apparatus.la: *Haec delectationis definitio est S. Doctori ceterisque Scholasticis familiaris et convenit cum ea, quam exhibet Avicenna in fine Metaph. VIII, c. 7, circa finem:* Delectatio non est nisi apprehensio convenientis, secundum quod conveniens est. *— Quae ab Avicenna data definitio fundari videtur in illa, quam Arist., Rhet. I, c. 11 tradit:* Est autem delectatio motus quidam animae et constitutio simul tota, sensibilis, in existentem naturam *(haec definitio explicatur ab Henr. Gand., S. a. 50, q. 2). Ed. Paris. 1878 sic Arist. interpretatur:* Positum sit igitur nobis, voluptatem esse motionem quandam animi et constitutionem subitam sensuque percipiendam in statu conveniente naturae. *Cfr. etiam Eth. Nic. VII, c. 11 seq., et praecipue Eth. Nic. X, c. 1–5, ac Magn. Moral. II, c. 7, ubi plura ad delectationem (voluptatem) pertinentia explicantur. — Mox, contradicentibus antiquioribus mss. et ed. 1, habet Vat. cum recentiore cod. cc* facturam *pro* creaturam. *Paulo post cod. R* infinita *loco* summa.
apparatus.en: This definition of delight is familiar to the Holy Doctor and the other Scholastics, and agrees with the one given by Avicenna near the end of *Metaphysics* VIII, ch. 7: "Delight is nothing other than the apprehension of what is befitting, insofar as it is befitting." — The definition given by Avicenna appears to rest on the one Aristotle offers in *Rhetoric* I, ch. 11: "But delight is a certain motion of the soul and a simultaneous whole constitution, sensible, into the existing nature" (this definition is explained by Henry of Ghent, *Summa* a. 50, q. 2). The Paris 1878 edition renders Aristotle thus: "Let it be posited by us that pleasure is a certain motion of the mind and a sudden constitution to be perceived by the sense in a state befitting nature." Cf. also *Nicomachean Ethics* VII, ch. 11 ff., and especially *Nic. Eth.* X, chs. 1–5, and *Magna Moralia* II, ch. 7, where many things pertaining to delight (pleasure) are explained. — A little later, against the older mss. and ed. 1, Vat. with the later cod. cc reads *facturam* ("a thing made") in place of *creaturam* ("a creature"). A little further on, cod. R reads *infinita* ("infinite") in place of *summa* ("highest").

apparatus.la: *Arist., De Anima II, text. 123 (ed. Paris. Firmin-Didot, III, c. 2), ubi iuxta ed. Venet. 1489 legitur:* Manifestum autem ex his, et propter quid excellentiae sensibilium corrumpunt sensitiva... Et manifesta est ex hoc causa, propter quam sensibilia intensa corrumpunt instrumenta sensuum. *Et text. 143 (ed. Paris. loc. cit.):* Proportio autem est symphonia... unde et delectabilia quidem sunt, dum dicuntur sincera et mixta entia ad rationem... excellentia autem contristant aut corrumpunt. *Tandem libr. III, text. 29:* Et est delectari aut tristari agere sensitiva medietate ad bonum et malum in quantum talia. *— Vat. rationem additam contra mss. et ed. 1 ita exhibet:* quia vera delectatio non est nisi in mediis. *Cod. X circa finem huius argumenti loco* in carne *ponit* in corpore.
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *On the Soul* II, text 123 (Paris, Firmin-Didot ed., III, ch. 2), where according to the Venice 1489 edition it reads: "It is clear from these things why the excessive [intensities] of sensibles corrupt the sense-faculties… And the cause is evident from this: that intense sensibles corrupt the instruments of the senses." And text 143 (Paris ed., loc. cit.): "Proportion is a certain symphony… whence [things] are delightful when they are called genuine and mixed in being with respect to ratio… but excessive ones cause pain or corruption." Finally, bk. III, text 29: "To delight or to suffer pain is to act sensitively by the mean, toward the good or the evil, insofar as they are such." — Vat., against the mss. and ed. 1, gives the added reason thus: *quia vera delectatio non est nisi in mediis* ("because true delight exists only in things of a mean"). Cod. X near the end of this argument reads *in corpore* ("in the body") in place of *in carne* ("in the flesh").

apparatus.la: *Arist., Phys. III, text. 63 (c. 6):* Infinitum igitur id est, cuius secundum quantitatem accipientibus semper aliquid accipere extra est; cuius autem nihil est extra, id est perfectum et totum. *— Mox praeter fidem antiquiorum mss. et ed. 1 non ita bene Vat. cum recentiore cod. cc* ergo non fruitio.
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *Physics* III, text 63 (ch. 6): "The infinite, then, is that of which, according to quantity, for those taking it, there is always something more to take outside; but that of which nothing is outside is perfect and whole." — A little later, against the older mss. and ed. 1, and not so well, Vat. with the later cod. cc reads *ergo non fruitio* ("therefore not enjoyment").

apparatus.la: *Id est,* quietat.
apparatus.en: That is, [he] *brings to rest*.

apparatus.la: *Corruptam lectionem Vat. et recentioris cod. cc, in qua ponitur* et *pro* vel *et omittitur* communem, *restauravimus ex antiquioribus mss. et ed. 1. Paulo ante cod. X* dicendum, quod convenientia dicitur vel per. *— De convenientia vide Arist., de Praedicam. c. 1, et Phys. VII, text. 21–34 (c. 4).*
apparatus.en: We have restored the corrupted reading of Vat. and the later cod. cc (in which *et* ("and") is put in place of *vel* ("or") and *communem* ("common") is omitted) from the older mss. and ed. 1. A little earlier, cod. X reads *dicendum, quod convenientia dicitur vel per* ("it must be said that befittingness is spoken of either by"). — On befittingness, see Aristotle, *Categories* ch. 1, and *Physics* VII, text 21–34 (ch. 4).

apparatus.la: *Plurimi codd. cum ed. 1 omittunt* se habet, *quod Vat. cum aliquibus tantum codd. hic addit.*
apparatus.en: Very many codices, with ed. 1, omit *se habet* ("stands"), which Vat., with only some codices, here adds.

apparatus.la: *Plures mss. ut A F G H K S T Y etc. cum ed. 1* simili. *Mox mendum Vat., quae post* se ipsa *addit* anima, *castigamus ex mss. et ed. 1; cod. X* sed est se ipsa similis. *In lectione in textum recepta* similitudo *sumitur concrete et sensus est: simile ratione similitudinis convenit immediate cum consimili. — Paulo post cod. T* homo *pro* anima; *plures vero codd. ut C L R S U omittunt* anima, *sed non bene.*
apparatus.en: Several mss. (A, F, G, H, K, S, T, Y, etc.) with ed. 1 read *simili* ("with the like"). A little later, we correct Vat.'s error — which after *se ipsa* ("by itself") adds *anima* ("soul") — from the mss. and ed. 1; cod. X reads *sed est se ipsa similis* ("but it is itself similar"). In the reading received into the text, *similitudo* ("likeness") is taken concretely, and the sense is: a like thing, by reason of likeness, agrees immediately with what is like. — A little further on, cod. T reads *homo* ("man") in place of *anima* ("soul"); and many codices (C, L, R, S, U) omit *anima*, but not well.

apparatus.la: *Cod. X hic repetit* unum.
apparatus.en: Cod. X here repeats *unum* ("one").

apparatus.la: *Codd. W X Z adiungunt* ibi, *et mox cod. A post* sequitur *repetit* delectatio.
apparatus.en: Codd. W, X, Z add *ibi* ("there"), and then cod. A after *sequitur* ("follows") repeats *delectatio* ("delight").

apparatus.la: *Cod. X addit* etiam. *Paulo post codd. aa bb* spiritualis *loco* immaterialis. *Mox codd. inter se non conveniunt; nam codd. A C G I L S T U W post* tristatur *omittunt* in; *codd. R et ff ponunt* ab; *cod. bb vero* ex; *plures autem ut F H K etc. cum ed. 1* in.
apparatus.en: Cod. X adds *etiam* ("also"). A little later, codd. aa, bb read *spiritualis* ("spiritual") in place of *immaterialis* ("immaterial"). A little further on, the codices do not agree among themselves: codd. A, C, G, I, L, S, T, U, W after *tristatur* ("is pained") omit *in* ("in"); codd. R and ff give *ab* ("by"); cod. bb instead *ex* ("from"); while many — such as F, H, K, etc. — with ed. 1 read *in*.

apparatus.la: *De hac differentia inter sensum et intellectum vide Arist., De Anima II, text. 123 et 143 paulo supra relatos, et libr. III, text. 4 (ed. Paris. c. 4):* Necesse est itaque, quoniam (intellectus) omnia intelligit, immixtum esse; *et text. 7:* Quod autem non similis sit impassibilitas sensitivi et intellectivi, manifestum est ... [sensus] tire ex vehementi sensibili... sed intellectus cum aliquid intellexerit valde intelligibile, non minus intelligit inferiora, sed et magis; sensitivum enim non sine corpore est, hic (intellectus) ... est.
apparatus.en: On this difference between sense and intellect, see Aristotle, *On the Soul* II, texts 123 and 143, just cited above, and bk. III, text 4 (Paris ed., ch. 4): "It is necessary, therefore, since (the intellect) understands all things, that it be unmixed"; and text 7: "And that the impassibility of the sensitive and of the intellective [powers] is not alike is manifest … [the sense] suffers from a vehement sensible … but the intellect, when it has understood something highly intelligible, does not understand lesser things less — but even more; for the sensitive [faculty] is not without a body, but this [intellect] … is."

apparatus.la: *Auctoritate antiquiorum mss. et ed. 1 substituimus* intelligibile *loco* intelligentiae.
apparatus.en: On the authority of the older mss. and ed. 1, we have substituted *intelligibile* ("intelligible") for *intelligentiae* ("of intelligence").

apparatus.la: *Ita codd. C H K O S T U Y aa bb et ed. 1; sed codd. A F I L M R V W X Z* participando; *Vat. autem cum cod. cc* per. *Mox codd. X et Y* confortatur *loco* fortificatur.
apparatus.en: So read codd. C, H, K, O, S, T, U, Y, aa, bb, and ed. 1 [i.e., *percipiendo*, "in perceiving"]; but codd. A, F, I, L, M, R, V, W, X, Z read *participando* ("by sharing"); while Vat. with cod. cc reads *per*. A little later, codd. X and Y read *confortatur* ("is strengthened") in place of *fortificatur* ("is fortified").

apparatus.la: *Cod. cc* scilicet quantum *pro* secundum quod. *Codd. F et I* qui, *satis bene, et conveniunt quoad sensum cum cod. T, qui habet* quia.
apparatus.en: Cod. cc reads *scilicet quantum* ("namely, as much as") in place of *secundum quod* ("insofar as"). Codd. F and I read *qui* — which is quite good — and agree in meaning with cod. T, which has *quia* ("because"). ---

questions.notes:
- **Chunk scope.** This chunk covers Q. I of Art. III in its entirety, spanning the bottom of printed p. 38 through the top of p. 39 (PDF pp. 140–141): the brief opening frame, three *videtur quod* arguments, three *Sed contra* arguments, Conclusio, Respondeo, and the three *Ad obiecta* replies. The Scholion block at the top of p. 39 is included. This closes the second of the three confirmed gaps in d. 1 identified in the rebuild audit. The article-level divisio textus that introduces Articulus III at the top of p. 38 ("*De fruibili*... primo, utrum Deo contingat frui; secundo, utrum fruendum sit ipso solo") is deliberately kept out of this chunk and will live in its own `bon-sent-I-d1-a3-divisio` file when that pattern is established for the rebuild.

- **Key terms** (per project glossary): *frui* → enjoy; *fruibile* → enjoyable / what is to be enjoyed; *delectatio* → delight; *convenientia* → befittingness / agreement (the technical term for the fit between two natures); *conveniens cum convenienti* → "what is befitting with what is befitting" (Bonaventure's definition of delight, via Avicenna and Aristotle's *Rhetoric*); *quietatio* → rest / stilling; *finire* → to bring to an end (with the paired sense of *quietare*, glossed in fn 7); *medietas / in mediis* → mean / in things of a mean; *per privationem perfectionis / limitationis* → by the privation of perfection / of limitation; *analogia proportionis / proportionalitatis* → analogy of proportion / of proportionality.

- **The Avicennan definition of delight.** Objection 1 *contra* and the reply ad 1 both turn on the definition *delectatio est coniunctio convenientis cum convenienti*. Fn 4 traces the pedigree from Aristotle's *Rhetoric* I through Avicenna's *Metaphysics* VIII to the scholastic commonplace. Bonaventure's reply distinguishes two kinds of *convenientia*: univocal (by shared nature) and analogical (by common comparison) — the latter itself subdivided into three kinds. The doctrine of analogy of proportionality here is a key early statement of the distinction later developed in d. 14, d. 29, d. 46, and d. 48.

- **Sense vs. intellect (Reply to 2).** The threefold contrast — on the side of power, of object, and of mode of apprehension — is the heart of this question and is densely cross-referenced by the Quaracchi editors to *De Anima* II–III. Fn 14 assembles the relevant Aristotelian loci: II text 123, text 143, III text 4, and text 7 (the passage on the intellect's unmixed impassibility). The English preserves the scholastic distinction between *virtus apprehensiva*, *apprehensum / obiectum*, and *modus apprehendendi*.

- **Two senses of "infinite" (Reply to 3).** Fn 17 documents competing readings at *secundum quod est possibile* near the end of the reply. Bonaventure's distinction — between the infinite by privation of perfection (matter) and the infinite by privation of limitation (God) — is the germ of the solution and is preserved carefully in the English.

- **Footnote placement — uncertainty flag.** Several markers on p. 39 (notably [^11] *unum*, [^12] *sensus*, [^13] *in excellenti*, and [^14] *De Anima* reference) were placed by reasoning about the sense of each apparatus entry rather than by direct visual match to marker glyphs in the PDF, which at small point size are difficult to read. These placements should be verified on a higher-resolution image pass. Footnote [^17] merges what the raw OCR shows as two adjacent apparatus entries — "Cod. cc *scilicet quantum* pro *secundum quod*" and "Codd. F et I *qui*, satis bene..." — since both document manuscript variants on the same phrase *secundum quod est possibile* in Ad 3.

- **Vision transcription status.** First-pass vision re-OCR of printed pp. 38–39 (PDF pp. 140–141), reconciled against `raw/bonaventure_vol1_raw.txt` lines 14595–14895 for words obscured by ligature or tight point size in the footnote region. Apparatus footnotes were read from the PDF at small point size and should be considered best-effort. Several manuscript sigla may still need cross-check against the Quaracchi Vol. I sigla key (forthcoming in `tools/apparatus-sigla.json`).

For a likeness does not agree with its counterpart in virtue of a third term, but by itself. So it is in the present case, because the soul is an expressed likeness of God. This agreement places inclination and need in one extreme, and rest and sufficiency in the other, because one has been made for the sake of the other, and is therefore ordered toward the other. And since, where there is sense, delight either accompanies or follows the quieting of inclination and the supplying of need, the soul, when it is quieted by God in this manner, enjoys Him.

2. To the objection that an exceedingly intense sensible destroys the sense — therefore, etc. — it must be said that the cases of intellectual understanding and sensing are not alike. And for understanding there is a threefold account of this: one is from the side of the apprehensive power, another from the side of the apprehended object, and a third from the side of the mode of apprehending.

From the side of the apprehensive power: because the sense can be destroyed, but the intellect cannot. The account of this is that the sense depends upon an organ, in which there is a certain mean and harmony, which is corrupted not only by what is contrary to it but also by what is excessive; but the intellect does not depend upon an organ, because it is an immaterial power, and therefore does not suffer in the presence of what is excellent.

From the side of the object the cases are not alike, because an excellent object helps and strengthens, since the influence of such a knowable thing proceeds from within and enters into the power itself, and therefore strengthens and fortifies it. Just as if a great mountain were to give the power to carry itself, it would be carried more easily than a small one; so it is with the intelligible, which God is. A sensible object, however, only arouses from without, and therefore the one destroys while the other does not.

From the side of the mode of apprehending there is similarly a dissimilarity, because the sense in apprehending its object tends toward the exterior, and in perceiving it is dispersed outwardly and not fortified inwardly, and therefore is weakened. But the object of the intellect, since it is most interior to the intellect itself, in the perception of it the power is not dispersed but gathered, and the more united the power is, the stronger it is.

3. To the objection concerning the infinite: it must be said that "infinite" is used in two ways — namely, by way of privation of perfection, and in this way matter is said to be infinite, and such an infinite thing has no power to bring to an end, but rather needs to be brought to an end, to the extent that this is possible. In another way "infinite" is used by way of privation of limitation; and what is infinite in this sense properly has the power to bring to an end, because beyond it, since nothing greater can be conceived, one cannot desire anything further. Hence such infinity belongs to the ultimate end, which most of all has the character of that which brings to an end.

[Scholion omitted]

QUESTION II.

Whether God alone, or uncreated good alone, is to be enjoyed.

Finally it is asked whether God alone, or uncreated good alone, is to be enjoyed; and that this is so seems [evident].

1. That alone is to be enjoyed which is to be loved for its own sake; but that alone is to be loved for its own sake which is good for its own sake; and that is good for its own sake whose goodness it possesses neither from another nor is that goodness ordered toward anything else; but this is God alone: therefore, etc.

2. Likewise, that alone is to be enjoyed which quiets the soul's appetite; but the soul's appetite is not sufficiently quieted except in that which is a more perfect and greater good than it; but this is God alone: therefore, etc.

3. Likewise, the appetite is not sufficiently quieted except by something that fills the soul, because the soul falls short of rest to the extent that it falls short of fullness; but the soul is capable of God according to its appetite: therefore, since every created thing is infinitely less than He, none supplies the soul's appetite. And this is what Augustine says: "Nothing less than the Trinity can fill a soul capable of the whole Trinity."

4. Likewise, a good that can be thought can be desired: therefore if a greater good than some good can be conceived, something greater than it can be desired; but something greater than every finite thing can be conceived: therefore something greater can be desired: therefore no finite thing sufficiently terminates the soul's appetite: therefore only the infinite good, which is God, is to be enjoyed, for once He is possessed, nothing further can be conceived or desired.

On the contrary: 1. It seems that it is possible to enjoy a created good, because, although the appetite of matter is infinite, it is nevertheless sufficiently terminated by an incorruptible created form: therefore it similarly seems that there is some created good that will sufficiently terminate the soul's appetite; but every such thing is to be enjoyed: therefore some created good is to be enjoyed.

2. Likewise, human appetite is of finite capacity, therefore it only grasps the finite, or if it grasps the infinite, it grasps it finitely; therefore if it is terminated by what it grasps, it is terminated by a finite good: therefore it seems that some finite good is to be enjoyed.

3. Likewise, it seems in particular that a human being is to be enjoyed, because everything that God enjoys is to be enjoyed; but God enjoys a human being, because He loves a human being; but He loves a human being with the same love by which He loves Himself, because there is not in Him a twofold love; but the first is of enjoyment: therefore the second is as well.

4. Likewise, it seems in particular concerning virtue; because everything that is to be desired for its own sake is to be enjoyed; this is evident in itself; but every honest good is to be desired for its own sake, "because the honorable is that which by its own force draws us and by its own dignity allures us," as Tullius says, and Augustine divides the honorable against the useful; but virtue falls under the genus of the honorable: therefore virtue is to be enjoyed.

5. Likewise, it seems in particular concerning beatitude. Everything is to be enjoyed whereby, once possessed, the mind rests and delights and can seek nothing further; but created beatitude is of this kind: therefore, etc.

CONCLUSION.

God alone is properly to be enjoyed; it is permissible to enjoy spiritual goods improperly, insofar as they delight and are joined to the end.

It must be said that God alone is to be enjoyed, taking "enjoy" in its proper sense, as it denotes movement with both delight and rest. But taking "enjoy" in its common sense, as it denotes movement with delight only, a human being may not wrongly enjoy all those things that delight spiritually and are joined to the end, such as fruits, gifts, and beatitudes; but in the first sense, God alone.

And the account of this is that nothing can sufficiently bring the soul to its end except the good for which it exists. But this is the highest good, which is above the soul, and the infinite good, which exceeds the soul's powers. For the soul's natural cognition is unrestricted cognition; hence it is naturally suited in some way to know all things, and therefore its cognition is not filled by any knowable thing except that which has within itself all knowable things and by the knowledge of which all things are known. Similarly its affection is naturally suited to love every good; therefore the affection is not sufficiently terminated by any good except that which is the good of every good and which is all in all. Concerning this good it is said in Exodus thirty-three: "I will show you all good." But this is the highest good: therefore, etc.

Likewise, nothing sufficiently brings the soul to its end except the infinite good, because for it to be brought to its end, it is necessary that it be terminated according to estimation; otherwise it would not be blessed unless it reckoned itself blessed. But estimation surpasses every finite thing, because greater than any finite thing can always be conceived: therefore, since affection can extend itself wherever estimation can, the affection of the soul necessarily surpasses every finite thing; and if this is so, it is not sufficiently terminated by any finite good. Therefore God alone is to be enjoyed, because He is the highest and infinite good.

And not only is God alone to be enjoyed because of perfect termination, but also because of perfect delight. For delight requires the delightful thing and its conjunction with that which is delighted. But everything that delights the soul delights under the account of the good and the beautiful; and since God alone is goodness and beauty itself, therefore in God alone is there perfect delight.

Likewise, because there is conjunction; but God alone is He who is conjoined most perfectly. For He is conjoined according to truth and intimacy. For God alone, on account of His supreme simplicity and spirituality, glides into the soul, so that according to truth He is in the soul and more intimate to the soul than it is to itself.

All four of these accounts reduce to one, namely this: because the soul is naturally suited to receive the infinite good, which is God, therefore it ought to rest in Him alone and enjoy Him.

1. To the objection concerning the appetite of matter: it must be said that the appetite of matter is ordered toward form as toward its substantial perfection, from which together with matter one thing is made; and therefore it is necessary that the form be of the same genus as matter, and it is not altogether above matter: therefore every such form is finite. But such a form, if it is incorruptible, by reason of its union restricts the appetite of matter and, having restricted it, terminates it; hence it is not terminated in its full amplitude. But the appetite of the soul is not so restricted by its union with the desirable object; on the contrary it is expanded; and therefore it must be perfected by something altogether supreme.

2. To the objection that it grasps only finitely: it must be said that it grasps the infinite good finitely, since the soul itself is finite. But since that good is infinite, the soul is therefore totally absorbed by it, so that its capacity is now bounded on all sides. Hence it will not merely rejoice, but as Anselm says, it will enter into the joy of the Lord. For if it were only grasping and were not overcome and absorbed, there could still arise an appetite to grasp something more. It is therefore clear that in order for the soul to be fulfilled, even though it has finite capacity, it is nonetheless necessary that the infinite good be present.

3. To the objection concerning the human being: it must be said that God loves a human being, and God's love is a love of enjoyment; yet He does not enjoy the human being, because in loving Himself He loves the human being, that is, in enjoying Himself He uses the human being. This is clear as follows: because the love of God toward a creature is not an affection but a communication of effect. Communication according to its habitual account is understood with respect to goodness, because the good is what is naturally suited to communicate itself. According to its actual account, however, it is understood with respect to or regards the will, because it is because He wills that He acts. Therefore the account of communicating comes from will and goodness, just as the account of knowing comes from the exemplar and understanding. Because, therefore, He loves us from the turning of His will upon His own goodness, He loves us in enjoying Himself.

4. To the objection concerning virtue, that virtue is an honest good: it must be said that "honest good" is used in two ways — either that which is purely good, or that in which its likeness shines forth. In the first sense the honest is to be enjoyed, taking "enjoy" properly, because this alone terminates and quiets. In the second sense it is not, unless "enjoy" is taken commonly, as it denotes delight. For things of this kind, by reason of their assimilation to God, have a beauty by which they delight and allure us; yet one must not rest in them, because then they lose their beauty, since "virtues, when referred to themselves, are proud and inflated."

5. To the objection concerning beatitude: it must be said that created beatitude does not terminate the appetite through itself, but through conjunction with uncreated beatitude: hence the soul loves it for the sake of God, not for its own sake.

DOUBTS CONCERNING THE MASTER'S TEXT.

DOUBT I.

In this part several doubts arise concerning the text, and first concerning what he says: "But of these there are some whose every use consists in signifying, not in justifying." But on the contrary: All sacraments are medicines, because according to Hugh of Saint Victor the sacraments have been medicines in every age; but every medicine has its effect in curing: therefore the sacraments likewise; but this curing is justification: therefore in every age the sacraments have had the power to justify.

I respond: It must be said that the sacraments of the Old Law can be considered in two ways — namely in themselves or by reason of the work done (ex opere operato), and in this sense they were only for signifying; or by reason of the faith attached or charity or by reason of the work of the one performing (ex opere operantis), and in this sense the legal sacraments were for justifying, apart from Circumcision.

DOUBT II.

"Every sign, therefore, is something." An objection is raised against this division. For it seems that the Master divides badly, because a superior is not divided against its inferior; but "thing" is superior to "sign": therefore, etc.

I respond: It must be said that it is true that a superior taken in its full generality is not divided against its inferior; but a contracted superior can well be divided. Here, however, "thing" is contracted to stand for a thing that does not signify.

DOUBT III.

Likewise, a doubt arises concerning what the Master says: "But not conversely is every thing a sign." For he seems to speak badly, because a sign is that which leads to the knowledge of something else; but every thing leads to something else, because every thing is either a cause or an effect. But a cause leads to the knowledge of the effect and conversely. If you say that not everything that leads is a sign, but only what leads to what is prior — then every creature is a sign, since it leads to God.

I respond: It must be said that sign is twofold, namely natural and instituted. The first is not what is intended here, but the second; hence the objection does not apply to the matter at hand, since what is intended here is the sign by institution, such as vocal and sacramental signs.

DOUBT IV.

Likewise, the Master seems to speak badly in what he says: "First concerning things, afterward concerning signs." For he seems to have ought rather to say the reverse, because a sign leads to the knowledge of a thing: therefore one ought first to treat or speak of signs than of things.

I respond: It must be said that knowledge of the sign is prior to the thing with respect to which it is a sign; but this need not be true of every thing. Hence he first treats of things of which the sacraments are not signs.

DOUBT V.

Likewise, it seems that this division of things — "Some are those which are to be enjoyed, etc." — is badly assigned with respect to the thing divided, because the thing divided is simpler than the dividing members and something is common to the dividing members; but nothing is simpler than God, nor is anything common to God and creature: therefore, etc.

I respond: It must be said that there is a division of one common thing according to name alone, and this is a division of an equivocal; there is another division of what is common according to both name and thing, and this is a division of a univocal; and there is also a third, in a middle manner — and this is the division of an analogical, where there is no community according to unity of nature, but according to similarity of proportion; and this community is one of reason.

DOUBT VI.

Likewise, it seems that the division is bad with respect to its members: for it seems that the third member is superfluous. For every thing is either to be used or to be enjoyed: therefore the third is superfluous.

Likewise, just as there is a thing that enjoys and uses, so too there is a thing that is both to be enjoyed and to be used, such as Christ: therefore, for the same reason that the third member is posited, a fourth ought to be posited.

I respond: Every thing which is some nature is either an end — and so it is a thing to be enjoyed; or something leading to the end — and so it is a thing to be used; or something arriving at the end — and so it is a thing that enjoys and uses, such as the human being: and so the members are taken. And this division is sufficiently fitting for this science, because since theology is about the Creator and about creatures, it is useful for the theologian to teach how the human being tends toward God through other things.

DOUBT VII.

Likewise, an objection is raised concerning what he says: "Things which are to be enjoyed" — because if the three are things through themselves and not through accident, and from the diversity of things there is diversity or multiplicity of enjoyment: therefore just as there are three things, so there will be three enjoyments.

Likewise, there are three articles of faith, because they concern three persons: therefore by analogy there are also three enjoyments.

I respond: That "thing" is here taken commonly for both essence and person on account of its generality; and because this word "thing" is taken from an act of the soul, therefore three are called things because there are three persons, yet nonetheless one thing, because there is one goodness in them. Because therefore there is one goodness, therefore also one enjoyment, although there are three things. — And since an article of faith states something from the side of the distinguishing soul, namely the intellect, and enjoyment regards the divine essence itself and goodness and the union of affection commonly, therefore enjoyment is one.

DOUBT VIII.

Likewise, an objection is raised concerning what he says: "Everyone who enjoys also uses" — because this seems false, since foolish human beings as well as beasts enjoy, because they are delighted in the delightful for its own sake, but they do not use. If you say it is said by way of transfer; why is the word "using" not similarly transferred?

I respond: "To use" in its general sense implies freedom, and in its specific sense implies freedom with relation to another; "to enjoy" implies freedom with delight; and although neither freedom nor comparison belongs to brutes, delight does belong to them. Therefore "to use" in no way belongs to brutes; but "to enjoy" belongs to them in some way, though improperly.

DOUBT IX.

Likewise, it seems that he speaks badly in saying that hope is not to be placed in a human being, because of the Blessed Virgin the Church sings "Life, sweetness, and hope" — and the Church does not err.

Likewise, in Jonah chapter one: "The helmsman approached him"; Gloss: "It is natural for a human being to trust more in others than in himself in dangers."

I respond: It must be said that to hope in someone is twofold — either as in a helper, or as in a savior. The first hope can be in a human being, the second cannot. — Or: to hope for the final reward — and this ought to be only in God; or for a temporal benefit — and this can be in a human being. If the first is placed in a human being, it merits a curse, according to [the Scripture].

DOUBT X.

Likewise, it is asked why he says concerning a human being: "Therefore, brother, I shall enjoy you in the Lord," rather than concerning a donkey or some other creature, since in all creatures the vestige of the divine goodness shines forth.

I respond: What causes one to enjoy something in God is not representation, but rather indwelling. Hence the converse expression is the proper one, namely: "I shall enjoy the Lord in you," while I know through works that God dwells in you; and the other is a figurative manner of speaking.

DOUBT XI.

Likewise, a question arises concerning this solution of Augustine, by which he resolves the aforementioned authority through that qualification "in the Lord." But in Ecclesiasticus chapter eight it is said simply: "Enjoy the great man." Likewise, in Deuteronomy chapter twenty-eight: "You will beget sons and daughters, and you will not enjoy them" — from this it implies that if they did not sin, they would enjoy them.

I respond: It must be said that the aforementioned solution is not general, but only applies to the proposed authority. And therefore one must have recourse to the solution given outside the letter in the questions — that since "enjoy" is used commonly and properly, in the aforementioned passages it is used only commonly.

DOUBT XII.

Likewise, what the Master says does not seem to hold: "For if he neither enjoys nor uses, etc." — because God loves Himself, yet does not use Himself, because He does not love Himself for the sake of something else; nor does He enjoy Himself, because where there is enjoyment, there is adherence and need, as Augustine says; but God lacks both, etc.

I respond: It must be said that enjoyment in its general account denotes a union of love, namely of the enjoyable with the one enjoying. Since therefore it is possible for something to be united to itself and to another, it is possible not only to enjoy another but also oneself; but where there is union to another, there is dependence, adherence, and need; where however it is union to oneself, if that thing is the highest good, there is no adherence or dependence or need, but utter sufficiency. But if the good is deficient, it stands in need; and hence it is that God alone perfectly enjoys Himself, while nothing other than Him can perfectly enjoy itself. For God alone is the highest good and loves Himself in enjoying Himself, and also loves other things in enjoying Himself: and thus neither God's enjoyment nor His use is accompanied by need, as our enjoyment and use are.

DOUBT XIII.

Likewise, an objection is raised concerning what he says: "Because He is good, we exist": therefore because He is good from eternity, we exist from eternity.

I respond: It must be said briefly that this is so because "good" states a cause. But there is a natural and necessary cause, and a voluntary cause. The divine goodness is the cause of our existing and our being good by way of will, not of nature; but a voluntary cause does not immediately produce its effect when it exists.

DOUBT XIV.

Likewise, it is further objected: why does it similarly not follow: "Because He is just, we are just"? If you say that justice is not His disposition insofar as He is cause; on the contrary: wisdom is a disposition of God insofar as He is cause: therefore by equal reasoning, because He is wise, we are wise. If you say that it is not an immediate disposition, as goodness is; an objection is raised concerning will, which is most immediate, and yet it does not follow: because He is willing, we are willing.

questions.notes:
- **"Expressed likeness" (expressa similitudo):** Bonaventure's characteristic term for the soul's relation to God — stronger than *vestigium* (trace) or generic *similitudo*, implying a direct imprint or stamp. Rendered "expressed likeness" to preserve this technical weight.
- **"Brings to an end" / "terminates" (finire, finitur):** The Latin *finire* serves double duty as both "to terminate/limit" and "to fulfill/complete." Rendered contextually as "bring to an end," "terminate," or "fulfill" depending on whether the sense is limiting or fulfilling — the argument in q. 2 turns precisely on this ambiguity with *infinitum*.
- **"Enjoys" / "enjoyment" (frui, fruitio):** Following standard Augustinian-scholastic usage. Bonaventure's distinction between *proprie* (proper) and *communiter* (common) senses of *frui* is central to the *Conclusio* and preserved explicitly in translation.
- **"Honest good" (bonum honestum):** Scholastic term from Cicero via Augustine for intrinsically valuable good (as opposed to *utile*, useful). Rendered "honest good" to preserve the technical term; the Cicero quotation is translated directly from Bonaventure's citation.
- **Anselm citation (Proslogion c. 26):** Bonaventure quotes Anselm on "entering into the joy" — a reversal of the intuitive reading of Matthew 25:21 ("enter into the joy of your Lord"), making the soul enter *into* joy rather than joy entering the soul. The translation preserves this nuance.
- **"Glides into the soul" (illabitur animae):** Technical term for divine immanence. *Illabi* carries the sense of flowing or slipping into something imperceptibly; "glides into" is more idiomatic than "flows into" while preserving the connotation.
- **Doubt XII resolution:** The argument that God enjoys Himself without need (*indigentia*) by being united to Himself rather than to another is a subtle distinction; the translation preserves the logical structure carefully.

DIST. I. DOUBTS.

DOUBT XV.

Likewise, an objection is raised concerning what he says: "That it should be loved for its own sake alone" — because as "through itself" is to "through accident," so "for its own sake" is to "for the sake of another." But nothing that belongs to something through accident belongs to it through itself: therefore nothing that belongs to something for the sake of another belongs to it for its own sake. If therefore virtues are to be desired for the sake of another, then not for their own sake.

I respond: As the Philosopher says, "the end and the 'for the sake of which' are the same." But the end is twofold: in one way the ultimate end, which is the end in the most proper sense, in which there is rest; in another way an end under an end, which is called properly a terminus. Thus "for the sake of which" is also diversified; hence in one way it excludes the end, in another it does not, as the Master says.

As for the objection concerning "through itself": I say that, just as "through itself" in one sense is opposed to what is "through another" — and in this sense "through itself" is the same as "according to what it itself is," or "the first universal" — and in another sense is opposed to what is "through accident": so too "for its own sake" is taken in two ways. In one way it is opposed to what is "for the sake of another," and in another way it is opposed to what is "through accident," because it is ordered toward that thing only accidentally. According to this, the Master distinguishes "for its own sake," and consequently the honorable or the enjoyable, and enjoyment itself.

DOUBT XVI.

Likewise, an objection is raised concerning what he says: "And there are certain things through which we enjoy, such as the virtues." It seems that the soul could enjoy with its powers alone. For without any virtue it can enjoy a created good; therefore, since uncreated good is more enjoyable, and the soul is more naturally suited to this, it will be able to enjoy it with its powers alone.

I respond: It must be said that the highest good is that which is above us; therefore, in order for us to be united to it, a twofold medium necessarily intervenes: one medium through which the soul is naturally suited to be united to something diverse from itself — and this is the power; another special one beyond this, which elevates it — and this is virtue. The objection does not apply, because a power can of itself fall short and incline, but not of itself be elevated.

[Critical apparatus omitted]

DISTINCTION II.

CHAPTER I.

On the Trinity and Unity.

This therefore is to be held with true and pious faith: "that the Trinity is the one and only true God, as Augustine says in the first book On the Trinity — namely the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit; and that this Trinity is said to be, is believed to be, and is understood to be of one and the same substance or essence, which is the highest good, which is seen by the most pure minds. For the weak gaze of the human mind is not fixed upon so excellent a light unless it has been cleansed through the righteousness of faith." The same in the first book of the Retractions: "I do not approve of what I said in the prayer: 'O God, who hast willed that only the pure should know the truth.' For it can be replied that many who are not pure know many true things. Concerning this highest and most excellent matter, therefore, one must proceed with modesty and fear, and with most attentive and devoted ears must it be heard, where the unity of the Trinity — namely of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit — is sought, because nowhere is error more dangerous, nowhere is anything sought with more labor, and nowhere is anything found more fruitfully." Therefore let everyone who hears and reads the things said of the ineffable and inaccessible light of the Godhead strive to imitate and preserve what the venerable Doctor Augustine says of himself in the first book On the Trinity: "It will not trouble me, he says, wherever I am uncertain, to seek; nor will I be ashamed, wherever I err, to learn. Whoever therefore hears or reads these things: where he is equally certain, let him go on with me; where he is equally uncertain, let him seek with me; where he recognizes his own error, let him return to me; where mine, let him call me back. So let us enter together on the path of charity, tending toward Him of whom it is said: Seek His face always."

CHAPTER II.

What the intention was of those who wrote on the Trinity.

"All the Catholic writers, as Augustine says in the same work, who have written on the Trinity which is God, have intended to teach according to the Scriptures that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are of one substance and are one God in inseparable equality, so that there is unity in essence and plurality in persons; and therefore they are not three gods, but one God, even though the Father has begotten the Son, and therefore the Son is not who the Father is; and the Son has been begotten by the Father, and therefore the Father is not who the Son is; and the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but only the Spirit of the Father and the Son, co-equal to both and belonging to the unity of the Trinity." "Let us hold, therefore, that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are by nature one God, as Augustine says in the book On Faith to Peter; and yet that the Father Himself is not the Son; nor is the Son Himself who the Father is; nor is the Holy Spirit Himself who the Father is or who the Son is. For there is one essence of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, which the Greeks call *ousia*, in which the Father is not one thing, the Son another, the Holy Spirit yet another, even though the Father is personally other, the Son other, the Holy Spirit other."

CHAPTER III.

What order is to be observed when treating of the Trinity.

Furthermore, as Augustine teaches in the first book On the Trinity: "First, according to the authorities of the holy Scriptures, it must be demonstrated whether the faith is as it presents itself. Then, against garrulous reasoners, more elated than capable, Catholic reasoning and fitting comparisons must be used for the defense and assertion of the faith, so that, satisfying their inquiries, we may more fully instruct the gentle, and so that those who could not find what they seek may complain of their own minds rather than of the truth itself or of our exposition."

CHAPTER IV.

On the testimonies of the Old Testament by which the mystery of the Trinity is declared.

Let us therefore set forth in the midst the authorities of the Old and New Testaments by which the truth of the divine Unity and Trinity is demonstrated. And let the very opening of the Law come first, where Moses says: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one God." Likewise: "I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt; you shall have no other gods before me." Behold, here he signified the unity of the divine nature. "For 'God' and 'Lord,' as Ambrose says in the first book On the Trinity, is a name of nature, is a name of power." Likewise, elsewhere God speaking to Moses says: "I am who I am; and if they ask my name, go and say to them: He who is has sent me to you." For in saying "I am," not "We are," and "He who is," not "He who are," he most openly declared that there is one God alone. In the Canticle of Exodus also it is read: "The Lord, Almighty is His name" — he does not say "of the Lord," wishing to signify unity. The Lord also showed at once the plurality of persons and the unity of nature in Genesis, saying: "Let us make man according to our image and likeness." For in saying "let us make" and "our," He showed the plurality of persons; in saying "image," the unity of essence. For as Augustine says in the book On Faith to Peter: "If in that nature of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit there were only one person, it would not be said: 'Let us make man according to our image and likeness.' For when He says 'according to the image,' He shows that there is one nature according to whose image man was to be made; but when He says 'our,' He shows that the same God is not one but several persons." Hilary too in the third book On the Trinity says these words signify that in the Trinity there is neither diversity nor singularity or solitude, but likeness and plurality or distinction. For he says thus: "He who said 'Let us make man according to our image and likeness' showed that they are mutually like each other in that He says 'our image and likeness.'" "For an image alone does not exist, and a likeness does not exist for itself alone: nor does the likeness of one to another permit diversity to be mixed in the two." Likewise the same author in the fourth book: "He wished it to be understood more absolutely that this signification was not to be referred to Himself alone, in saying: 'Let us make man according to our image and likeness'; for the profession of partnership removed the understanding of the singular, because no partnership can exist for a solitary person alone, nor again does the solitude of a solitary person use 'let us make,' nor does anyone say 'our' of one alien from himself. Both expressions — namely 'let us make' and 'our' — just as they do not allow for one who is solitary and the same, so they do not signify one who is different and alien from himself. To a solitary being it is fitting to say 'I will make' and 'my'; but to one who is not solitary it is fitting to say 'let us make' and 'our.' Both expressions, as they do not signify one who is solitary, so neither do they signify one who is different or diverse. For us, therefore, He must be confessed as neither solitary nor diverse. And so God is found to work toward the making of man according to the image and likeness common to Himself with God, so that neither does the signification of the agent admit the understanding of solitude, nor does the operation constituted toward the same image or likeness allow for diversity of divinity."

In these words Hilary wished the plurality of persons to be understood by the name of partnership, and signified that by the name of partnership or plurality something is not posited, but removed. For when the plurality or partnership of persons is spoken of, solitude and singularity are denied; when we say that there are several persons, we signify that there is not only one. Therefore Hilary, wishing these things to be understood subtly and rightly, says: "The profession of partnership removed the understanding of the singular" — he does not say "posited something." So too when we say three persons, we remove singularity and solitude, and signify that the Father is not alone, nor is the Son alone, nor is the Holy Spirit alone, and that it is not only Father and Son, nor only Father and Holy Spirit, nor only Son and Holy Spirit. This matter will be treated more fully below, where it will also be shown in what sense the three persons are said to be alike, and whether there is in any way diversity or difference among them.

But now let us return to the matter at hand and, to demonstrate the plurality of persons and the unity of the divine essence, let us bring forward other authorities of the Saints. Moses says: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth" — by *God* signifying the Father, by *beginning* the Son. And for what among us is called *God*, the Hebrew truth has *Elohim*, which is the plural of the singular *El*, which is *God*. Therefore because it does not say *El*, which is God, but *Elohim*, which can be interpreted as "gods" or "judges," this is referred to the plurality of persons. To this also seems to belong what the devil said through the serpent: "You will be like gods," for which the Hebrew has *Elohim*, as if to say: you will be like the divine persons. That greatest of prophets and kings also, David, who claims understanding beyond others, saying: "I have understood beyond the elders" — showing the unity of the divine nature, says: "Lord is His name" — he does not say "of the Lord." Elsewhere also, showing at once its unity and eternity, he says from the person of God: "Israel, if you will hear me, there shall be in you no new God, nor shall you worship a foreign God." "One of these, as Ambrose says in the first book On the Trinity, signifies eternity, the other the unity of undifferentiated substance, so that we do not believe the Son or the Holy Spirit to be later than the Father or of another divinity. For if the Son or the Holy Spirit is later than the Father, He is new; and if He is not of one divinity, He is foreign; but He is not later, because He is not new, nor is He foreign, because the Son was born from the Father, the Holy Spirit proceeded from the Father." Elsewhere also, hinting at the distinction of persons, he says: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of His mouth all their power." Elsewhere also he says: "May God bless us, our God, may God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear Him." For the threefold confession of God expresses the Trinity of persons; but the unity of essence it discloses when, in the singular, he subjoins *Him*. Isaiah also says that he heard the Seraphim crying: "Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God." By saying *Holy* three times he signifies the Trinity; by subjoining *Lord God*, the unity of essence. David also openly hints at the eternal generation of the Son, speaking from the person of the Son: "The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you." Concerning this ineffable generation Isaiah says: "Who shall declare His generation?" In the book of Wisdom also the eternity of the Son with the Father is shown, where Wisdom speaks thus: "The Lord possessed me at the beginning of His ways, before He made anything from the beginning: I was set in order from eternity, before the earth was made; the depths did not yet exist, and I was already conceived: not yet were the fountains, not yet the mountains or the hills, and I was already brought forth: He had not yet made the earth and the cornerstones of the world: when He prepared the heavens, I was there; when He was laying the foundations of the earth, I was with Him composing all things, and I delighted through all the days, playing before Him." Behold an open testimony concerning the eternal birth, whereby Wisdom herself testifies that before the world she was conceived and brought forth — that is, begotten — and that she exists eternally with the Father. Wisdom also says elsewhere: "I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before all creation." The Prophet Micah also indicated at once the eternal generation of the Word and the temporal birth from Mary, saying: "And you, Bethlehem Ephrata, are small among the thousands of Judah: from you shall come forth one who is to be ruler in Israel, and his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity."

We also have express testimonies concerning the Holy Spirit in the Old Testament. For in Genesis it is read: "The Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters." And David says: "Where shall I go from your Spirit?" And in the book of Wisdom it is said: "The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from deceit, for the spirit of wisdom is kind." Isaiah also says: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me," etc.

[Critical apparatus omitted]

questions.notes:
- **Doubt XIV continuation / Doubt XV opening:** The text opens mid-argument (Doubt XIV's response), transitioning into Doubt XV. The fragment at the start — "is most proximate to act... just as God as one imprints unity, so God as good imprints goodness" — completes the threefold account of why the inference "because He is good, we exist" holds. Translated to preserve the logical structure.
- **"First universal" (primum universale):** Bonaventure is invoking an Aristotelian-Thomistic technical term from the *Posterior Analytics* concerning per se predication. Rendered literally as "first universal" to preserve the scholastic reference. The editor's note indicates this refers to the strict adequation of predicate and subject.
- **"Power" vs. "virtue" (potentia / virtus):** Doubt XVI turns on this Bonaventurian distinction: *potentia* is the soul's natural capacity for union; *virtus* (infused virtue) is the additional supernatural elevation required. Both translated consistently throughout. Bonaventure's point is that natural capacity is insufficient for union with the supernatural highest good.
- **Distinction II, Chapter IV — Peter Lombard's text:** From this point forward the translation is of the *Sentences* of Peter Lombard himself (the *Magistri* text), not Bonaventure's commentary. This is the base text on which Bonaventure comments. It consists largely of patristic *catenae* (Augustine, Ambrose, Hilary) stitched together.
- **"Elohim" discussion:** The Lombard's Hebrew etymology (*hel* / *heloym*) is pre-critical and inaccurate by modern standards but is translated faithfully as written (*El* for the singular, *Elohim* for the plural).
- **"*Ousia*" (usian in the Latin):** The Lombard preserves the Greek transliteration. Translated as "*ousia*" with the Greek term retained as the Lombard himself calls attention to it.
- **Hilary quotations:** These lengthy passages from Hilary's *De Trinitate* are translated from Bonaventure's edition of the Lombard, not from Hilary directly; minor divergences from the critical text of Hilary are expected and left as-is per the brief's instruction to translate what is given.
- **OCR artifacts corrected:** "DUBI.\" → "DUBIA"; "Jiwenitur" corrected to context; page-header intrusions ("SENTENTIARUM LIB. I.") silently omitted as formatting artifacts. "pro eo quod" rendered contextually.

questions.english:
DIST. II. DIVISION OF THE TEXT.

On the testimonies of the New Testament pertaining to the same.

Now, after the testimonies of the Old Testament concerning the faith of the holy Trinity and Unity, let us come to the authorities of the New Testament, so that the truth may be known in the midst of the two living creatures (that is, of the Testaments), and that the coal may be taken from the altar with tongs to touch the lips of the faithful. The Lord Christ, therefore, openly indicates the unity of the divine essence and the trinity of persons, saying to the Apostles: "Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." "He says 'in the name,' as Ambrose says in the first book On the Trinity, not 'in the names'" — so that the unity of essence may be shown; through the three names which He placed there, He declared that there are three persons. "He also says: 'I and the Father are one.' He said 'one,' as Ambrose says in the same book, so that no separation of power and nature might arise; and He added 'are,' so that you might know the Father and the Son — namely, that the perfect Father is believed to have begotten a perfect Son, and that the Father and the Son are one, not by confusion of person, but by unity of nature." John also in his canonical Epistle says: "There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one." He also at the beginning of his Gospel says: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" — where he openly shows that the Son was always and eternally with the Father, as one with another. The Apostle also openly distinguishes the Trinity, saying: "God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts." And elsewhere: "If His Spirit, who raised Jesus, dwells in us," etc. Likewise, elsewhere he most evidently commends both the Trinity and the unity, saying: "Because from Him, and through Him, and in Him are all things, to Him be glory." "He says 'from Him,' as Augustine says in the book On the Trinity, on account of the Father; He says 'through Him' on account of the Son; 'in Him' on account of the Holy Spirit." By the fact that he does not say "from them, through them, and in them," nor "to them be glory," but "to Him," he indicated that this Trinity is one Lord God. But since nearly every syllable of the New Testament concordantly indicates this truth of the ineffable Unity and Trinity, let us abstain from accumulating further testimonies on this matter and show by fitting arguments and analogies — to the extent that our weakness allows — that it is so.

COMMENTARY ON DISTINCTION II.

On the Unity and Trinity according to what is believed.
"This therefore is to be held with true and pious faith," etc.

DIVISION OF THE TEXT.

This is the second part, in which the Master, having investigated the material of the first book, begins to pursue it further; and this part is divided into two parts, because things to be enjoyed can be considered in two ways — namely in themselves, and in comparison to creatures: in themselves, by reason of trinity and unity; in comparison to creatures, by reason of knowledge, power, and will. First, therefore, he treats of the holy Trinity and Unity; second, of knowledge and power and will, below at distinction thirty-five: "And since above we have discussed."

Concerning the most sacred Trinity itself, it is possible to treat of it in three ways, since one can first believe it, second understand what is believed, and third express or enunciate what is understood. To believe is through authority; to understand is through reason; to express is through Catholic and rational discourse. Therefore he first treats of the Trinity and Unity itself as it is believed; second, of the same as what is believed and understood through reason, at distinction three: "For the Apostle says"; third, as what is believed and understood is expressed rationally and in a Catholic manner, below at distinction twenty-two: "After what has been said above, it seems to us that we must discuss the diversity of names." And the order is clear. For it is prior and more fundamental to believe than to understand — for many believe who do not understand; and similarly it is prior to understand than to express in speech.

The first part, namely according to what is believed, contains the present distinction; and since the matter is most difficult, he first sets out the mode of proceeding; and second, he carries it out, at: "Let us therefore set forth in the midst."

Likewise, the first part has three sub-parts according to the three chapters. In the first he touches on the mode of treatment — that it must be conducted with modesty, fear, and diligence — premising the subject matter around which he intends to proceed. In the second he subjoins the intention of those who have written on the Trinity, at the second chapter: "All the Catholic writers, however." Third, he touches on the order, at: "Furthermore, as in the first book."

The mode of writing about the Trinity must be grounded in the understanding of faith and conducted with modesty and fear on account of the danger. The intention of those writing about the Trinity is to show that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are three persons and one God. The order of writing is, first, to demonstrate the truth through authorities, then through arguments and fitting analogies.

"Let us therefore set forth in the midst." This is the second part, in which the Master intends to show the Trinity and Unity through the authorities of sacred Scripture; and since sacred Scripture has two parts — namely the New and the Old Testament — he therefore first shows this through the authorities of the Old Testament, then through the authorities of the New, at: "But now after the testimonies," etc. And since the Old Testament has two parts — namely the Law and the Prophets, in which the faith is unfolded — he therefore shows it first through the testimonies of the Law, and second through the testimonies of the Prophets, at: "That greatest of prophets." The first part again, in which he proves through the testimonies of the Law, has two parts: for he first proves the unity of the essence; second, unity together with trinity, at: "The Lord also showed at once the plurality of persons." Similarly, that part concerning the testimonies of the Prophets has two: in the first he proves the unity of essence and the plurality of persons in general; in the second, he shows in particular the generation of the Son and the procession of the Holy Spirit, at: "David also openly hints at the eternal generation of the Son." Similarly, that part in which he proves through the authorities of the New Testament has two parts: for first he proves through the authorities or testimonies of Jesus Christ; second, through the authorities of the Apostles, at: "John also in his canonical Epistle." The authorities and their explanations, their number and varieties, are sufficiently clear in the text.

TREATMENT OF THE QUESTIONS.

For the clarification of what the Master says about the holy Trinity and Unity, four questions can be raised concerning this part.

First, it is asked whether the unity of essence or nature is to be posited in God.

Second, whether a plurality of persons is to be posited in God.

Third, whether infinity is to be posited in the divine persons.

Fourth and finally, whether a trinity is to be posited in the divine persons.

THE SINGLE ARTICLE.

On the unity of the divine essence and the plurality of persons.

QUESTION I.

Whether there is only one God.

Concerning the first — that the unity of essence or nature is to be posited in God — it seems demonstrable by reason, given a threefold supposition that must be made: on account of His simplicity; on account of the common conception of the mind, which is that God is that than which nothing greater can be conceived; and on account of the principle of rest, which exists only in the supreme and first.

questions.notes:
- **Placement of this chunk:** The *Divisio Textus* for Distinction II is a structural commentary by Bonaventure on the Lombard's text, explaining the logical and thematic organization of the material before proceeding to the questions. It also includes the concluding section of the Lombard's own text on New Testament Trinitarian testimonies. Both are translated in sequence as given.
- **"In the midst of the two living creatures" (in medio duorum animalium):** An allegorical reading of Habakkuk 3:2 (LXX: *in medio duorum animalium*) applied to the two Testaments as living creatures flanking the truth. This is Augustine's application of the verse (*De Civitate Dei* XVIII.32). The allusion to the coal from the altar (*forcipe de altari*) is from Isaiah 6:6. Both rendered literally to preserve the typological imagery.
- **Structure of the *Divisio Textus*:** This genre is Bonaventure's architectural map of the Lombard's text — a scholastic *divisio* that identifies every logical subdivision before the commentary proceeds to questions. It is not argumentation but structural analysis, and is translated in that register (analytical, declarative).
- **"Catholic and rational discourse" (catholicam et rationabilem locutionem):** Bonaventure's third mode for treating the Trinity — after *credere* (believe) and *intelligere* (understand through reason) — is *dicere* (express properly). This threefold schema (belief → understanding → expression) organizes the whole of Distinction II, mapping onto Distinctions 2, 3, and 22 respectively.
- **"That than which nothing greater can be conceived" (quo maius excogitari non potest):** Anselm's famous formulation from the *Proslogion*, here cited as a "common conception of the mind" (*communis animi conceptio*). Retained in the standard English translation.
- **Question I opens at the very end:** The chunk ends mid-sentence in the opening of Question I (*Suppositio prima est, quod Deus est simplicis-*). Translated as given; the full argument and response are in subsequent chunks not included here.
- **OCR artifacts corrected:** "nomen eit" → "nomine"; "nr*" (page artifact) silently removed; "Mss." abbreviations silently resolved.

questions.english:
DIST. II. THE SINGLE ARTICLE. QUESTION I. (continued)

most simple. From this it is argued that since it cannot share anything with any other thing that differs from it — because if it shares, it also differs, and therefore not in the same respect, so there is composition there — and if it can share nothing, then neither deity nor entity; therefore if there are two gods, since one is a being, the other is not a being; if one is God, the other is not God: therefore if there are two gods, there are not two gods.

2. Likewise, the second supposition is that God is omnipotent. From this it is argued: therefore He could bring it about that every power other than His could do nothing: therefore if there are two gods diverse in nature, one can do this to the other — that the other could do nothing — and conversely. But that from which power can be taken away is not God: therefore if there are two gods, neither is God.

3. Likewise, the third supposition is that God is simply supreme. From this it is argued: therefore all things are below Him; therefore all things are from Him and toward Him. If therefore there are two gods, one is below the other and conversely; one is from the other according to a diverse nature and conversely; one is toward the other and conversely; but what is below another in nature and from another and toward another is not God: therefore, etc.

4. Likewise, this can be proved by reduction to the impossible. If there are two gods, either one is where the other is, or not. If one is where the other is: then one is in the other, since they have the same mode of being: therefore one is material to the other: therefore the other is not God. If one is not where the other is: then each is limited, and therefore neither is infinite.

5. Likewise, if there are several good gods, either one understands the other or not. If not: then each is ignorant. If it does understand: either through presence, or through a species, or through itself as through an exemplar of that other. If through presence: then one is in the other, and God glides into God and perfects God; if through a species: then it is composite; if through an exemplar: then one is the exemplar of the other, and therefore also its principle.

6. Likewise, if there are two different gods, each of whom is the highest good: either one loves the other as it ought to be loved, or not. If so — since each is the highest good, each is to be loved with the love of enjoyment: therefore each enjoys the other; but one who enjoys another good beside itself is in need of it: therefore one is in need of the other: therefore each is needy, and therefore neither is God.

On the contrary: 1. God can do more than our intellect can think. But the human intellect — as that of the pagans — understands several omnipotent gods: therefore God can bring this about. But whatever can be in the divine nature is there, because it is eternal: therefore, etc.

2. Likewise, more goods are better than fewer; but several gods are more goods: therefore two would be something better than one. But according to Anselm, everything that is better must be attributed to God: therefore several gods are to be posited.

3. Likewise, those whose operation is diverse have diverse power and diverse nature; but the operation of the three persons is diverse, since the appearance in the dove was of the Holy Spirit alone, and the Son alone assumed human nature: therefore they are diverse in substance: therefore there are several gods.

4. Likewise, great is the power that can produce something great, greater what can produce something greater, and greatest what can produce the greatest; but God is supremely powerful above all things: therefore He can produce the supreme; but this is God: therefore since "in eternal things being and being able are the same," therefore, etc.

CONCLUSION.

That there are several gods is impossible — indeed, if one correctly understands what God is, it is not even conceivable.

I respond: It must be said that it is impossible for there to be several gods, and if the signification of this name "God" is correctly understood, it is not only impossible but not even conceivable. For "God" signifies the simply supreme both in reality and in the estimation of the one thinking. Because He is supreme in reality, all things are from Him and in Him and toward Him, and in Him rest is altogether; therefore it is impossible to understand, while preserving this concept, that anything other than Him be equal to Him. Likewise, nothing greater than God can be conceived, nor even anything equal, because He is the supreme in estimation. Therefore it is impossible and inconceivable to posit several gods.

1. To the objection, therefore, concerning the pagans: it must be said that this was not an act of understanding but of fiction; moreover, they were not understanding God according to the divine dignity — and therefore the objection does not hold.

And to the argument that God can do more, etc.: it must be said that there are two kinds of understanding — rational and phantasmatic. The first is true, but not the second; because we can imagine many things through the phantasy that God cannot bring about, since it does not belong to Him, "in whom what is unfitting is impossible."

2. To the objection that more goods are better than fewer: it must be said that this holds in the case of created and finite good, which by reason of its finitude admits an increase of goodness through the addition of another good; but it does not hold in the case of the infinite good, because however much you add infinite good to the infinite, I always understand there to be as much goodness in one as you do in many.

3. To the other objection concerning the diversity of operations: it must be said that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit agree in every operation, but differ in relation. Hence in the Incarnation there is the operation of producing that nature and there is the union; in the first the three persons agree, in the second they do not. — Similarly in the dove there is the formation of the dove and its signification; in the first they agree, in the second they do not. Augustine's example from On the Trinity is that for the formation of the word "memory," memory, understanding, and will all concur; yet the word "memory" signifies one of the powers. The case is similar in the matter at hand.

4. To the objection that great power, etc.: it must be said that to produce a person is threefold — either from oneself, or from some created thing, or from nothing. From Himself God can produce the simply supreme; but that one will not be another in nature, on account of the simplicity of the nature. From another thing or from nothing He cannot produce the simply supreme, but only the supreme in a genus — not on account of a defect of the acting power, but on account of a defect of the creature, which must necessarily be limited; and therefore He cannot produce another God.

[Scholion omitted]

questions.notes:
- **Opening (Q. I continued):** The chunk opens mid-argument, in the third sentence of the first *fundamentum* argument for the unity of the divine essence. Translated seamlessly from the prior chunk's end.
- **"Shares / communicates" (communicare):** The Quaracchi editors' footnote notes that *communicare aliquid cum aliquo* here means "to have something in common with another / to agree with another in something" — not the theological sense of divine self-communication used elsewhere. Rendered "share" or "have in common" throughout this argument to reflect this usage.
- **"In eternal things being and being able are the same" (in aeternis idem est esse et posse):** An Aristotelian axiom (*Physics* III) cited in both argument 4 *contra* and the *Conclusio*. Retained as a quotation. The point is that God's eternal omnipotence entails the actuality of whatever He can do — hence if He can produce another God, there already is another God.
- **"What is unfitting is impossible" (inconveniens est impossibile):** From Anselm's *Cur Deus Homo* I.20 — "however small an unfittingness in God is impossible." Bonaventure's compressed version distinguishes rational understanding (which cannot conceive multiple omnipotent gods without contradiction) from phantasmatic imagination (which can picture anything). Rendered following the Anselmian source.
- **"Rational and phantasmatic understanding" (intellectus rationalis / phantasticus):** A characteristic Bonaventurian distinction between genuine conceptual understanding (governed by logical constraints) and mere imaginative picturing (which has no such constraints). The pagans' polytheism was the latter, not the former.
- **Reply to objection 3 (diverse operations):** The argument that distinct Trinitarian operations (Incarnation of the Son, apparition of the Holy Spirit as dove) imply distinct natures was "the strongest objection of the Arians, Nestorians, Eutychians, and Paulianists," per Albert the Great (noted by the Quaracchi editors). Bonaventure's reply distinguishes the productive act (common to all three persons) from the relational terminus (proper to one person). The Augustine example of the word "memory" — where all three faculties contribute to forming the word, yet only memory is its referent — illustrates the distinction.
- **Reply to objection 4 (supreme production):** Bonaventure distinguishes three modes of production: from oneself (generation of the Son, which yields one who is supreme but not numerically other in nature), from a created thing, and from nothing. Only the first yields the simply supreme; the other two yield only the supreme in a genus. The conclusion — God cannot produce "another God" — rests on the impossibility of numerical otherness in nature without limitation.
