questions.english:
DIST. II. THE SINGLE ARTICLE. QUESTION II.

[Scholion omitted]

QUESTION II.

Whether a plurality of persons is to be posited in God.

Second, it is asked whether a plurality of persons is to be posited in God. And that this is so is shown by supposing four things concerning God: the first is that in Him there is supreme beatitude; the second is supreme perfection; the third is supreme simplicity; the fourth is supreme primacy.

1. From the first supposition the argument runs thus: if there is in Him supreme beatitude — but wherever there is supreme beatitude, there is supreme goodness, supreme charity, and supreme joy. But if there is supreme goodness, since it belongs to goodness supremely to communicate itself, and this is especially so in producing from itself an equal and in giving its own being: therefore, etc. If there is supreme charity, since charity is not private love but is toward another: therefore it requires plurality. Likewise, if there is supreme joy, since "the possession of no good is joyful without a companion": therefore for supreme joy, fellowship is required, and thus plurality.

2. Likewise, from the second supposition thus: if there is in Him supreme perfection — but "it belongs to perfection to produce another such as itself in nature": therefore it is necessary that there be multiplication there; but this cannot be according to another essence: therefore it must be according to another person or supposit.

3. Likewise, from the third supposition thus: if there is in Him supreme simplicity — but it belongs to simplicity that a nature be in many, as is evident in the universal; but it is from a defect of simplicity that it is numbered in them: therefore if in God there is simplicity deficient in nothing, there will be an essence in many that is not numbered: therefore, etc.

4. Likewise, from the fourth supposition thus: if there is in Him supreme primacy — but the more prior something is, the more fruitful it is and the more it is the principle of others: therefore just as the divine essence, because it is first, is the principle of other essences, so the person of the Father, since He is first because He is from no one, is a principle and has fruitfulness with respect to the persons; but fruitfulness in God with respect to God cannot exist except conjoined to act: therefore it is necessary that there be several persons.

On the contrary: 1. It seems that from the same suppositions the contrary could be argued, and thus the arguments and the conclusion are undermined. For if there is supreme beatitude there, since that which is blessed through its essence suffices to itself alone for beatitude: therefore it is not necessary to posit another person for beatitude or joy.

2. Likewise, against the second supposition the objection runs thus: if there is supreme perfection there, the essence is equally fully and perfectly in one person as in many. If therefore beyond perfection any addition is superfluous, plurality is superfluous; and if this is so, since in divine things nothing is superfluous, plurality is not in divine things.

3. Likewise, against the third argument thus: if there is supreme simplicity there, since plurality is opposed to simplicity and "opposites cannot obtain with respect to the same thing": therefore if God is one and in Him there is simplicity, then not plurality — since He is simple in every respect.

4. Likewise, against the fourth supposition thus: if there is supreme primacy there — therefore, since rest is in the first principle and rest is in unity: therefore primacy does not posit plurality but unity: therefore it seems that there is only one person.

CONCLUSION.

That a plurality of persons is to be posited in divine things is both taught by faith and shown to be fitting by arguments of congruence.

I respond: It must be said that in divine things a plurality of persons is to be posited, as faith declares and the foregoing arguments show, if one considers them without contradiction. For by reason of simplicity the essence is communicable and capable of being in many. By reason of primacy, a person is naturally suited to produce another from itself; and I here call primacy "innascibility," by reason of which, as the ancient opinion holds, there is fontal fullness in the Father for every emanation — and this will be made clear below. By reason of perfection it is apt and ready for this; by reason of beatitude and charity, voluntary. With these conditions in place, it is necessary to posit a plurality of persons.

1. To the contrary objection, therefore, that what is blessed through its essence suffices to itself alone, and therefore has no need of another, etc.: it must be said that it is true that it has no need; nor is another posited on account of need, nor as one who beatifies, but as one sharing in beatitude.

2. Similarly, to the objection that the deity is equally fully in one as in many: it must be said that even if it is equally fully present, it is nevertheless not so fully declared. And moreover, by the very fact that it is fully in the Father, it overflows into the other persons by the overflow of perfection.

3. To the objection that plurality is incompatible with simplicity: it must be said that there is a certain plurality by addition, and this is incompatible; and a certain plurality by origin, and this neither adds nor composes nor is incompatible with simplicity, but rather with solitude; and so it is in divine things, as will be made clear below.

4. To the objection that in the first there is rest: it must be said that just as in essences there is one essence that is first, from which the others are and to which they are ordered, so too in the persons there is one person from which the others are and to which they are ordered; and in that person there is the rest of origin, because that person is from no one — and this is the person of the Father. Hence Augustine appropriates unity to that person, saying: "In the Father, unity," etc.

[Scholion omitted]

QUESTION III.

Whether the number of the divine persons is infinite.

Next, in the third place, it is asked whether in the divine persons one ought to posit infinity. And that this is so is shown in the following way.

1. Because a creature is finite, and whatever is in it is actually finite: therefore, from the opposites, since the divine essence is infinite, whatever is in it is infinite: therefore, since in God there is a number of persons, it will be infinite; and thus the persons will be infinite.

2. Likewise, since infinity is twofold — virtual and numerical — virtual infinity is in God: therefore by equal reasoning numerical infinity is as well: therefore in God there are infinite persons.

[Critical apparatus omitted]

questions.notes:
- **Opening fragment (Scholion reference list):** The text opens with a string of bibliographic cross-references in the Quaracchi editorial format (*Breviloq., Itiner., Alex. Hal.,* etc.). These are editorial apparatus, not Bonaventure's text, and have been omitted per the brief.
- **"Fontal fullness" (fontalis plenitudo):** A technical Bonaventurian term for the Father's inexhaustible originating capacity — He is the fount from which both Son and Spirit proceed. Rendered literally; this is a term of art Bonaventure uses throughout the Trinitarian questions.
- **"Innascibility" (innascibilitas):** Bonaventure identifies *primitas* (primacy) with *innascibilitas* — the property of being from no other principle. This is a standard scholastic term for the Father's distinctive personal property; retained untranslated.
- **"Plurality by addition / plurality by origin" (pluralitas per additionem / per originem):** The key distinction in reply to objection 3. Plurality by addition would imply composition and thus conflict with simplicity; plurality by origin (the persons proceeding from one another) involves no such addition. This is central to Bonaventure's Trinitarian theology.
- **"Overflow of perfection" (redundantia perfectionis):** *Redundare* carries the sense of overflowing or spilling over — the Father's perfection so fully realized that it necessarily communicates itself to the Son and Spirit. Rendered as "overflow" to preserve this image.
- **Seneca citation:** The phrase "the possession of no good is joyful without a companion" is from Seneca's *Epistulae ad Lucilium* I.6, cited here as the Quaracchi editors note. Translated directly from Bonaventure's quotation.
- **Question III:** The text ends mid-question (only the two opening arguments are present before the chunk ends). Translated as given; the response and solution to Question III are not in this chunk.
- **"Virtual and numerical infinity" (infinitas virtualis et numeralis):** A distinction between God's infinite power/perfection (virtual infinity) and an infinite number of instances (numerical infinity). The argument proposes these should stand or fall together — Bonaventure's reply (not yet in this chunk) will deny the inference.

DIST. II. THE SINGLE ARTICLE. QUESTION III. (continued)

3. Likewise, an infinite power, when it emanates according to its entire infinity, produces not only the infinite intensively but also extensively; but the power of the Father in the production of persons emanates according to its entire omnipotence: therefore it produces not only persons infinite in power, but also infinite in number.

4. Likewise, this same point is shown thus: the multiplication of persons is either a matter of power or it is not. If it is not, then it ought not to be posited in divine things; if it is a matter of power through itself, then greater multiplication will belong to greater power, and infinite multiplication to supreme power: therefore, etc.

On the contrary, this is shown by four conditions, which are taken from the principle that what is nobler must always be attributed to God — conditions that necessitate positing the finitude of the persons. The first is distinction, the second order, the third connection, the fourth supreme completion.

1. From the first condition it is shown thus: if there is distinction there, then not confusion; but where there is infinity, there is confusion: therefore, etc.

2. Likewise, from the second thus: where there is order, there is termination, because where termination is lacking, mediation is also lacking, and consequently order is lacking; but where there is termination, there is no infinity: therefore if in the divine persons there is order, there is no infinity.

3. Likewise, from the third thus: where there is connection, it is necessary that all the persons proceed from one; for if one proceeds from another and so on successively, then there is an infinite distance between the first and the last — but this is incongruous: therefore all proceed from one. Either, then, they proceed by the same modes or by different modes. If by the same modes: then there is no distinction; if by different modes — but the different modes of emanating are finite: therefore, etc.

4. Likewise, from the fourth thus: if there is supreme completion there, then the divinity is naturally suited to complete another — therefore, since the completion of persons consists in beatitude, it is naturally suited to beatify. But if the persons were infinite, it would be impossible for any person to be beatified by God; for the knowledge of any given person belongs to the substance of beatitude, since the whole goodness that is the substantial reward is in each of the persons; therefore either the soul would know all of them, or it would not be blessed; but it would be impossible to know all of them, since the soul's power is finite: therefore, etc.

CONCLUSION.

That the number of the divine persons is finite is both held by faith and persuaded by reason.

I respond: It must be said that in the divine persons, with respect to number, one ought not to posit infinity but finitude.

The account of this is that numerical infinity is incompatible with perfection and order, because it arises from recession from unity or from its origin. Likewise, infinity of mass; and therefore neither is in God. But infinity of power arises from approach toward unity and origin; and therefore, since this belongs to perfection, it is to be posited in God — the other is not.

1. and 2. To the objection, therefore, that whatever is in God is infinite: it must be said that this is true — it is infinite, but not with just any infinity, but with that infinity by which God is infinite; and this is the infinity of immensity, and in this way the Trinity is infinite — not with numerical infinity, which does not belong to God.

3. To the objection that an infinite power, emanating infinitely, produces infinite things: it must be said that to divine power there belongs only the production of the perfect; and therefore there belongs to it only the production of such infinity as is consistent with supreme perfection. But this is not numerical infinity, and therefore it is not in God.

4. To the last objection, that it belongs to power to multiply itself: it must be said that it does not belong to power in every way, but it belongs to power to multiply itself perfectly; and therefore it does not follow that to multiply itself more is a greater perfection, unless "perfectly" is understood. But to multiply itself infinitely according to number is to do so imperfectly; and therefore this does not belong to God.

[Scholion omitted]

QUESTION IV.

Whether there are only three divine persons.

Fourth and finally, it is asked whether in the divine persons one ought to posit a trinity. And that there is not — that there is rather a duality — is shown thus:

1. The Father gives to the Son everything He is able to give; but one who gives everything he is able to give cannot give more: therefore He cannot produce another person either, since that would be a form of giving.

2. Likewise, the Father begets the Son as the Word, equal to Himself in all respects and expressing and articulating Him fully; but the multiplication of persons is for the declaration of power: therefore it seems superfluous to produce another.

3. Likewise, it is shown that there ought to be a quaternity there, by an argument from emanation. For since the Son emanates by generation and not by procession, therefore, even though He does not generate, He nonetheless produces by spirating; by the same reasoning it seems that the Holy Spirit, even though He does not produce by spirating, could generate or does generate, since He is not generated.

4. Likewise, since in divine things there is a twofold mode of producing — one by way of nature, and another by way of will — and since a complete account of production ought to be present there, it seems also that there ought to be a third mode of producing, by way of art. And if so, a fourth person would have to be posited according to this mode of producing.

On the contrary: that there is only a trinity there is shown from the suppositions made above — that in that Trinity there is beatitude, perfection, simplicity, and primacy.

1. From the first supposition it is shown thus: if there is supreme beatitude there, then there is supreme concord; therefore there is supreme kindredship and supreme charity. But if there were more than three, there would not be supreme kindredship; if fewer, there would not be supreme charity: therefore there are only three. Proof of the minor premise. If there is a fourth person, it either proceeds from one, from two, or from three. If from one or two only, then it does not agree perfectly and equally with all; but if from three, then the two intermediate persons share more in common with each other than with the extremes, since they both produce and are produced; and thus there is no perfect bond. — Likewise, if there were fewer than three, there would not be perfect charity, because perfect love is both generous and shared: because it is generous, it tends toward another; because it is shared, it wills that the beloved be loved by another and that the other love it as itself and from itself: therefore there is love and co-love; but this cannot exist with fewer than three.

questions.notes:
- **Opening (Q. III continued):** Arguments 3 and 4 are the continuation of Question III from the previous chunk. Translated seamlessly from where the prior chunk ended.
- **"Infinity of immensity" (infinitas immensitatis):** Bonaventure's term for God's properly divine infinity — not quantitative but qualitative, denoting the absence of any limiting boundary or deficiency. Distinguished here from *infinitas numeralis* (numerical infinity) and *infinitas molis* (infinity of mass/extension). All three terms rendered literally to preserve the technical taxonomy.
- **"Recession from / approach toward unity" (recessus ab unitate / accessus ad unitatem):** The key structural contrast in the *Conclusio* of Question III. Numerical and material infinities represent flight from the unity and determinacy that characterize perfection; virtual/intensive infinity represents concentration toward the primordial unity. A characteristically Neoplatonic framework running through Bonaventure's Trinitarian theology.
- **"Supreme completion" (summa completio):** The fourth property cited against numerical infinity — rendered "supreme completion" rather than "fullness" to preserve the active sense of *completio* (bringing to completion, fulfilling). The argument is that infinite persons would make beatific knowledge impossible for any finite soul.
- **"Co-love" (condilectio):** A technical term from Richard of St. Victor's Trinitarian theology (*De Trinitate* III), denoting the love that two persons share toward a third. Bonaventure's argument here tracks Richard's famous argument that perfect love requires a third person as the shared object of mutual love. Rendered "co-love" to preserve this technical usage; the footnote confirms the Quaracchi editors' awareness of this source.
- **"Kindredship" / "germanitas":** *Germanitas* literally means the relationship of brothers born of the same parents — rendered "kindredship" to convey this sense of close consanguineal bond among the persons, which would be disrupted if any person shared less fully in the common procession.
- **Question IV ends mid-text:** The chunk ends after argument 2 of the "on the contrary" section, in the middle of Question IV. Translated as given; the resolution and objection responses are not in this chunk.
- **Aristotle citation (Physics II):** The phrase "every agent acts either by way of nature or by way of will" is cited as from the *Philosopher* — following Bonaventure's standard attribution. The objection (argument 4) proposes a third mode of divine production "by way of art," which Bonaventure will reject in the response (not yet translated) on the grounds that divine art is not distinct from divine will.

DIST. II. THE SINGLE ARTICLE. QUESTION IV. (continued)

modes and only these does He produce; but the person produced by each of these modes is most perfect: therefore, if beyond perfection everything is superfluous and everything falling short is deficient, it is necessary that there be only two persons emanating and no more and no fewer, and one from whom they emanate: therefore only three.

3. Likewise, from the third supposition thus: if there is supreme simplicity there, the Father gives everything to each: therefore those who proceed or emanate are not distinguished by what they receive, but by the mode of receiving or of emanating; but there are only two modes of emanating: therefore there can be only two persons emanating and a third producing: therefore, etc.

4. Likewise, from the fourth supposition thus: if by reason of primacy there is supreme fruitfulness there, no person can produce by any kind of production by which it is itself produced, because with respect to that production it is not prior: therefore, since two persons emanate according to two modes of emanating, it is impossible for them to produce by these modes, and there are no other modes: therefore they cannot produce another person: therefore there are only three.

CONCLUSION.

That there are only three divine persons is both taught by the Catholic faith and shown to be fitting by reason.

I respond: It must be said that, as the Catholic faith declares, only three persons are to be posited — no more and no fewer. And to this end both a reason of necessity and a reason of fittingness are brought forward.

The reason of necessity, as to why there cannot be fewer than three, is supreme beatitude and supreme perfection. For supreme beatitude requires love and co-love; supreme perfection requires a twofold emanation, namely of nature and of generosity; and for this at least three persons are required. — Likewise, the reason of necessity as to why there cannot be more is supreme simplicity, which does not permit persons to be distinguished except according to modes of emanating; and again, principal fruitfulness, which does not permit a person to produce by any kind of emanation unless it is, according to the order of understanding, prior to that emanation. Hence the first person, because it is unbegotten and unbreathed-forth, generates and spirates; the second, because it is capable of being breathed forth but is begotten, does not generate but does spirate; the third person, however, because it is breathed forth and proceeds from the one who generates, neither generates nor spirates. And therefore it is impossible for there to be more than three.

The reason of fittingness is taken from the sufficiency of combinations and from the perfection of the number three.

From the sufficiency of combinations: since, as Richard says, "love is in all the persons," and there are only three kinds of love — namely "gratuitous, owed, and mixed from both" — there will be only three persons: one that only gives, in which there is gratuitous love; another that only receives, in which there is owed love; and a middle one that both gives and receives, in which there is love mixed from both. — Likewise, the persons can be combined in another way according to the account of origin; and the sufficiency of this kind of combination consists in three. For one can conceive of a person that is a principle of a person and is not itself something principiated; and again a person that is something principiated and is not a principle of a person; and a third way, a person that is both something principiated and a principle. A fourth mode, however — that a person be neither a principle nor something principiated — is altogether impossible and inconceivable.

The reason of fittingness on the part of number is that this number — three — has both first and supreme perfection, whether it is considered in itself, in continuous quantity, or in creatures.

Considered in itself, it has first perfection, because it is the first number that is constituted from all its own parts — namely unity and duality, which together make three. The number six, however, is called the first among the perfect numbers, because it is constituted from all its aliquot parts — namely three, two, and one. — Likewise, supreme perfection is in it, because unity, which is the principle and completion of every number, reflected back upon itself by perfect reduplication — such as occurs in a solid square — is tripled according to reason while remaining one according to truth, as when one says: once one, once. And this is very similar to the uncreated Trinity, in which in the unity of substance there is a trinity of accounts; yet it is not altogether similar, because there, together with the unity of substance, there is a trinity of accounts and of things, namely of persons; here only of accounts.

Similarly, if this number is considered in continuous quantity, it has in itself first and supreme perfection: first, because every quantity has a beginning, a middle, and an end; supreme, because the highest perfection of continuous quantity consists in the threefold dimension, namely length, breadth, and height. And this is what the Philosopher says at the beginning of On the Heavens: "We say that everything perfect is determined by three, and with this number we have been accustomed to magnify God, the one creator of all things, who transcends the properties of what has been created."

Similarly, if this number is considered in creatures, it has in itself first and supreme perfection: first, because a trinity of vestige can be found in every creature, however small, however minimal; supreme, because the highest and most noble perfection of the creature — namely beatitude — is found in accordance with the trinity of the image as reformed and made God-like.

1. To the objection, therefore, that the Father gives to the Son everything He is able to give: it must be said that this is true, but He does not give in every way in which He is able. And therefore there is a fallacy of accident in the inference: "He cannot give more, therefore He cannot produce another person" — because this would not be giving more, but giving in another way.

2. Similarly, the following reply is clear: the Son does not declare in every way, because, even if He does so according to the account of nature, He does not do so according to the generosity of will — except insofar as from the Word itself the Spirit proceeds.

3. To the objection that the Holy Spirit ought to generate: it must be said that the cases are not alike, because the person of the Son precedes spiration, and therefore has the character of primacy; the person of the Holy Spirit follows generation, and therefore does not generate, because He is not unbegotten.

4. To the objection concerning the third mode of emanating, namely by way of art: it must be said that art has fruitfulness for emanating or producing only through will; and therefore that mode ought not to be distinguished from the mode of producing by way of generosity or will.

Or, alternatively and better: the mode of producing by way of art agrees with the mode of producing by way of nature in this, that in both cases something like the producer is produced. But it differs, because in natural production what is produced is like in substance and nature but other in person; whereas in production by way of art what is produced is like according to the account of the exemplary form, but unlike in substance and nature. But such a mode of producing is incompossible with the divine essence, which does not admit diversity of essences.

[Scholion omitted]

DOUBTS CONCERNING THE MASTER'S TEXT.

DOUBT I.

In this part the first doubt concerning the text arises from what the Master says: that the highest good "is seen by the most pure minds." For he seems to speak badly, because no mind, while still on the way, is most pure — that is only in the homeland.

I respond: It must be said that the mind, in order to contemplate God perfectly, needs to be purified with respect to intellect and affection; therefore he says "through the righteousness of faith" — that is, through faith, which makes one righteous in action and of itself purifies the intellect, while righteousness purifies the affection. And there are three degrees of each kind of purification. For the intellect is purified when it is abstracted from sensible species; more purified, when it is cleansed of phantasmatic images; most purified, when it is cleansed of philosophical reasoning. The degrees of purification of affection are these: the affection is purified when it is cleansed of fault; more purified, when it is cleansed of attachment; most purified, when cleansed of occasion — and in this state it is fitted for contemplation.

DOUBT II.

Likewise, an objection is raised concerning what he says: "the weak gaze of the human mind is not fixed upon so excellent a light," etc. For it seems that even when cleansed it cannot be fixed there, because however much it may be cleansed, that light still exceeds the mind's gaze beyond all proportion: therefore, if on account of its excellence it cannot be seen by one who lacks faith, neither can it be seen by one who has faith.

I respond: There is a difference between considering, being fixed, and comprehending. It can be considered by an unclean mind; but it cannot be fixed upon except by a pure mind; it cannot be comprehended except by the immense. The account of why it cannot be fixed is twofold: one, because it is above the intellect, and therefore the intellect is not fixed in it unless it has the adhesive of affection — otherwise it falls back immediately; another account, because a sound eye is proportionable to that light qualitatively, even if not quantitatively; but a weak or bleary eye is disproportionable in both ways, and therefore cannot be fixed.

DOUBT III.

Likewise, an objection is raised concerning this statement of Ambrose: "God and Lord is a name of nature and a name of power" — because Damascene says that the name "God" is imposed from His operation, whence it is derived either from *aithein*, which means to burn, or from *theein*, which means to cherish, or from *theasthai*, which means to see.

I respond: It must be said that concerning this name and similar ones there are two ways of speaking: either with respect to that to which it is imposed — and in this sense it is a name of nature, because it is imposed upon that which is supreme nature; or with respect to that from which it is imposed — and in this sense it is a name of operation, because it is imposed from operation.

DOUBT IV.

Likewise, a question arises concerning this circumlocution: "I am who I am" — whether this name "I am," etc., is a name of essence or of person. That it is of a person seems evident, because a demonstrative pronoun signifies a certain person. And again, speaking is an act of a person. If you perhaps say that "I," because it signifies origin, stands for the person of the Father; "am," because it signifies an act going forth, for the person of the Son; and "who," as a relative connecting both, for the person of the Holy Spirit — this amounts to nothing, because the relative and the antecedent stand for the same thing.

I respond: It must be said that the name "He who is" and "I am who I am" is properly a name of essence — for this is a certain circumlocution, signifying entity in every kind of perfection and absoluteness, and this is the proper name of the divine substance. And to the objection that a pronoun signifies a certain person: it must be said that "person" there refers to a certain supposit of the Word, and this is substance and nature.

DOUBT V.

Likewise, a question arises concerning the authority: "Let us make man according to our image and likeness" — whether "image" there stands for essence or for person. If for essence, then to say "our image" is the same as to say "our essence"; if for person, then it ought to say "my" and not "our"; if for a created image, this is nothing to the matter at hand, since by this the unity of nature would not be proved.

I respond: It must be said that, according to the way the Saints understand it here, "image and likeness" denotes both essence and relation. For "image" imports unity with distinction, and "likeness" similarly, because of the intrinsic relation. And therefore in the name "image and likeness," with respect to some part of its signification, the unity of essence is indicated, and with respect to another part, the plurality of persons is indicated. And therefore Augustine expounds it in one way, and Hilary in another. Augustine considers the part of the signified, namely the unity of essence; but Hilary considers the whole. Hence Hilary says that by the name of image and likeness both unity and plurality are simultaneously understood. Similarly Augustine, in the expressions "let us make" and "our," considers only the co-signified — and therefore plurality. Hilary, however, considers both the signified and the co-signified, and therefore in both expressions he says that both plurality and unity are to be understood.

DOUBT VI.

Likewise, Hilary says: "Nor does the likeness of one to another permit diversity to be mixed in the two."

But on the contrary: likeness is the same quality in different things: therefore likeness is compatible with difference.

- **Opening (Q. IV continued):** Arguments 2–4 of the "On the contrary" section of Question IV, followed by the full *Conclusio* and replies to objections 1–4. Translated seamlessly from the prior chunk's end-point.
- **"Co-love" (condilectio) and Richard of St. Victor:** The argument that perfect love requires both love (*dilectio*) and co-love (*condilectio*) — i.e., a shared love for a third — is explicitly credited to Richard of St. Victor (*De Trinitate* V.16, 23). The footnote confirms this attribution. "Co-love" retained as before.
- **"Incompossible" (incompossibilis):** A scholastic technical term meaning "incapable of existing together with" — stronger than merely "impossible" in isolation. The Quaracchi editors restored this reading over the simpler *impossibilis* found in the Vatican codex. Rendered "incompossible" to preserve the technical precision.
- **Number theology (ternarius):** Bonaventure's elaborate argument for three as the perfect number draws on ancient Pythagorean-Neoplatonic arithmetic (via Aristotle's *De Caelo*, Isidore, Augustine, and ultimately Euclid). The argument that 1×1×1 = 1 while "tripling" unity is central to his analogy for the Trinity: three in reason/account (*rationes*), one in truth. The Scholion (omitted per brief) explains this arithmetic in considerable detail.
- **"Solid square" (solidum quadratum):** A reference to perfect reduplication — a number multiplied by itself twice (the cubic number). The Quaracchi editors note that *quadrata* is a scribal interpolation; the correct term is simply "perfect reduplication" (*reduplicatio perfecta*). The point is that 1 cubed = 1, making three the "perfect" self-reflection of unity.
- **"Trinity of vestige / trinity of image" (trinitas vestigii / trinitas imaginis):** Two degrees of Trinitarian trace in creatures — the vestige (found in all created things: unity, truth, goodness) and the image (found in rational creatures, especially as reformed by grace and glory). These are Bonaventurian technical categories; retained as "vestige" and "image" throughout.
- **Doubt IV on "I am who I am":** Bonaventure's solution — that "He who is" is a name of essence, not of any particular person — follows Augustine (*De Trinitate* V) and will be elaborated at dist. 22, q. 3. The trinitarian reading of the three grammatical elements (ego/sum/qui) is dismissed as a fallacy of identity between relative and antecedent.
- **Doubt V on "image and likeness":** Bonaventure's resolution of the Augustine/Hilary apparent conflict — Augustine takes "image" to signify unity of essence (the *signified*), while Hilary takes it to co-signify both essence and relation (signified + *co-signified*). The scholastic distinction between *significatum* and *consignificatum* is central here.
- **Doubt VI ends mid-text:** The chunk ends in the middle of Bonaventure's response to Doubt VI. Translated as given.

And since in the divine essence there is supreme simplicity, there can be neither likeness according to accident nor according to part: and therefore likeness does not admit diversity of nature.

DOUBT VII.

Likewise, an objection is raised concerning what the Master says: that by the name of partnership, something is not posited but removed — because from this it seems that, according to him, every numerical expression posits nothing but only negates; but this seems false. For since in divine things there is a true plurality of persons, they seem to be spoken of not only privatively but also positively.

I respond: This was the Master's position, which is not commonly held, because it does not have truth, as will be more clearly shown below. Nevertheless the Master is excused, because he said that numerical names posit nothing because they import number, which is not properly in divine things. For number is caused by the aggregation and distinction of units; and the distinction of units comes about in three ways: by division of the continuous, by disparity of forms, and by grade or order. Since therefore in divine things there is neither aggregation nor such distinction, there is accordingly no number properly speaking.

DOUBT VIII.

Likewise, a question arises concerning what he says: "In the beginning God created" — why this name "God" stands or supposes for the person of the Father rather than for the person of the Son, and how the Trinity is to be understood from this.

I respond: To this it must be said that the plurality of persons is indicated to us in Scripture in eight ways. In the first way by signification, as in the last chapter of Matthew: "In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." In the second way by co-signification, as in Genesis at the beginning, where we have "God" but the Hebrews have *Elohim*, which is the nominative plural of the singular *El*. In the third way by supposition, as when it is said "God begot God"; in Proverbs eight: "Before all hills the Lord begot me." In the fourth way by appropriation, as there: "In the beginning God created," etc. — for "God" there is appropriated to the Father and "beginning" to the Son. In the fifth way by iteration, as in Isaiah six: "Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of hosts." In the sixth way by order of words, as in the Psalm: "May God bless us, our God, may God bless us." In the seventh way by connotation in the act of mission, as when it is said in Galatians four: "God sent," etc. In the eighth way by apparition, as the three men appeared to Abraham in Genesis eighteen.

DOUBT IX.

Likewise, an objection is raised concerning what he says: "That greatest of the Prophets" — because on Matthew chapter seventeen: "Moses and Elijah appeared to them," the Gloss says: "Elijah was the greatest of the Prophets" — not David, therefore.

I respond: The spirit of prophecy, given in greater abundance, makes a prophet of the Lord more excellent. It can therefore be given in greater abundance in two ways: either because it extends to more things, or because it extends to higher things. To Elijah it was given with respect to more things, namely foreknowledge of future events and the working of miracles; but to David with respect to higher things, because, as is clear from his prophecy, he saw more and more clearly, since his was intellectual prophecy.

DOUBT X.

Likewise, an objection is raised concerning what he says: "The Lord possessed me" — because possession is of an inferior thing, ordering is of a posterior thing, and conception similarly sounds of the fragility of the female sex, as does parturition — none of which is fitting to divine things.

I respond: Wisdom is described by comparison to her effects and by comparison to her principle. And since by comparison to her effects she has in herself an inexhaustible treasury in terms of multitude, and has order in terms of discretion, she is therefore described by the verb of possessing and ordering. By comparison to her principle she emanates by an intrinsic emanation, in that she is of the substance of the one emanating; and therefore she is described by the verb of conception and parturition.

DISTINCTION III.
PART I.

On the knowledge of the Creator through creatures, in which the vestige of the Trinity appears.

"For the Apostle says" that the invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are seen through the things that are made, being understood by the intellect — His eternal power and divinity as well. By "creation of the world" is understood the human being "on account of the excellence by which he excels among other creatures, or on account of the affinity he has with every creature." The human being, therefore, could or indeed did behold the invisible things of God with the intellect of the mind through the things that are made — that is, through visible or invisible creatures. For he was helped by two things, namely by nature, which was rational, and by the works made by God, so that truth might be made manifest to the human being. Therefore the Apostle said: "because God revealed it to them" — namely while He made the works in which the judgment of the craftsman shines forth to some degree.

For as Ambrose says: "So that God, who is invisible by nature, might also be known from visible things, He made a work that by its own visibility manifested its maker, so that through the certain the uncertain might be known, and that He who made what is impossible for a human being to make might be believed to be God of all things." They were therefore able to know, or they did know, that beyond every creature there is one who made those things which no creature is able to make or destroy. Let any creature you will come forward and make such a heaven and such an earth, and I shall say that it is God. But since no creature can make such things, it is established that the one who made them is above every creature; and through this, the human mind was able to know that He is God.

In another way also they were able to know, or did know, the truth of God through the guidance of reason. For as Augustine says in the book On the City of God: "The greatest philosophers saw that no body is God, and therefore transcended all bodies in seeking God; they saw too that whatever is mutable is not the highest God and principle of all things, and therefore transcended every soul and mutable spirits; then they saw that everything mutable cannot exist except through that which exists immutably and simply. They understood, therefore, that He both made all these things and could not have been made by anyone."

"They also considered that whatever exists in substances is either body or spirit, and that spirit is something better than body, but far better is the one who made spirit and body."

"They also understood that the form of a body is sensible and the form of a spirit is intelligible, and they preferred the intelligible form to the sensible. By sensibles we mean what can be perceived by the sight and touch of the body; by intelligibles, what can be understood by the gaze of the mind. Since therefore in their gaze both body and spirit were more or less beautiful, and if they could lack all form they would be altogether nothing, they saw that there is something whereby those things were made beautiful, where the first and immutable form is, and thus incomparable; and they most rightly believed that to be the principle of things which was not made and from which all made things were made." Behold, in so many ways the truth of God could be known. Since therefore God is one simple essence, consisting of no diversity of parts or accidents, the Apostle nonetheless says in the plural "the invisible things of God," because the truth of God is known in multiple ways through the things that are made. For from the perpetuity of creatures the eternal Creator is understood; from their magnitude, the omnipotent one; from their order and disposition, the wise one; from their governance, the good one. But all these pertain to demonstrating the unity of the Godhead.

There remains now to show whether through the things that are made some vestige or faint indication of the Trinity could be had. Concerning this, Augustine in the sixth book On the Trinity says: "It is fitting that we who contemplate the Creator through the things that are made should understand the Trinity. For a vestige of this Trinity appears in creatures. For all these things that have been made by divine art show in themselves a certain unity and form and order. For each of these created things is both something one, as are the natures of bodies and souls, and is formed by some form, as are the figures or qualities of bodies and the disciplines or arts of souls, and seeks or holds some order, as are the weights or positions of bodies and the loves or delights of souls; and so in creatures the vestige of the Trinity shines forth. For in that Trinity there is the supreme origin of all things and most perfect beauty and most blessed delight." Now the supreme origin, as Augustine shows in the book On True Religion, is understood as God the Father, from whom are all things, from whom are the Son and the Holy Spirit. Most perfect beauty is understood as the Son — that is, the truth of the Father, in no part unlike Him, whom together with Him and in Him the Father we venerate, who is the form of all things that were made from the one and are referred back to the one, which things nonetheless would neither come to be from the Father through the Son nor be kept safe within their proper bounds unless God were supremely good — He who neither envied any nature that would be good from Him, and gave to each, to some as much as it willed, to others as much as it could, the ability to remain in that good; and this goodness is understood as the Holy Spirit, who is the gift of the Father and the Son. Therefore it is fitting for us to honor and hold fast to the gift of God itself, co-equally immutable with the Father and the Son. Through the consideration of creatures, therefore, we understand the Trinity of one substance — namely the one God the Father, from whom we are, and the Son through whom we are, and the Holy Spirit in whom we are; that is, the principle to whom we return, the form we follow, and the grace by which we are reconciled: the one, namely, at whose command as author we were founded, and His likeness through whom we are reformed unto unity, and the peace by which we adhere to Unity — namely, God who said "let there be," and the Word through whom everything was made that exists substantially and naturally, and the Gift of His kindness by which what was made from Him through the Word was pleased and reconciled to its author so that it would not perish. Behold, it has been shown how in creatures the image of the Trinity is indicated to some degree; for through the contemplation of creatures a sufficient knowledge of the Trinity could not be had or could be had without the revelation of doctrine or of interior inspiration. Hence those ancient philosophers saw the truth as if through a shadow and from afar, falling short in their contemplation of the Trinity, like the magicians of Pharaoh at the third sign. Yet we are helped in the faith of invisible things through the things that are made.

On the image and likeness of the Trinity in the human soul.

"But now let us come to that discussion in which we find the image of the Trinity in the human mind, which knows God or can know Him." For as Augustine says in the fourteenth book On the Trinity: "Although the human mind is not of the same nature as God, yet the image of that nature than which nothing is better is to be sought and found there, where our nature has nothing better — that is, in the mind. For in the mind itself, even before it participates in God, His image is found; for although, with the loss of participation in God, it is deformed, the image of God nonetheless remains. For the mind is the image of God precisely insofar as it is capable of Him and can be a participant in Him. Let us therefore inquire in it for the Trinity that is God. Behold, then, the mind remembers itself, understands itself, loves itself; if we see this, we see a trinity — not yet God, indeed, but the image of God. For here there appears a certain trinity of memory, understanding, and love." Let us therefore treat especially of these three: memory, understanding, and will.

"These three, then, as Augustine says in the tenth book On the Trinity, are not three lives but one life; not three minds but one mind; one essence. Memory, however, is said in relation to something, and understanding and will or love are similarly said in relation to something; but life is said with reference to itself, and so are mind and essence. These three are therefore one in that they are one life, one mind, one essence; and whatever else they are each said to be with reference to themselves, they are also said together — not in the plural, but in the singular. But they are three in that they are referred to one another."

"They are also equal — not only individually to individually, but also individually to all together; otherwise they would not mutually contain each other; but they do mutually contain each other. For both individually and all together they are contained by each and all. For I remember that I have memory and understanding and will; and I understand that I understand and will and remember; and I will that I will and remember and understand."

"And I remember my entire memory and understanding and will together. For what I do not remember of my memory is not in my memory; but nothing is so present in memory as memory itself: therefore I remember it entirely. Likewise, whatever I understand, I know that I understand, and I know that I will whatever I will; but whatever I know, I remember. Therefore I remember my entire understanding and my entire will."

"Similarly, when I understand these three, I understand them all together. For there is nothing among the intelligibles that I do not understand, except what I am ignorant of. But what I am ignorant of I neither remember nor will. Whatever therefore of the intelligibles I do not understand, consequently I neither remember nor will. Whatever, therefore, of the intelligibles I do remember and will, consequently I understand."

"My will also grasps my entire understanding and my entire memory when I use all that I understand and remember. Since therefore mutually, individually and all together, all things and their wholes are grasped by each, the entire individual things are equal to the entire individual things, and the entire individual things are equal together to all the entire things; and these three are one — one life, one mind, one essence." "Behold, the human mind is the image — though unequal — of that supreme Unity and Trinity in which there is one essence and three persons." Now mind is here taken for the soul itself, in which that image of the Trinity is found; "but mind is properly said, as Augustine says, not of the soul itself, but of what is most excellent in it" — in which sense it is often used. It should also be known that memory is not only of absent and past things, but also of present things, as Augustine says in the fourteenth book On the Trinity — otherwise it could not contain itself.

Here it must be carefully noted in what sense it is to be understood that those three things — namely memory, understanding, and will — are said to be one, one mind, one essence. This does not seem to be true according to the proper meaning of the expression. For mind — that is, the rational spirit — is a spiritual and incorporeal essence. But those three are natural properties or powers of the mind itself and differ from one another, because memory is not understanding or will, nor is understanding will or love.

"And these three are also referred to themselves," as Augustine says in the ninth book On the Trinity: "For the mind cannot love itself or remember itself unless it also knows itself — for how does it love or remember what it does not know?" In a wondrous manner, therefore, these three are inseparable from themselves; and yet each individually and all together are one essence, even though they are said in relation to one another.

But now it must be seen in what sense these three are said to be one substance — namely because they exist substantially in the soul or mind itself, not like accidents in subjects, which can be present and absent. Hence Augustine in the ninth book On the Trinity says: "We are admonished, if we can see even this much, that these things exist in the soul substantially, not as in a subject, as color in a body, because even though they are said in relation to one another, each of them nonetheless exists substantially in its own substance." Behold, in what sense those three things are said to be one or one substance. "These three, as Augustine says in the fifteenth book On the Trinity, are divinely established in the mind by nature; and whoever vividly perceives how great is that in it from which even the eternal and immutable nature can be recalled, perceived, and desired — for it is recalled through memory, perceived through understanding, embraced through love — surely finds in it the image of that supreme Trinity."

CHAPTER III.

On the likeness between the creating and the created trinity.

"Yet let him beware lest he compare this image, made by the same Trinity, to it in such a way that he thinks it altogether like, but rather in whatever likeness there is, let him perceive a great unlikeness as well."

"This can be shown briefly. One human being through those three remembers, understands, loves — he who is neither memory nor understanding nor love, but has these. There is therefore one human being who has these three, not who himself is these three. But in that supreme simplicity of nature which is God, although God is one, there are nonetheless three persons, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit," and these three are one God. "The thing of the Trinity, therefore, is one thing; the image of the Trinity in another thing is another. On account of this image, even that in which these three are is called an image — namely the human being. Just as both the panel and the picture painted on it are called an image; but the panel is called by the name of image on account of the picture that is in it."

"Again, this image — which is a human being having those three — is one person. But that Trinity is not one person but three — the Father of the Son and the Son of the Father and the Spirit of the Father and the Son. So in this image of the Trinity, those three are not one human being but belong to one human being. But in that supreme Trinity whose image this is, those three do not belong to one God but are one God; and those three are three persons, not one." "For those three are not the human being, but belong to or are in the human being. But can we say that the Trinity is thus in God such that those three are something of God, and not God Himself?" Far be it from us to believe this. Let us say, then, that in our mind there is the image of the Trinity — but a slight and imperfect one — which bears a likeness to the supreme Trinity in such a way that it is for the most part unlike it. It must also be known that "this Trinity of the mind, as Augustine says in the fourteenth book On the Trinity, is not the image of God merely because the mind remembers and understands and loves itself, but because it can also remember and understand and love Him by whom it was made."

There is also another way in which the trinity in the soul — which is an image of that supreme and ineffable Trinity — can be distinguished under other names. For as Augustine says in the ninth book On the Trinity: "Mind and its knowledge and love are certain three things. For the mind knows itself and loves itself; nor can it love itself unless it also knows itself — for how does it love or remember what it does not know?" "When therefore the mind knows and loves itself, a trinity remains — namely mind, love, and knowledge." "But mind here is taken not for the soul but for what is more excellent in the soul." Now these three, although they are distinct from one another, are nonetheless said to be one, because they exist substantially in the soul.

And the mind itself is, as it were, the parent; and its knowledge is, as it were, its offspring. "For when the mind knows itself, it begets knowledge of itself, and is the sole parent of its own knowledge. The third is love, which proceeds from the mind itself and from knowledge, when the mind knowing itself loves itself; for it could not love itself unless it knew itself. It also loves its pleasing offspring — that is, its knowledge; and so love is a certain embrace of parent and offspring."

"Nor is the offspring less than the parent, when the mind knows itself as great as it is; nor is love less than the parent and the offspring — that is, than the mind and the knowledge — when the mind loves itself as much as it knows itself and as great as it is."

"These are also each in themselves: for the loving mind is in love, and love is in the knowledge of the one who loves, and knowledge is in the knowing mind." Behold, in these three some vestige of the Trinity appears.

The rational mind, therefore, considering these three and that one essence in which they exist, extends itself to the contemplation of the Creator and sees unity in trinity and trinity in unity. For it understands that God is one, one essence, one principle. It understands that if there were two, either each would be insufficient, or one would be superfluous — for if something were lacking to one that the other had, supreme perfection would not be there; but if nothing were lacking to one that the other had, since everything would be in one, the other would be superfluous. It understood, therefore, that there is one God, the one author of all things; and it saw that without wisdom He would be, as it were, a foolish thing; and therefore it understood that He has wisdom, which was begotten from Him; and because He loves His wisdom, it also understood that there is love there.

On the unity of the Trinity.

"Therefore, in accordance with this consideration, as Augustine says in the ninth book On the Trinity, let us believe the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit to be one God, creator and ruler of the whole creation; and the Father not to be the Son, and the Holy Spirit not to be either the Father or the Son, but a Trinity of persons related to one another." For as he himself says in the book On Faith to Peter: "There is one nature or essence of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit — not one person. For if there were one person just as there is one substance of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, a Trinity would truly not be said. Again, there would indeed be a true Trinity, but the Trinity itself would not be one God, if just as the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are distinguished from one another by the property of their persons, so they had been also separated by diversity of natures." "But the faith of the Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles proclaims the one God to be the Trinity." "In that holy Trinity, therefore, there is one God the Father, who alone begot essentially from Himself one Son; and there is one Son, who alone was essentially born from the one Father; and there is one Holy Spirit, who alone essentially proceeds from Father and Son. But all of this one person cannot do — that is, beget itself and be born from itself and proceed from itself." For as Augustine says in the first book On the Trinity: "There is nothing that begets itself so as to exist."

COMMENTARY ON DISTINCTION III.

PART I.

On the knowledge of God through remote likenesses.

"For the Apostle says that the invisible things of God," etc.

DIVISION OF THE TEXT.

Above, the Master treated of the holy Trinity and Unity insofar as it is believed. In this second part he treats of the same insofar as it is understood. And this part is divided into three parts: in the first he brings forward fitting likenesses and arguments for understanding the Trinity. In the second he resolves the emerging doubts, below at the beginning of distinction four: "Here there arises a quite necessary question. It is established," etc. In the third, those doubts having been resolved, he determines the properties and conditions of the Trinity and Unity, below at distinction eight: "Now concerning the truth or the property," etc.

Likewise, the first part has two. In the first he brings forward remote likenesses; in the second, near or express likenesses, which are found in the image, at: "But now let us come to that discussion."

Likewise, the first part has two parts. In the first he shows Unity; in the second, Trinity, at: "There remains now to show whether through the things that are made," etc.

The first part has four sections. In the first he proves by the authority of the Apostle in Romans one that God is knowable through creatures. In the second he adduces various modes of knowing and arguments, at: "For as Ambrose says." In the third he states that those modes are implied in the authority of the Apostle, at: "Behold, in so many ways." In the fourth he indicates what can be proved through the aforesaid arguments — namely the unity of essence, not the Trinity — at: "But all of these pertain to demonstrating the unity," etc.

"There remains now to show whether," etc. Above, the Master showed the unity or entity of the divine essence through arguments. In this second part he shows the Trinity through a remote likeness, which is found in the vestige; and this chapter has four sections. In the first the Master shows the character of the vestige in creatures. In the second he shows what in the Creator corresponds to the vestige — namely the trinity of appropriated attributes: origin, beauty, and delight, so that individual items are matched to individual ones — at: "For in that Trinity there is the supreme origin." In the third he teaches the contemplation of the Trinity in God through the consideration of the vestige in creatures, at: "Through the consideration of creatures, therefore," etc., where he shows the trinity of appropriated attributes in God both with respect to the act of creation and with respect to the act of reformation. In the fourth section he shows that the consideration of the Trinity through the vestige is not sufficient but is remote, at: "Behold, it has been shown how in creatures."

"But now let us come to that discussion." This is the second part of the present distinction, in which the Master proves the Trinity and Unity through a near and express likeness, of the kind that is an image. And this part is divided in two: in the first he shows the trinity and unity in the Creator through the trinity and unity considered in the powers of the soul; in the second, through the habitual dispositions, at: "It can also be distinguished in another way and under other names."

The first part again has four sections. In the first the Master shows where the image is to be sought in the soul — namely in the superior part and in its three powers: memory, understanding, and will. In the second he touches on the conditions of the image, which are trinity, unity, and equality, at: "These three, then, as Augustine says." In the third he raises and resolves the doubt that arises from the foregoing — namely whether the soul is its own powers — at: "Here it must be carefully noted." In the fourth he teaches how to guard against the error that could be caused or arise from the presentation of the created trinity — that it would be altogether like the uncreated — where he shows that the unlikeness of the image to God is very great, at: "Yet let him beware."

"It can also be distinguished in another way and under other names," etc. This is the second part of the second part of this distinction, in which the Master intends to investigate the image in the habitual dispositions of the soul as far as is possible; and this part is divided into four sections. First, he touches on those things in which the image of the Trinity is found — namely mind, knowledge, and love. Second, those having been indicated, he shows that the image is found in these on account of their consubstantiality, order, and equality, at: "Now these three, although they are distinct from one another." Third, he shows how the rational mind, in the contemplation of the created trinity, advances toward seeing and knowing the uncreated Trinity in Unity, at: "The rational mind, therefore, considering these three." Fourth, he briefly recollects what has been demonstrated above, at: "Therefore, in accordance with this consideration."

TREATMENT OF THE QUESTIONS.

For the understanding of what is touched upon in this first part of the distinction, four things are asked.

The first is whether God is knowable by a creature.

The second is whether He is knowable through a creature.

The third is whether the mode of knowing through creatures belongs to the human being with respect to every state — namely the state of innocence, the state of fallen nature, and the state of glorified nature.

The fourth is what is knowable about God through creatures.

THE SINGLE ARTICLE.

On the knowability of God.

QUESTION I.

Whether God is knowable by a creature.

Concerning the first — that God is not knowable by a creature — it is shown:

1. By the authority of Dionysius in the Divine Names: "It is impossible either to speak or to understand God."

2. Likewise, it is shown by reason through a fourfold supposition that must be present in cognition — namely proportion, union or reception, judgment, and information. For the intellect understands only what is proportionable to it, and what is in some way united to it, and about which it judges, and by which the gaze of understanding is informed.

From the first supposition the argument runs thus: it is necessary that there be a proportion between the knower and the knowable; but there is no proportion between God and the intellect, because God is infinite and the intellect is finite: therefore, etc. Furthermore, if there is some proportion, it does not seem to be sufficient, because the uncreated truth is more distant from the human intellect than any created intelligible is from the sense. But the sense, which is perceptive of the sensible, is never elevated to knowledge of the created intelligible: therefore neither will the intellect ever be elevated to knowledge of the uncreated intelligible.

3. Likewise, from the second supposition thus: it is necessary that there be a union of the knowable with the knower, so that one is in the other; but the knower is not in the knowable, but conversely; but it is impossible for the infinite to be contained by the finite itself: therefore it is impossible for it to be in it: therefore for God to be in the intellect is impossible, since He is infinite.

4. Likewise, from the third supposition thus: for cognition it is necessary that there be in the knower a judgment concerning the known; but every one who judges has power over what is judged; but the finite does not have power over the infinite: therefore it does not judge concerning it; but judgment was required for cognition: therefore the finite intellect does not know the infinite God, over whom it has no power.

5. Likewise, from the fourth thus: it is necessary that the intellect that knows be informed by the known; but everything that informs another does so either through its essence or through a likeness; but God does not inform through His essence, because He is united to nothing as a form; nor through an abstracted likeness, because an abstracted likeness is more spiritual than that from which it is abstracted; but nothing is or can be more spiritual than God: therefore, etc.

On the contrary: 1. The rational soul is made in the image of God. But as Augustine says in the book On the Trinity — and it is in the text of the present distinction — "The mind is the image of God precisely insofar as it is capable of God and can be a participant in Him." But to be capable of Him is not according to substance or essence, since this applies to all creatures: therefore it is through knowledge and love: therefore God can be known by a creature.

2. Likewise, it is shown by reason thus: all spiritual knowledge comes about by reason of light, and by reason of uncreated light, as Augustine says in the Soliloquies; but light is supremely knowable, and God is supreme light: therefore He is supremely knowable by the soul itself: therefore, etc.

3. Likewise, since some things are known through presence and others through likeness, those are known more truly that are known through presence, as Augustine says; but God is united to the soul itself through presence: therefore God is known more truly than other things that are known through likeness.

4. Likewise, as supreme goodness stands to love, so does supreme truth stand to knowledge; but supreme goodness is supremely lovable by the affective power: therefore supreme truth is supremely knowable by the intellect.

5. Likewise, each thing acts more efficaciously with respect to that toward which it is naturally ordered; but our intellect is naturally ordered toward the knowledge of the supreme light: therefore that light is most

questions.notes:
- **Opening (Doubt VI continued):** The chunk opens with the tail of Bonaventure's response to Doubt VI from the prior chunk, distinguishing likeness according to accident or part (which admits diversity) from likeness according to the whole (which does not). Translated seamlessly.
- **Doubt VII — the Master's position on numerical expressions:** Bonaventure explicitly distances himself from Peter Lombard's position that numerical expressions in Trinitarian discourse are purely privative. He excuses the Master on narrow grounds while signaling that the fuller treatment follows at dist. 24. The phrase "This was the Master's position, which is not commonly held" is a rare moment of direct critique of the Lombard.
- **Doubt VIII — eight modes of Trinitarian signification in Scripture:** A compact taxonomy unique in the Sentences commentary tradition. Alexander of Hales is noted by the Quaracchi editors as listing seven of these modes; Bonaventure adds the eighth (apparition). All eight rendered with their technical scholastic names.
- **"Intellectual prophecy" (prophetia intellectualis):** Bonaventure's distinction between David (prophecy through intellectual vision — the highest Augustinian grade) and Elijah (prophecy through imaginative vision — more numerous but lower miracles and foreknowledge). Follows Augustine's taxonomy from *De Genesi ad litteram* XII.
- **Distinction III begins mid-chunk:** From "For the Apostle says" onward, the text transitions entirely into Bonaventure's commentary on Distinction III — first the Lombard's base text on the vestige of the Trinity in creation and the image in the soul (lengthy Augustine *catenae*), then Bonaventure's own *Divisio Textus* and the opening of Question I. All translated continuously.
- **Augustine *catenae*:** The extended passages from *De Trinitate* (IX, X, XIV, XV) and *De Vera Religione* are translated from Bonaventure's version of the text, which diverges slightly from the critical edition of Augustine in places. Per the brief, these divergences are left as-is.
- **"Remote likenesses / near likenesses" (similitudines longinquae / propinquae):** Bonaventure's technical distinction between the *vestigium* (trace of the Trinity found in all creatures) and the *imago* (image of the Trinity found in the rational soul). The vestige is a remote, one-way likeness; the image is a near, reflexive likeness. Both terms retained throughout.
- **Question I ends mid-text:** The chunk ends in the midst of the fifth *contra* argument of Question I (*illa maxime*). Translated as given.

questions.english:
DIST. III. THE SINGLE ARTICLE. QUESTION IV. (continued from prior chunk)

in creatures. And the arguments that seem to prove the contrary do not prove it, but rather prove that God is known by them in creatures.

1. To the objection concerning the state of innocence — that the mind is formed immediately, etc.: it must be said that medium is twofold, namely an efficient medium and a disposing medium. What Augustine said must be understood of the first kind of medium, but not of the second; for God is the efficient medium and the object of the mind itself. Augustine says this against the philosophers, whose opinion was that the mind is not joined immediately to the first principle, but through the mediation of some intelligence.

2. To the objection that the order is not proper: it must be said that the human being can be considered in two ways — either as a being in himself, or as a being outside himself. In the first way he does not arrive at God through creatures external to himself, but the being that is outside himself, through the knowledge of creatures, is gathered back into himself and elevated above himself.

Or it can be said, in another way, that other creatures can be considered either as things or as signs. In the first way they are inferior to the human being; in the second they are means on the way to the destination — not at the destination itself — because those creatures do not themselves arrive, but through them the human being arrives at God, leaving them behind.

[Scholion omitted]

QUESTION IV.

Whether the trinity of persons together with the unity of essence can be known naturally through creatures.

Fourth and finally, it is asked what is knowable about God through creatures. The Apostle says that "eternal power and divinity" can be known. And it is asked whether the plurality of persons can be known through creatures. And it seems that it can.

1. Because the philosophers had no knowledge of God except through creatures, and they knew the Trinity: therefore, etc. The minor premise is clear from Augustine in the City of God: "The philosophers say that philosophy is threefold" — in which there is knowledge of the Trinity.

2. Likewise, the magicians failed at the third sign, in Exodus eight; and it is interpreted that they failed in the knowledge of the third person — either with respect to proper attributes or with respect to appropriated attributes. Not with respect to appropriated attributes, because goodness shines forth for us most evidently in creatures: therefore it was with respect to proper attributes: therefore they knew at least two persons.

3. Likewise, this same point seems evident by reason: because the vestige, since it expresses distinction, is a principle for knowing God distinctively or in distinction; but in God there is no distinction except the distinction of persons: therefore through the vestige they were able to know the distinction of persons.

4. Likewise, through the image there is knowledge of the Trinity with respect to order, distinction, and equality; but knowledge through the image is knowledge through creatures: therefore through creatures they were able to know the Trinity.

5. Likewise, knowledge of the hidden properties of creatures is more difficult than knowledge of the plurality of persons, because the former is grasped only by the great and subtle, while the latter is grasped even by the simple and unlearned: therefore if through the visible properties of creatures they were able to arrive at the invisible ones, much more were they able to arrive at the knowledge that persons are multiple. And this is what is said in Wisdom thirteen: "For if they were able to know so much as to evaluate the world, how did they not more easily find its Lord?"

On the contrary: 1. Knowledge of the Trinity is knowledge of faith; but knowledge of faith concerns things that are above reason; and what is above reason cannot be known through creatures: therefore, etc.

2. Likewise, there are only two ways of knowing something about God through creatures — either by affirming what is in the creature or something like it, or by removing; but the Trinity is not known by removal but by positing; but in no creature is there found a plurality of supposits together with unity of essence: therefore, etc.

3. Likewise, written law is above the law of nature, and the book of sacred Scripture is above the book of worldly creation; but no one lacking faith comes to knowledge of the plurality of persons through sacred Scripture: therefore much less through the book of worldly creation.

CONCLUSION.

The trinity of persons is not knowable through creatures, but only the trinity of appropriated attributes — namely unity, truth, and goodness.

I respond: It must be said that the plurality of persons together with the unity of essence is the exclusive property of the divine nature, of which no likeness is or can be found in creatures, nor can it be rationally conceived; and therefore the trinity of persons is in no way knowable through creatures by rationally ascending from creatures to God. But although it has no likeness at all, it does have in creatures something that is believed to be a likeness in some way. Hence I say that the philosophers never knew the trinity of persons through reason, nor even their plurality, unless they had some habitual disposition of faith, as some heretics have; hence what they said, they either said without understanding, or they said it illumined by a ray of faith.

There is another trinity — that of appropriated attributes, namely unity, truth, and goodness — and this they did know, because it has a likeness.

1. To the objection, therefore, that through threefold philosophy the philosophers knew the Trinity: it must be said that it is true that through that and through other things they arrived at knowledge of the appropriated attributes; but believers arrived through it at knowledge of both trinities.

2. To the objection concerning the third sign: it is well said that the wise men are said to have failed at the third sign because they failed in the knowledge of the most powerful effect of goodness — namely redemption.

3. To the other objection: it must be said that the vestige expresses the distinction of essential properties, and to this corresponds the trinity of appropriated attributes — not the trinity of proper attributes or persons.

4. To the objection concerning the image: it must be said that the soul can be known either according to what it is — and this knowledge belongs to reason — or according to what it is as an image — and this knowledge belongs to faith alone.

[Critical apparatus omitted]
