questions.notes:
- **Opening (Q. III / transition):** The chunk opens with the tail of Bonaventure's replies to objections in Question III — specifically replies 1 and 2 concerning the state of innocence and the proper order of knowledge. Translated seamlessly.
- **"Efficient medium / disposing medium" (medium efficiens / disponens):** A key Bonaventurian distinction for reconciling Augustine's claim of immediate divine illumination with the role of creatures as means of knowing God. God is the efficient medium (the active cause of knowledge); creatures are disposing media (occasions or preparatory conditions). Rendered with these technical labels.
- **"Gathered back into himself and elevated above himself" (recolligitur in se et elevatur supra se):** The characteristic Bonaventurian itinerary of the mind: from creatures to self (*in se*) to God (*supra se*). This is the structure of the *Itinerarium mentis in Deum*. Rendered literally to preserve this technical vocabulary.
- **"Creatures as things / as signs" (res / signa):** A recall of the fundamental distinction from Distinction I (Augustine's *De Doctrina Christiana*). Creatures as *res* are inferior to the human being; as *signa* they are media that one passes through and leaves behind on arrival at God.
- **"Trinity of appropriated attributes" (trinitas appropriatorum):** Bonaventure's core conclusion. The trinity knowable through creatures — unity (appropriated to the Father), truth (to the Son), and goodness (to the Holy Spirit) — is not the trinity of *proper* Trinitarian persons (Father, Son, Spirit in their distinct relations) but of attributes *appropriated* to the persons by convention and analogy. Philosophers could arrive at the former; only faith yields the latter.
- **"Habitual disposition of faith" (habitus fidei):** Bonaventure's careful hedge regarding the ancient philosophers who appeared to speak of the Trinity: they either spoke without understanding (i.e., their tripartite philosophy accidentally paralleled Christian doctrine) or had some *habitus fidei* — perhaps through contact with Hebraic tradition or divine illumination. This protects both the exclusivity of faith for Trinitarian knowledge and the possibility of occasional divine illumination outside formal revelation.
- **"Third sign" (tertium signum):** The magicians of Pharaoh failed at the third plague (gnats, Exodus 8:18), interpreted allegorically as failure to know the Holy Spirit or the effect of divine goodness (redemption). Bonaventure takes the latter interpretation: they failed not in knowing a Trinitarian *person* but in knowing the *effect* most proper to the appropriated attribute of goodness.
- **"The book of worldly creation" (liber mundanae creaturae):** Bonaventure's characteristic image of creation as a *liber* — a book in which God's attributes can be read. The argument *a fortiori*: if even the higher "book" of Scripture cannot lead the faithless to Trinitarian knowledge, the lower book of creation certainly cannot. This image recurs throughout the *Itinerarium* and the *Breviloquium*.

DIST. III. PART I. THE SINGLE ARTICLE. QUESTION I.

CONCLUSION.

God, supremely knowable in Himself, would also be supremely knowable by us, if there were no defect on the part of our intellect.

It must be said that God in Himself, as supreme light, is supremely knowable; and as a light that supremely fulfills our intellect, He would be, so far as He Himself is concerned, supremely knowable even by us, unless there were some defect on the part of the knowing power — a defect that is not perfectly removed except by the God-likeness of glory. The arguments that God is knowable by creatures and even most clearly knowable, so far as He Himself is concerned, unless something impedes or is lacking on the part of the intellect, are therefore to be conceded — as will be shown afterward.

1. To the objections raised on the contrary: it must be said that there is knowledge by comprehension and knowledge by apprehension. Knowledge by apprehension consists in the manifestation of the truth of the thing known; but knowledge by comprehension consists in the inclusion of totality.

For the first kind of knowledge, a proportion of fittingness is required; and such proportion exists in the soul with respect to God, because "the soul is in some way all things" — through its assimilation to all things, since it is naturally suited to know all things, and is most capable of God through assimilation, because it is the image and likeness of God. For the second kind of knowledge — knowledge by comprehension — a proportion of equality and equivalence is required; and this does not exist in the soul with respect to God, because the soul is finite while God is infinite; and therefore the soul does not have this proportion. It is of this second kind that Dionysius speaks, and the objection runs against it — but not against the other.

2. To the objection concerning the distance between the intelligible and the sensible: it must be said that distance can be measured according to the account of being and according to the account of the knowable. In the first way there is greater distance; in the second there is not, because both — namely God and the soul — are intelligible. This is not so in the case of intellect and sense, because the sense is a determined power, but the intellect is not.

3. To the objection that the infinite cannot be grasped by the finite: some say that to grasp the infinite is twofold — namely with respect to essence, and in this way the infinite is grasped; and with respect to power, and in this way it is not grasped — just as a point is entirely reached according to substance by a line, but not totally according to power. But this solution does not seem to resolve the difficulty, because in God essence and power are the same, and each is infinite.

Therefore it must be said that infinite is twofold: one kind that stands in opposition to the simple, and such an infinite is not grasped by the finite — this is infinite mass; another kind that has infinity together with simplicity, such as God; and such an infinite, because it is simple, is wholly everywhere, and because it is infinite, is in no thing in such a way that it is not also outside that thing. This is how the cognition of God must be understood. And therefore it does not follow that if He is known wholly, He is comprehended — because the intellect does not include His totality, just as no creature includes His immensity.

4. To the objection that one who judges has power, etc.: it must be said that to judge about something is twofold: in the first way, by discerning whether it is or is not — and in this way judgment belongs to every intellect that knows with respect to every object; in another way, by approving or disapproving whether it ought to be so — and in this way one does not judge about truth, but according to it judges about other things, as Augustine says in On True Religion: "The judge does not judge about the law, but according to it judges about other things." And concerning this mode it is true what Augustine says, that "no one judges about that truth, yet no one judges without it." And it is of this second mode that what is objected holds true — that the one who judges has power over what is judged; but of the first mode it is not true that it has power over it — it can nonetheless be directed toward it as toward an object with the assistance of that truth.

5. To the last objection concerning information: it must be said that God is present to the soul itself and to every intellect through truth; therefore it is not necessary for a likeness to be abstracted from Him by which He may be known. Nevertheless, when He is known by the intellect, the intellect is informed by a certain knowledge, which is as it were a likeness — not abstracted, but impressed — inferior to God, because it is in an inferior nature, yet superior to the soul, because it makes the soul better. And this is what Augustine says in the ninth book On the Trinity, chapter eleven: "Just as when we learn bodies through the senses of the body, some likeness of them is formed in our mind: so when we know God, some likeness of God is formed; yet that knowledge is inferior, because it is in an inferior nature."

[Scholion omitted]

QUESTION II.

Whether God is knowable through creatures.

Second, it is asked whether God is knowable through creatures. And it seems He is not.

1. Because the way to error is not the way to knowledge; but knowledge through creatures is a way to error: therefore, etc. Proof of the minor premise: from Wisdom fourteen: "The creatures of God are a snare and a trap and a stumbling block for the feet of the foolish." Furthermore, Augustine in On Free Will speaks of those who are occupied in creatures: "Turning their back to you, they are fixed in their bodily work as in their own shadow."

2. Likewise, darkness or a dark thing is not a way to knowing what is luminous or light; but the creature is darkness, while God is light: therefore God is not knowable through creatures.

3. Likewise, the middle term through which something is known or proved of an extreme must share in something with that whose knowledge it serves; but Creator and creature have nothing in common: therefore God is not known through creatures.

4. Likewise, every middle term through which one ascends to an extreme is distant from it by a finite number of degrees; but every creature, however noble, is distant from God by infinite degrees — for however much it may be doubled, it will never arrive at His nobility: therefore through creatures one does not ascend to knowledge of God.

On the contrary: 1. From Wisdom thirteen: "From the greatness of the beauty and of the creature the Creator of these things can be seen and known." Hence Isidore in On the Highest Good: "From the beauty of the bounded creature, God causes His own beauty — which cannot be bounded — to be understood."

2. Likewise, it is shown by reason thus: it is possible to know not only the effect through the cause, but also the cause through the effect: therefore if God acts as cause according to His own nobility, and the creature is the effect, God can be known through creatures.

3. Likewise, the sensible is a way of knowing the intelligible; but the creature is sensible and God is intelligible: therefore through the creature one arrives at knowledge of the Creator.

4. Likewise, it is possible to know like through like; but every creature is like God — either as a vestige or as an image: therefore through every creature it is possible to know God.

There is therefore a question as to what the difference is between vestige and image; and since the vestige is in every creature, it is asked why the image is not similarly in every creature, and in what respect the vestige is to be discerned.

CONCLUSION.

God can be known through creatures by the natural light of reason.

I respond: It must be said that, because the cause shines forth in the effect and the wisdom of the craftsman is manifested in his work, God — who is the craftsman and cause of creatures — is known through them.

And for this there are two reasons: one from fittingness and the other from need. From fittingness, because every creature leads more toward God than toward anything else; from need, because since God, as supremely spiritual light, cannot be known in His spirituality by the intellect, which is as it were material, the soul needs to know Him through creatures.

1. To the objection that knowledge of creatures is a way to error: it must be said that knowing creatures is twofold — either with respect to their special properties and those that belong to imperfection, or with respect to their general conditions, which belong to completion. If with respect to the special properties of imperfection: either by attributing them to God, or by removing them. In the first way it is a way of error; in the second way it is a way of knowledge — and in this way God is known through removal.

But if creatures are known with respect to the conditions of perfection, this can happen in two ways — as a painting can be known in two ways: either as a painting, or as an image. Hence one either rests in the beauty of the creature, or through it one tends toward something else. In the first way it is a way of deviation; hence Augustine in On Free Will: "Woe to those who love your signs instead of you, and wander in your vestiges and abandon you who are their guide." In the second way — insofar as it is a way toward something else — it is a principle of knowing through supereminence, because every noble property in a creature is to be attributed to God in the highest degree; and in this way that is clear.

2. To the objection that a dark medium is not a way of knowing light: it must be said that there is a well-disposed eye and a bleary eye. For the well-disposed eye this is true, but not for the bleary one, for which a covering cloud or a reflecting earth serves as a medium for seeing the sun — so it is for our intellect, which is like the eye of an owl with respect to the most manifest things of nature.

3. To the objection concerning the lack of community: it must be said that there is no community by univocation, yet there is community by analogy — which expresses a relation of two things to two things, as in the case of a sailor and a teacher, or of one thing to one, as in the case of an exemplar to what is patterned after it.

4. questions.notes:
- **Opening (Q. I conclusion and replies):** The chunk opens with Bonaventure's *Conclusio* for Question I and replies to the five objections. The *Conclusio* is the resolution of the opening question (whether God is knowable by creatures): God is supremely knowable in Himself; the defect is on our side, fully overcome only by the *deiformitas gloriae* of beatific vision.
- **"Knowledge by apprehension / by comprehension" (cognitio per apprehensionem / per comprehensionem):** A key Bonaventurian distinction drawn from Augustine (*De Videndo Deo* IX.21). Apprehension requires only proportio convenientiae (fittingness); comprehension requires proportio aequalitatis (equality) — the latter impossible for any finite intellect with respect to an infinite God. Dionysius's claim that God cannot be understood applies only to comprehension. Rendered with these technical terms.
- **"The soul is in some way all things" (quodam modo est anima omnia):** The Aristotelian formula from *De Anima* III.8, expressing the intellect's openness to all intelligible form — the ground of the soul's proportio convenientiae with God.
- **Infinite of mass vs. infinite with simplicity:** Bonaventure's second solution to objection 3 distinguishes *infinitum molis* (quantitative infinity, which is opposed to simplicity and cannot be grasped by a finite intellect) from *infinitum cum simplicitate* (God's infinity, which is simple and therefore wholly present everywhere without being bounded). This is a recurring distinction throughout the Trinitarian questions. The point: God can be wholly known without being comprehended, just as God is wholly everywhere without being bounded.
- **"The judge does not judge about the law" (iudex non iudicat de lege):** Augustine, *De Vera Religione* XXXI.58. Bonaventure uses this to distinguish discernment (*discernendo*) — which requires no superiority over the object — from approval/disapproval (*approbando*), which does. The intellect knows God by the first mode; only God employs the second with respect to eternal truth.
- **Reply 5: "not abstracted but impressed" (non abstracta sed impressa):** Bonaventure's careful account of how God is known without species abstraction — the soul receives an *impressed* likeness (not derived from God by abstraction, as from a sensible object, but imprinted by God's presence). This is the basis for the Scholion's long defense against ontologist readings (Malebranche, etc.): divine illumination means participation in a created light that reflects uncreated truth, not direct vision of God.
- **Question II begins:** The second question of the article — whether God is knowable *through* creatures (as opposed to *by* a creature, Question I) — opens with four objections and four *contra* arguments. The chunk ends mid-reply to objection 4. Key discussions: the analogy of the bleary eye (*oculus lippus*) for our intellect's need for creaturely mediation; the analogy/univocation distinction for the objection about lack of community between Creator and creature; the painting/image distinction (one may rest in the creature as in a painting, or pass through it as through an image toward God).
- **"Like the eye of an owl" (sicut oculus noctuae):** Aristotle, *Metaphysics* II.1 — the intellect is to the most manifest things as the owl's eye is to daylight. Bonaventure applies this to show why the soul, despite its natural kinship with God, still needs the mediation of creatures as a cloud or earth mediates the sun's light for a diseased eye.

The first degree with respect to the ascent toward the aspect of presence is in the consideration of visible things; the second in the consideration of invisible things, such as the soul or another spiritual substance; the third is from the soul to God, because "the image is formed by truth itself and is immediately joined to God."

To the question raised last about the difference between vestige and image: some assign this difference by saying that the vestige is in sensible things and the image in spiritual things. But this distinction and position does not hold, because the vestige is also in spiritual things. For unity, truth, and goodness — in which the vestige consists — are the most universal and intelligible conditions.

Others say that it is called a vestige because it represents according to part, and an image because it represents according to the whole. But again this difference does not hold, because since God is simple He has nothing that represents Him according to part; and since He is infinite, He cannot be represented according to the whole by any creature whatsoever — not even by the whole world.

Therefore it must be understood that since a creature leads to the knowledge of God in the manner of a shadow, in the manner of a vestige, and in the manner of an image, the difference among these — from which they also take their name — is more clearly taken according to the mode of representing. For something is called a shadow insofar as it represents in a certain remoteness and confusion; a vestige insofar as it represents in remoteness but with distinction; an image insofar as it represents in nearness and with distinction.

From this first difference a second is derived, which concerns the conditions in which these are found. For creatures are called a shadow with respect to properties that regard God in some genus of causation according to an indeterminate account; a vestige with respect to the property that regards God under the account of a threefold cause — efficient, formal, and final — such as are unity, truth, and goodness; an image with respect to the conditions that regard God not only in the account of cause but also of object — which are memory, understanding, and will.

From these two differences two others follow: the first regarding what they lead to — for a creature as shadow leads to the knowledge of common attributes as common; a vestige to the knowledge of common attributes as appropriated; an image to the knowledge of proper attributes as proper.

The other difference concerns the things in which they are found. For since every creature stands in relation to God both in the account of cause and in the account of threefold cause, every creature is therefore either a shadow or a vestige. But since only the rational creature stands in relation to God as to an object — because it alone is capable of God through knowledge and love — it alone is an image.

[Scholion omitted]

QUESTION III.

Whether the human being in every state knows God through creatures.

Third, it is asked whether knowledge of God through creatures belongs to the human being with respect to every state. That it belongs to the human being with respect to the first state is shown thus:

1. The human being in the state of innocence did not know God face to face: therefore if he knew God, he knew Him through the effect, therefore through the vestige, therefore through creatures.

2. Likewise, in the human being in the state of innocence, sensible cognition was not an impediment but an aid to intellectual cognition; but intellectual cognition — for the sake of which the human being was made — is knowledge of God: therefore every act of sensible cognition in the first human being was ordered toward this; but knowledge of God with the aid of sensible things is knowledge through creatures: therefore, etc.

Likewise, that it belongs to the human being with respect to the state of beatitude seems evident:

1. Because the Blessed know creatures but do not rest in them, but refer them to God: therefore they know God through creatures.

2. Likewise, the blessed souls praise God through creatures; but to praise God through creatures is to know Him through creatures: therefore, etc.

On the contrary — that it does not belong to the human being in the first state — is shown thus:

1. Knowledge through the vestige is knowledge through a medium; "but the mind, as Augustine says, is formed immediately by truth itself": therefore such knowledge does not belong to human nature with respect to that state — nor with respect to any other.

2. Likewise, it is not a proper order that what is nearer should arrive at its end through a more remote medium; but the human being in the first state was nearer to God than all other creatures: therefore it did not befit him to arrive at knowledge of God through other creatures.

Likewise, that such knowledge does not belong to the human being with respect to the state of beatitude seems evident:

1. Because knowledge through the vestige is knowledge through a guiding process: therefore it is not perfect knowledge — therefore it is partial: therefore it does not remain in the Blessed, because in them what is partial will be done away with.

2. Likewise, the vestige or creature is like a ladder for ascending or a road for arriving at God; but when one has arrived at the destination, the road is no longer of use: therefore similarly, when the human being is already above, he has no need of the ladder; but the knowledge of the Blessed is immediately directed toward God: therefore it is not through creatures.

CONCLUSION.

God is known in creatures by those who comprehend — perfectly; by those who are on the way — partially; but God is properly known through creatures by those on the way, and differently before the fall than after.

I respond: For the understanding of what has been said, it must be noted that it is one thing to know God in creatures and another to know Him through creatures. To know God in creatures is to know His presence and influence in creatures. And this belongs to those on the way partially, but to those who comprehend — perfectly; hence Augustine says at the end of the City of God that then God will be seen expressly, when God will be all in all. But to know God through creatures is to be elevated from the knowledge of creatures to the knowledge of God as if by an intermediate ladder. And this belongs properly to those on the way, as Bernard says to Eugenius.

This belongs differently, however, to the human being in the state of established nature and in the state of fallen nature: for in the first state he knew God through creatures as through a clear mirror; but after the fall he knew Him as through a mirror and an enigma, as the Apostle says in the first letter to the Corinthians thirteen — on account of the clouding of the intellect and the deterioration of things.

questions.notes:
- **Opening (Q. II reply 4 continued):** The chunk opens completing the reply to objection 4 of Question II — that creatures are infinitely distant from God in degree and therefore cannot mediate knowledge of Him. Bonaventure's answer: ascent "according to presence" (any creature naturally leads to God; the degrees are not infinite in this sense) vs. ascent "according to equivalence" (in this sense the degrees are infinite, since no creature can be equivalent to the uncreated). Translated seamlessly.
- **Three degrees of ascent (shadow / vestige / image):** Bonaventure elaborates a threefold itinerary: (1) visible things → (2) invisible spiritual substances → (3) the soul immediately conjoined to God as image. This is the structure of the *Itinerarium mentis in Deum* (chapters 1–2, 3–4, 5–7). The Augustine citation is from the *83 Questions* (q. 51): the image is formed by truth itself with no nature interposed.
- **Four differences between shadow, vestige, and image:** A formally presented taxonomy — Bonaventure's own contribution, going beyond the two opinions he rejects:
  (1) **Mode of representing**: shadow = remote + confused; vestige = remote + distinct; image = near + distinct.
  (2) **Conditions**: shadow → indeterminate causal relation; vestige → threefold cause (efficient/formal-exemplary/final) = unity/truth/goodness; image → God as object of knowledge and love = memory/understanding/will.
  (3) **What they lead to**: shadow → common attributes as common; vestige → common attributes as appropriated; image → proper Trinitarian attributes.
  (4) **Where found**: shadow and vestige in every creature; image only in rational creatures.
- **"Formal cause" (causa formalis):** The Quaracchi editors' note clarifies that Bonaventure means extrinsic formal cause (= exemplar cause), not intrinsic formal cause. God is the exemplar of the creature's truth, not its intrinsic form.
- **Question III — three states:** Bonaventure distinguishes the state of innocence (*status naturae institutae*), the fallen state (*status naturae lapsae*), and the state of beatitude (*status beatitudinis* / comprehensors). The *Conclusio* gives a refined answer for each.
- **"Know God in creatures / through creatures" (in creatura / per creaturam):** The key distinction of the *Conclusio* — *in* = knowing God's presence and influence within the creature (belongs to comprehensors perfectly, to wayfarers partially); *per* = using creatures as an intermediate ladder to rise to God (belongs properly only to wayfarers). Bernard's *De Consideratione* V.1 is cited: "Citizens have no need of this ladder, but exiles do."
- **"Clear mirror / mirror and enigma":** 1 Corinthians 13:12. Before the fall: knowledge through a clear mirror (creatures undimmed). After the fall: through an obscured mirror, on account of (*propter*) two factors — the clouding (*obnubilatio*) of the intellect by sin and the deterioration (*peioratio*) of things (creatures themselves become less transparent to God's presence as a result of the disorder introduced by sin). Chunk ends mid-sentence in the reply to the beatitude objection.

CONCLUSION.

The account of image is found in these three powers — memory, intellect, and will — together with comparison to the unity of essence and the plurality of acts.

I respond: It must be said that, as Augustine says and the Master relates, the image is found in these three powers — but in comparison to the unity of essence and the plurality of acts, in which there is distinction and order and an origin of one from another by a certain mode of disposing. For the retention of a species disposes one toward understanding, and understanding disposes one toward loving, if what is understood is good.

1. And from this the solution to the objection that in these powers there is no distinction by origin is clear.

2. To the objection that image is found according to exterior disposition: it must be said that there is an image of a corporeal and sensible thing — and this, since it offers itself to cognition through external features, has an image that represents according to exterior disposition. There is also an image of a spiritual thing, which is most interior to each thing and is known according as the power is gathered back to interior things; and this has an image that represents with respect to interior dispositions.

3. To the objection that memory concerns sensible things: it must be said that memory is taken in three ways — in one way as receptive and retentive of sensible and past things; in another way as retentive of past things, whether sensible or intelligible; and in a third way as retentive of species, abstracting from every temporal difference — namely of innate species. And in this third way it is part of the image; but the objection runs against the other first two ways. In the first way memory follows sense; in the second way it follows understanding and will; in the third way it precedes and corresponds to the Father.

4. To the objection that memory is not reformed: it must be said that on the contrary memory is reformed, both with respect to the state of the way and with respect to the state of the homeland — in the first by hope; and this is clear through Augustine's exposition on that word of Matthew twenty-two: "You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart — that is, with intellect without error; with your whole soul — that is, with will without contradiction; with your whole mind — that is, with memory without forgetfulness." In the second state it is reformed with respect to retention; hence Bernard says that "God will be for the understanding a fullness of light, for the will a multitude of peace, for memory a continuity of eternity." Nor is it incongruous that memory, though it is first, is reformed through the last gift; because the order of reformation and deformation begins from the later, while the order of formation begins from the higher — and therefore reformation begins from the will and extends to memory.

5. To the objection that the image is in the power of knowing: it must be said that likeness denotes something gratuitous, and is therefore said to be in the will or in love through appropriation. The image, however, does not denote what is gratuitous, and is therefore said to be in the power of knowing.

Or alternatively, concerning the image: because the proper image is in the Son, and understanding — which is in the cognitive power — is appropriated to the Son, the image is therefore said to be in the power of knowing.

6. To the objection that the will is not equal to understanding: it must be said that the will, as it is taken commonly for willing and not-willing — both of which are acts of the will — is well equalized, insofar as it is said to be common to both, as Augustine says and is held in the text: that the will grasps other things when I use, etc. For whatever we remember or understand, we take into the capacity of the will for choosing or rejecting; and this is according to what it denotes as the common act of the will. But according to the special act, which is willing alone, it is not equalized; and the objection runs concerning this, because willing in this sense does not comprehend the whole will, just as remembering comprehends the whole memory and understanding the whole understanding.

QUESTION II.

Whether the image is found in these powers through their comparison to God.

Second, a question is asked concerning the powers in comparison to their object — namely whether the image is found in them through their comparison to God. And it seems that it is.

1. "The soul is an image precisely insofar as it is capable of God and can be a participant in Him," as Augustine says in the fourteenth book On the Trinity; but it is capable insofar as it pertains to the superior part: therefore, etc.

2. Likewise, in the same work: "The image of that nature than which nothing is better is to be sought and found in us where our nature has nothing better"; but this is the superior part: therefore, etc.

3. Likewise, the same point seems evident by reason, because an image is so called insofar as it leads to the prototype; therefore since that prototype is God, the image is not found in these powers except insofar as they lead to God; but through these powers the human being is led to God, when through them he is converted toward Him: therefore, etc.

4. Likewise, God is the object of the theological virtues, in which the image of reformation consists: therefore, since the object of both images is the same — because one leads toward and perfects the other — if God is the object of one, He is also the object of the other.

On the contrary: 1. Augustine in the ninth book On the Trinity assigns the image in mind, knowledge, and love, according as the soul remembers itself, understands itself, loves itself: therefore it seems that the image is found through the conversion of the soul upon itself.

2. Likewise, Augustine in the twelfth book On the Trinity, chapter four: "When we seek the Trinity in the nature of the human mind, we seek it in the whole mind, not separating the action of temporal things from the contemplation of eternal things so as to seek some third thing": therefore the trinity of the image is found according to the action of temporal things, and thus through conversion toward lower things.

3. Likewise, according as the soul is converted upon lower things or upon itself, in it there is equality and order and origin and everything that concurs to the account of image.

4. Likewise, the image is in sinners who are turned away from God, and even in those who cannot return at all, such as the damned: therefore the account of image is not found according to conversion toward God.

5. Likewise, for the perfect account of image it is necessary that the knower and the known be equalized, or the one expressing and the one expressed — for these two represent the Father and the Son; but in conversion toward God there is no such equalization: therefore, etc.

CONCLUSION.

The image is primarily and principally in the powers of the soul insofar as they are converted toward God; secondarily in them insofar as they are converted toward the soul itself; but insofar as they are converted toward lower things, the image is not in them — but the vestige of the Trinity.

I respond: For the understanding of the foregoing, three things must be presupposed in the account of image: first, the image is found according to express conformation to the thing imaged; second, that what is conformed to the image is consequently conformed to the original — hence one who sees the image of Peter consequently also sees Peter; third, that the soul according to its powers is rendered conformed to those things toward which it is converted, whether according to knowledge or according to love.

Since therefore, when the soul is converted toward God it is conformed to Him, and the image is found according to conformity: therefore the image of God consists in these powers insofar as they have God as their object.

Again, since the soul is the image of God, and what is conformed to the image is also conformed to the original, therefore the soul, insofar as it is converted upon itself, does not depart from conformity; and therefore the image consists in these powers insofar as they have the soul itself as their object.

But when it is converted toward lower creatures, it is conformed to them — in which there is not the image of God, but the vestige. Therefore the powers of the soul, insofar as they have lower things as their objects, depart from the account of image, because they depart from express conformity.

Although therefore in these powers, insofar as they are converted toward lower things, one can find a trinity and some conformity — as Augustine shows — yet since they fall short of express conformity, the account of image is not found in them. Hence Augustine investigates the trinity in all the powers of the soul — not because the image is in them, but in order to exclude them from the account of image. Hence, seeking the whole trinity in the whole soul, he seeks it in the superior and inferior part of reason and in sense. And this is what he says in that authority: "When we seek the Trinity in the nature of the human mind, we seek it in the whole" — he does not say "we seek the image." Hence Augustine says in the twelfth book On the Trinity, chapter four: "Although a trinity can be found in the inferior part of reason, the image cannot be found there."

It must be conceded, therefore, that the image consists in these powers insofar as they are converted toward the soul, but first and principally — as the first arguments show — insofar as they are converted toward God. Hence Augustine assigns the image in two ways: the first is in mind, knowledge, and love, according as the mind knows and loves itself; the second is in memory, understanding, and will. And at the end of his book he shows that the most complete account of image is found in comparison to God.

1. 2. 3. From these things the response to the first and second and third objections is clear: because the first argument is to be conceded, the second concludes that there is a trinity in the inferior part, and the third that there is conformity — but these have been resolved, because this conformity is not express.

4. To the objection concerning the aversion of sinners: it must be said that we do not speak of the image in these powers according to actual conversion, but according to aptitudinal conversion, which never abandons the powers — just as a human being is called capable of walking even if his feet are cut off, though he does not walk.

5. To the objection that in the image it is necessary for the knower and the known to be equalized: it must be said that it is not necessary for the known to be equalized to the knower by the equalization of thing to thing, but under the account of the knowable. Hence the known is in the understanding to the extent that it is represented by memory. That it should be simply equal is not required; yet it is equalized insofar as the soul is converted upon itself. Hence the account of image has something more in the conversion toward God, and something more in the conversion of the soul upon itself. In the conversion toward God it has more, because it has more of the account of beauty and conformity; in the conversion toward itself it has more of the account of consubstantiality and equality.

[Scholion omitted]

QUESTION III.

Whether memory, understanding, and will are the same in essence as the soul.

Third, a question is asked concerning the comparison of these powers to the soul or subject — namely whether they are the same in essence as the soul. And it seems they are.

1. Augustine says in the tenth book On the Trinity: "These three — memory, understanding, and will — are one mind, one life, one essence, and therefore one substance."

2. Likewise, Bernard in the Sermons on the Canticles: "I see three things in the soul — memory, understanding, and will — and these three are the soul itself." If you say that this is said causally, this amounts to nothing, because Augustine in On the Spirit and the Soul says that the soul "is, as it were, certain things that are its own — such as its powers — and certain things that are not its own — such as its virtues"; which if it were said causally, both could be so said.

3. Likewise, the Philosopher seems to want to say the same thing, because he says that the principle of being and the principle of operating are the same: therefore since the principle of being is the substantial form itself, the principle of operating will also be it; but the principle of operating is the power: therefore the power is the principle of being; but there is no principle of being except the substantial form in the human being: therefore power and substantial form are the same in substance.

4. Likewise, it is shown by reason: just as prime matter is naturally suited to receive all things in truth, so the soul according to likeness; but the potency of prime matter with respect to the forms to be received does not differ in essence from matter itself: therefore similarly it seems that the potency of the soul does not differ from the soul itself. Proof: for if it differed in essence, it would be either substance or accident. Not accident, because it precedes every form and every accident; if substance, then it is either matter or form. Furthermore, if it differed, there would have to be some matter capable of it.

5. Likewise, an accidental form is not simpler than a substantial form; but the power of operating does not differ from an accidental form — for the power of heating does not differ in essence from heat, nor the power of illuminating from light itself: therefore similarly it seems that the power of the soul does not differ from the soul itself.

6. Likewise, what is an accident is not substantial to any substance; but these powers are substantial: therefore they are not accidents of the soul: therefore they are substances — clearly none other than the soul itself. Proof of the minor: because in the human being the rational, sensible, and vegetative soul does not express a diversity of substances but of powers: therefore it is clear that in the human being these differences — vegetative, sensible, rational — are derived from the powers; but such differences are substantial: therefore the powers also are substantial: therefore, etc.

On the contrary: 1. Augustine in the fifteenth book On the Trinity assigns the difference of the created image from the Trinity — that is, the uncreated one — namely that in that Trinity the one having is what is had, whereas here the one having is not what is had: therefore if the soul has three powers, it is not essentially those powers.

2. Likewise, Dionysius says that in every created thing these three differ: substance, power, and operation: therefore in the soul also substance and powers differ.

3. Likewise, Boethius: "In every created thing that by which it is and that which it is differ" — or "what it is and its being": therefore similarly, and indeed much more so, that which it can do and that by which it can do.

4. Likewise, it is shown by reason: those that differ in genus differ in essence, and one is not predicated of the other essentially; but the powers and the soul are such, because the soul is in the genus of substance while its powers are in the second species of quality — namely natural power or impotence: therefore, etc.

5. Likewise, those things of which one is outside the other differ essentially and substantially; but power goes out beyond substance, because it operates upon an object that is outside; but it is impossible for it to operate where it is not; if therefore power is where it operates, and it operates outside the substance of each thing: therefore it goes out beyond substance: therefore, etc.

6. Likewise, for this there is another argument: if the soul and its powers were the same in essence, then one would be multiplied only according to the multiplication of the other; and so, since there is only one soul, it would have only one power; but this is false: therefore, etc.

CONCLUSION.

The powers of the soul are substantial and are in the same genus by reduction as the soul; they are not, however, altogether the same in essence as the soul itself.

I respond: For the understanding of what has been said, it must be noted that natural power is spoken of in two ways. In one way, as it denotes the mode of the existence of natural power in a subject — according to which the subject is said to be easy or difficult at doing something; and in this sense natural power denotes a mode of quality and is generally in the second species of quality, as is evident when one speaks of a runner and a boxer, each of which denotes a facility that follows from the mode of existence of the power of walking or of resisting or acting in a subject. In another way natural power is said to be a power naturally proceeding from a subject. And this can be of two kinds. For some power proceeds from a substance along with an accident, such as the power of heating — for fire does not heat through its substance alone but through heat; and this power is not of a different genus than the quality from which it proceeds; hence the power of heating is in the same genus as heat. In another way, natural power is that which naturally and immediately proceeds from the substance, such as the power of generating with respect to the induction of the ultimate form; and this indeed is not of a different genus than the substance, but is reduced to the genus of substance as a substantial difference.

This is how it must be understood in the case of the soul's powers. For in one way the soul's powers can be named according to the first mode — as they denote a facility, which denotes the mode of existence of the power in a subject, such as cleverness and slowness; and these are in the second species of quality. In another way the powers can be named insofar as they denote the order of substance to act, which is mediated by some accidental property, such as the power of syllogizing — which is in the soul when it has the habit of syllogizing; and this is in the same genus as the science of syllogizing, namely in the first species of quality. Again, one can name the powers of the soul as they immediately proceed from the substance — as in these three: memory, understanding, and will. And this is clear, because with every accident set aside, once it is understood that the soul is a spiritual substance, by the very fact that it is present to itself and joined to itself, it has the power to remember and understand and love itself. Hence these powers are consubstantial to the soul and are in the same genus by reduction as the soul. Yet since they proceed from the soul — for a power comports itself in the manner of what proceeds — they are not altogether the same in essence, nor yet do they differ so as to belong to a different genus, but they are in the same genus by reduction.

And a sufficiently clear example can be given in a thing and its likeness. For a thing does not have so great an identity with its likeness that they are numerically one, nor so great a diversity that they differ in genus. For the likeness of Martin is not so distant from Martin as to differ entirely from him. And so the likeness of a thing is in the same genus by reduction as that of which it is a likeness. Because it proceeds, it differs — but it does not pass into another genus. And I speak of likeness according to the account of likeness, not of intention — that is, as it proceeds from the subject and does not withdraw, like a radiance from a light. The arguments proving that the soul is not its powers through essence are therefore to be conceded.

1. and 2. To the objection therefore from Augustine and Bernard that the soul is its powers: it must be said that there is no predication of accident of subject there, nor of the same thing of itself through essence, but a substantial or essential predication.

For this it must be noted that "essential" is said in four ways. In the first way, essential denotes that which expresses the entire essence of a thing, such as the individual species. In the second way, essential denotes what belongs to the essence and constitution of a thing, such as matter and form. In the third way, essential denotes what a thing cannot be or be understood to be without — such as those things in which the account of vestige is found, namely unity, truth, and goodness. In the fourth way, essential denotes what a thing cannot be thought to have perfect being without — such as the powers in the soul, in which the image is found; and this is the least way of being substantial or essential — yet it does not pass into another genus: therefore the soul is said to be its powers.

questions.notes:
- **Opening (Q. I, continued objections 3–6):** The chunk opens with the tail of the sixth objection from the prior chunk's Question I. Objections 3–6 concern memory (temporal, hence not suitable for the image), theological virtues (not in memory), will (book *On the Spirit and the Soul* assigns image only to cognitive power), and equality (will is not equally activated by all objects). Translated seamlessly.
- **"Memory in three senses" (memoria tripliciter):** Bonaventure's key distinction resolving the Aristotelian objection: (1) receptive memory of past sensible things (follows sense); (2) retentive memory of intelligibles as past (follows understanding and will); (3) retentive of innate species, abstracting from time (precedes, corresponds to the Father). Only the third sense belongs to the image. This threefold distinction is a Bonaventurian original within the scholastic tradition.
- **"Order of reformation / order of formation":** A subtle distinction in reply 4: deformation (sin) and reformation (grace) begin from the will (the last in the psychological order), since sin is first a disorder of love; but formation (natural constitution of the image) begins from memory (the first/deepest power). This is why hope reforms memory: both involve "retention" or "holding" (*tentio*). Bernard is cited (*In Cant.* Serm. II.5).
- **Question II — three conclusions:** Bonaventure gives a graduated answer: (1) the image is *primarily* in the powers insofar as they are converted toward God (the most complete image); (2) *secondarily* insofar as they are converted toward the soul itself (Augustine's first assignment, *De Trin.* IX); (3) *not at all* insofar as they are converted toward lower creatures (there only the vestige is found). This is the framework of the *Itinerarium* I–IV.
- **"Aptitudinal conversion" (conversio aptitudinalis):** Key term in reply 4 to the objection from sinners and the damned: the image is not destroyed by turning away from God in act (*conversio actualis*) because it consists in an aptitude or capacity that remains even in the damned. The image can be deformed but not destroyed. Illustrated by the analogy of one who is "capable of walking" even with amputated feet.
- **Question III — powers and the soul's essence:** Bonaventure's *Conclusio* — the powers are neither purely identical to the soul (as Augustine and Bernard's language might suggest) nor accidental qualities distinct in genus from it. They are *consubstantial* to the soul, in the same genus by reduction (*per reductionem*), proceeding from the soul as a radiance proceeds from light. The four senses of "essential" are a key technical passage: only in the weakest (fourth) sense are the powers "essential" to the soul — not constituting but required for perfect being.
- **Chunks ends mid-reply:** The text ends mid-sentence in reply 3 to Question III's third objection. Translated as given.

DIST. III. PART II. ARTICLE I. QUESTION III. (continued)

For if the proximate principle were altogether the same, then being and operating would be the same in the thing. Similarly, if the proximate principle were the same, since a thing always has being, it would always have operating. Since therefore form denotes the proximate and immediate principle of being, while power denotes the proximate and immediate principle of operating, it is clear that it is impossible for them to be altogether the same.

4. To the other objection concerning the potency of matter: it must be said that matter is not its own potency through essence, since it is not itself the ordering toward form; yet the potency of matter is essential to matter itself, just as active power is to a substance. And indeed the potency of matter is less removed from matter than active power is from substance; for the potency of matter is a passive potency, which denotes an ordering toward another with privation, while active power denotes an ordering with a positive act — and therefore the potency of matter adds less beyond matter than active power adds beyond substance. And hence it is that diverse potencies are not so distinguished in the same matter as they are in the same substance.

5. To the objection concerning accidental form: it must be said that an accidental form is not its own potency. For its potency is its capacity to flow into another; yet that potency does not add as much as the potency of a substantial form, since the potency of an accidental form denotes an ordering toward act, but not one sufficient through itself, but rather through the power of substance. For just as an accident is not through itself, so it does not have the power of operating through itself, but through the power of substance — and so this is clear.

6. To the last objection: it must be said that the powers of the soul are not accidental. Yet the argument does not hold, because perhaps the rational, sensible, and vegetable are not derived from the powers but from diverse natures found in the soul.

That argument, however, which was made on the opposite side — that the powers differ because they are in diverse genera — must be resolved by destruction of the premise, because they are not in diverse genera but in the same one by reduction.

[Scholion omitted]

ARTICLE II.

On the second assignment of the image.

Next there is a question about the second assignment of the image through mind, knowledge, and love. And concerning this three things are asked.

The first is about these absolutely — namely whether the image is found in them as in powers, or in habits, or in powers and habits together, or in substance and habits.

The second is about these in comparison to one another.

The third is whether this trinity of the image necessarily leads to knowledge of the Trinity with respect to the persons.

QUESTION I.

Whether the image is found in mind, knowledge, and love as in powers, or as in habits, or in both together, or according to substance and habits.

Concerning the first the discussion proceeds thus.

1. It is shown first that the image is not found in these as in powers, because the foregoing assignment was in the powers: therefore if this one were also in powers, there would be nothing but a repetition of words.

Moreover, knowledge and love do not denote a power but habits, although mind can denote a power: therefore the aforesaid three cannot be posited under the account of powers.

2. Likewise, it is shown that they do not denote habits, because Augustine says in his assignment and approbation of the image: "The mind knows itself, loves itself"; but no habit's act is to know itself or to love itself: therefore, etc.

Likewise, if mind stands for a habit, I ask for which habit. If for the habit of memory — which seems more likely, since no other can be given — but the act of this habit is to remember, and no other; yet Augustine assigns to mind these acts, namely knowing and loving: therefore, etc.

3. Likewise, it is shown that the image is not in powers and habits together. For since the powers are three and the habits are three, there would not be a ternary but a senary.

4. Likewise, I ask for which power mind stands in that formula. For it stands either for all, or for two, or for one. If for all, then there is no trinity there; if for two, then there is a quaternity, since there are two habits; if for one, then it cannot have those two acts — knowing and loving: therefore the trinity is not taken according to habits and powers together.

1. Likewise, it is shown that the image is not according to the soul's substance and habits together. For since the habits of knowing and loving follow from the substance itself in time, and the substance can also exist without these habits, while the account of image is perpetual, inseparable, and co-created with the soul itself: therefore the image is not in habits and substance together.

questions.notes:
- **Opening (Q. III replies 3–6, continued):** The chunk opens completing the replies to Question III's objections. Reply 3 establishes that being and operating must have distinct proximate principles (form and potency respectively), since otherwise a thing would always be operating whenever it exists. Reply 4 distinguishes the potency of matter (passive, with privation) from the active potency of substance — the latter "adds" more to substance than the former adds to matter. Reply 5 argues that accidental forms also depend on the substance's power to operate, so the analogy between heat's power to heat and the soul's powers fails (it would only show dependence, not identity). Reply 6 dismisses the argument from *rational/sensible/vegetable* being substantial differences.
- **"Destruction of the premise" (interemptio):** Bonaventure uses the scholastic term *interemptio* for the refutation of an argument by denying one of its premises outright (as opposed to *distinctio*, which distinguishes a true from a false reading). The powers and the soul are not in diverse genera but in the same genus by reduction — so the premise of the final contrary argument is simply false. The Scholion explains this term via Peter of Spain's *Summulae*.
- **Article II — second assignment of the image:** The structure of Distinction III Part II shifts here. Article I concerned the first Augustinian assignment (memory/understanding/will as the soul's three powers). Article II concerns the second assignment (*De Trinitate* IX): mind (*mens*), knowledge (*notitia*), and love (*amor*) — taken not as distinct powers but as the soul knowing and loving itself. Three questions follow: (1) are these powers, habits, or what? (2) their mutual comparison; (3) whether this trinity proves the personal Trinity.
- **Question I — four options rejected in the arguments:** A formally elegant dialectical structure presents four possible interpretations of mind/knowledge/love and eliminates each: (a) pure powers — ruled out because it would duplicate Article I's treatment; (b) pure habits — ruled out because Augustine assigns self-knowledge and self-love to *mens* itself, not to a habit; (c) powers plus habits — ruled out because three powers + three habits = six, not three; (d) substance plus habits — ruled out because habits are temporally acquired while the image is co-created and perpetual. Bonaventure's own solution (not yet reached in this chunk) will locate the image in the soul's substance as known and loved by itself.
- **Chunk ends mid-argument:** The chunk ends mid-sentence in the second argument against the fourth option (substance + habits). The *Conclusio* and full resolution of Article II, Question I are in the next chunk.

DIST. III. PART II. ARTICLE II. QUESTION I. (continued)

there would be a quaternity. If you say that knowledge does not differ according as it is a habit of understanding and of memory — on the contrary: habits are dispositions of powers; since therefore there are three powers, there will be three habits.

3. Likewise, the Master says in the text that mind is taken not for the substance of the soul but for what is more eminent in it.

CONCLUSION.

In this second assignment of the image — which is mind, knowledge, love — the trinity is found with respect to the substance of the soul and with respect to two habits of knowledge and love.

I respond: It must be said that this assignment differs from the preceding one, according to some, because the prior was in the powers, while this one is in the habits. And they respond to the objections through a distinction of mind. For "mind" is diversified according to four modes of reception. It is said in one way from *mene*, which means moon or deficiency — and in this sense it is said of the whole substance of the soul on account of the changes it undergoes. In a second way it is said from "measuring" — and in this sense it stands for the judging power, and this is how Damascene takes it, placing it among the cognitive powers. In a third way it is said from "excelling" — and in this sense it stands for the superior part of reason, and this is how Augustine frequently takes it. In a fourth way it is said from "remembering" — and in this sense it stands for memory both with respect to act and with respect to habit. They say therefore that in the assignment of this trinity "mind" stands for the habit of memory; but in the application, when Augustine says "mind knows itself and loves itself," it stands for the power of remembering.

But this does not seem to be fittingly said, because the application ought to correspond to the assignment. And moreover, since the proper act of mind, as it stands for memory, is to remember, that act ought to be mentioned; but Augustine in this assignment never makes mention of anything except two acts, namely knowing and loving — which are not of memory but of other powers.

It must therefore be responded that that trinity is not in the powers — because love and knowledge do not denote powers; nor is it in habits — because mind cannot stand for a habit, since it is taken as the agent; nor can it be in both powers and habits, because mind cannot stand for one power, since acts of two powers are assigned to it; nor similarly can it stand for several powers, because then there would be no trinity.

It remains, therefore, that one must necessarily hold that this trinity is found with respect to the substance of the soul — by reason of the mind knowing and loving itself — and with respect to habits — by reason of knowledge and love; and so there is a trinity, since the substance is one and the habits are two.

This assignment therefore differs from the preceding one — because the preceding was through uniformity in the powers with comparison to habits and acts, while this one is in substance and habits. It differs further in that the preceding was through the conversion of the soul toward God, while this one is through the conversion of the soul upon itself; and the image in the human being is not found in multiple ways in the same manner, as was said above. It differs also in that the preceding assignment of the image is more proper and fitting than this one. For properly speaking, the image consists in the unity of essence and the trinity of powers, according to which the soul is naturally suited to be sealed by that supreme Trinity with the image of likeness — which consists in grace and the theological virtues. Hence Augustine places this assignment first in his investigation, in order through it to arrive at that other one in which he completes his speculation. Hence this assignment is not proper in the same way as the other; and therefore the Master places it second as something non-principal.

1. To the objection, therefore, that habits are not coeval, etc.: it must be said that habit is threefold. For a power of the soul has a certain habit from acquisition, a certain one from innate disposition, and a third from its own origin. And this is clear, because a habit is that by which a power is ready for act; but a power is ready in these three ways — for example, our affective power has facility for loving another's good through acquired disposition, such as through virtue; for loving its own good through innate disposition; and for loving itself through its natural origin. For since it is inseparably united to itself, it is always disposed toward loving itself. Similarly, since our intellect is always present to itself, it is always disposed toward knowing itself. And so the objection concerning coevity is resolved — for with respect to such habits, coevity holds well.

2. To the objection that there ought to be three habits corresponding to three powers: it must be said that in this trinity there is no place for a habit of memory, because the trinity is found in the soul itself according as it is converted upon itself — and therefore the very substance of the soul takes the place of memory, and the very presence and offering by which the soul always presents itself to its own understanding takes the place of the habit and act of memory. And so it is clear that only the habits of two powers fall there; and therefore there is a trinity.

3. To the last objection concerning the Master's word: it must be said that "mind" there is understood not for the whole substance of the soul. And if it were understood otherwise, the Master's word would not be true. This is clear through Augustine, who, on the occasion of this image, throughout nearly the entire tenth book On the Trinity shows that the soul has an innate knowledge of itself, which is knowledge of its own substance. And furthermore, nothing in the soul knows and loves except the substance: therefore if mind were to stand for one power, it would not have those two acts — namely knowing and loving.

[Scholion omitted]

questions.notes:
- **Opening (Q. I, continued objections 2–3):** The chunk opens with the tail of a prior question's objections — arguments 2 and 3 against the identification of the second Augustinian image-assignment (mind/knowledge/love) with a simple trio of habits. Translated seamlessly.
- **Four etymologies of "mens":** Bonaventure catalogs four derivations current in scholastic tradition: (1) from *mene* (moon/defect) = the whole mutable soul; (2) from *metiendo* (measuring) = the judging cognitive faculty (Damascene's usage); (3) from *eminendo* (excelling) = the superior part of reason (Augustine's frequent usage); (4) from *meminisse* (remembering) = memory in act and habit. The solution hinges on which sense is operative in Augustine's formula *mens novit se et diligit*. This taxonomy derives from the *De Spiritu et Anima* c. 11 and Isidore's *Etymologiae* XI.1.
- **The resolution — substance + two habits:** Bonaventure rejects two positions (the trinity is in powers alone; or in habits alone) and proposes that in the second Augustinian assignment, "mind" (*mens*) stands for the *substance* of the soul itself (not a power), while *notitia* (knowledge) and *amor* (love) stand for two consubstantial habits. This yields a trinity of one substance + two habits. The Scholion cites Bonaventure's own anecdote from the Prologue to *II Sentences* where he explicitly defends this interpretation against the charge of contradicting the Master.
- **Difference from the first assignment:** Bonaventure draws three contrasts between the two Augustinian image-assignments:
  (1) The first (memory/understanding/will) is in *powers* compared to habits/acts; the second (mind/knowledge/love) is in *substance* and habits.
  (2) The first is through conversion toward *God* (the most complete image); the second is through conversion of the soul upon *itself*.
  (3) The first is *more proper* — the image properly consists in the unity of essence and trinity of powers naturally suited to receive the seal of Trinitarian likeness through grace. The second is preliminary, as Augustine's own order of investigation confirms.
- **Threefold habit (ab acquisitione / ab innata dispositione / a sui ipsius origine):** The reply to objection 1 introduces a threefold taxonomy of habits to explain how the soul's self-knowledge and self-love can be "habitual" without being acquired: the third kind of habit — arising from the soul's own origin — is coeval with the soul, since the soul is always immediately present to itself and thus always disposed to know and love itself. This is the sense in which *notitia* and *amor* are described as "consubstantial" habits.
- **"The soul always understands itself":** The Scholion (omitted per brief) addresses whether the soul's self-knowledge is actual or merely habitual — a contested question among Bonaventure, Aquinas, Scotus, and Richard of Mediavilla. Bonaventure's position (noted by the Scholion) is that the intellect is always *in first act* ready to know itself, not necessarily *in second act* (actual intellection), which requires attention.
