questions.titleEn: Whether this expression can be admitted: God generates another God
questions.latin:
<!-- page 99 -->

**QUAESTIO II.** *Utrum admitti possit haec locutio:* Deus generat alium Deum.

Secundo quaeritur, utrum unitas essentiae admittat hanc: *Deus generat alium Deum*. Et quod non, videtur.

1. Anselmus *de Processione Spiritus sancti*[^1]: «Cum dicimus Deum de Deo, non intelligimus alium Deum, sed eundem de se ipso».

2. Item, si genuit alium Deum — sed ubi est unus et alius, ibi sunt duo: ergo si genuit alium, sunt duo dii.

3. Item, *alius* dicit alietatem in generali; ergo cum generale specificetur per adiunctum, hoc nomen *Deus* specificat ipsum; sed si specificat, specificat ratione formae: ergo notatur alietas in forma: ergo non est admittenda talis locutio, cum non sit ibi alietas in forma.

**Sed contra.**

1. Generatio importat distinctionem[^2]; sed distinctio alietatem aliquam: ergo et generatio; ergo si haec est vera: *Deus genuit Deum*, et haec per consequens: *Deus distinguitur a Deo*, vel *genuit alium Deum*. Si dicas, quod non sequatur, quia generare importat distinctionem ut modum, sed distingui vel esse alium ut rem; contra: ad

<!-- page 100 -->

consequentiam ut modum sequitur consecutio ut res; unde si haec est vera: *si homo est, animal est*[^3], ad hominem sequitur animal. Et praeterea, constat quod distinctio generationis non tantum est a parte intelligentis, verum etiam a parte rei: ergo illi distinctioni ut exercitae respondet distinctio realis.

2. Item, affirmativa est falsa: *Deus genitus est Deus generans*; ergo negativa est vera: *Deus genitus non est Deus generans*. Sed sicut affirmativa significat identitatem, ita negativa diversitatem: ergo sicut Deum generantem et genitum contingit ad invicem comparari mediante negatione, ita mediante alietate: ergo haec est vera: *Deus genuit alium Deum*.

3. Item, *Pater sive Deus genuit alium*; haec est vera, constat: ergo aut *alium Deum*, aut *alium non Deum*; sed non *alium non Deum*: ergo etc.

4. Item, *alius* est terminus masculini generis[^4]; sed terminus masculini generis stat pro persona in partitivis terminis: ergo *alius* dicit alietatem personalem; sed haec est vera: *Deus genuit Deum alium in persona*; ergo simpliciter est vera haec: *Deus genuit alium Deum*.

**Conclusio.**

*In stricto verborum sensu falsa est locutio:* Deus genuit alium Deum.

**Respondeo.** Dicendum, quod haec consuevit distingui: *Deus genuit alium Deum*, quia *alius* potest teneri adiective; et sic ponit alietatem circa formam istius termini *Deus*, et sic locutio est falsa; potest etiam teneri substantive[^5], ut substantivetur; et tunc est appositiva constructio, sicut *animal homo*, et est sensus hoc modo: *Deus genuit alium Deum*, id est, genuit alium qui est Deus; et in hoc sensu est locutio vera.

Sed licet ista distinctio in locutionibus theologicis propter quendam proprium modum loquendi locum habeat, tamen quantum esset de virtute[^6] sermonis, non esset distinguenda; quia adiectivum adiunctum substantivo, ut *homo albus*, non dicitur substantivari, nec appositiva constructio dicitur ibi esse[^7], maxime cum illa sit minus communis respectu magis communis. Unde cum hoc nomen *alius* sit adiectivum habens substantivum coniunctum, in praedicta locutione ponit alietatem circa ipsum ratione suppositi et formae.

Et propterea, si velimus artificialiter[^8] procedere, iudicanda est talis locutio falsa. Propter hoc ad intelligentiam dictae locutionis notanda est regula communis: *non habet locum*[^9] *distinctio, ubi non est ex diversis causis unio* — verbi gratia, Pater et Filius et Spiritus sanctus uniuntur in hoc nomine *Deus*, non ex diversis causis sive ratione diversorum, sed ratione unius deitatis sive essentiae. Unio ex diversis causis est, ut in homine uniuntur Petrus et Ioannes ratione diversarum humanitatum, quia alia est humanitas Petri, et alia Ioannis.

Et iuxta hanc regulam ab oppositis[^10] est alia regula accipienda: *non habet locum omnimoda unio, ubi est simul cum unione distinctio*, ut Pater et Filius et Spiritus sanctus uniuntur in una deitate sive essentia, sed distinctionem habent ratione pluralitatis personarum.

Secundum hoc est attendendum, quod in divinis quaedam vocabula important distinctionem solum, quaedam omnimodam unionem, quaedam medio modo. Quoniam igitur *Deus generans* et *Deus genitus*, etsi sint personaliter distincti, tamen in deitate uniuntur ex eadem causa, quia una deitate: ideo non recipiuntur[^11] nomina importantia simpliciter distinctionem. Ideo haec non admittitur: *Deus distinguitur a Deo*; similiter: *Deus genuit alium Deum*. Item, ratione distinctionis non recipiuntur vocabula omnimodam importantia unionem in supposito et forma: unde haec non recipitur: *Deus genuit se*. Sed illa quae medio modo se habent, recipiuntur, quale est hoc verbum *generat*, quia dicit distinctionem in persona cum[^12] unitate essentiae. Similiter haec conceditur: *Pater generat alterum se*. Unde Augustinus *ad Maximinum*[^13]: «Pater genuit alterum se»; et similiter super Ioannem: «Pater mittens Filium misit alterum se». Et ex hoc est, quod non sequitur ad verbum simpliciter importans distinctionem; et sic patet primum.

**Ad 2.** Ad illud quod secundo obiicitur de negatione, bene concedo, quod est alietas; sed tamen non sequitur, quod possit dici alietas in essentia sive forma deitatis. Unde non sequitur: *genitus est alius a generante, ergo*[^14] *alius Deus*, quia mutatur suppositio huius termini *Deus*.

<!-- page 101 -->

**Ad 3.** Ad illud quod obiicitur tertio: *aut alium Deum, aut alium non Deum*; dico, quod non sufficienter dividit; quia non est contradictio, nisi accipiatur negatio respectu totius. In hac enim: *genuit alium Deum*, duo dicuntur, scilicet quod *Deus*[^15] *Deum*, et quod *alium* in deitate: et ideo ad hoc, quod sumatur contradictio, necesse est, quod feratur supra totum. Unde sicut non valet, demonstrato monacho nigro qui est albus per naturam: *iste aut est albus monachus, aut albus non monachus*, quia utraque falsa; similiter intelligendum est in proposito. Nec valet: *est Deus et est alius*: ergo *est Deus alius*; immo est ibi accidens, sicut hic: *est bonus et est citharoedus*: ergo *est bonus citharoedus*[^16].

**Ad 4.** Ad illud quod ultimo obiicitur, dicendum, quod *alius*, quamvis sit masculini generis, tamen quia ponit rem circa substantivum[^17], ab illo trahit suppositionem; et ideo non tenetur personaliter, nisi secundum quod substantivatur, sicut et hoc nomen *unus*; unde sicut si dicatur *unus Deus*, *unus* dicit unitatem substantialem, ita si dicatur *alius Deus*, *alius* dicit alietatem substantialem. Et ratio huius venit non tantum quia adiectivum, sed quia generale, quod specificatur per adiunctum.
questions.english:
<!-- page 99 -->

**Question 2.** *Whether this expression can be admitted:* God generates another God.

Second, it is asked whether the unity of essence admits this: *God generates another God*. And it seems that it does not.

1. Anselm, *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*[^1]: "When we say *God from God*, we do not understand another God, but the same [God] from himself."

2. Again, if he generated another God — but where there is one and another, there are two: therefore if he generated another, there are two gods.

3. Again, *another* (*alius*) expresses otherness in general; therefore, since the general is specified by what is attached, the name *God* specifies it; but if it specifies, it specifies by reason of form: therefore otherness is marked in the form: therefore such an expression is not to be admitted, since there is no otherness in form.

**On the contrary.**

1. Generation imports distinction[^2]; but distinction imports some otherness: therefore so does generation; therefore if this is true — *God generated God* — then by consequence this is also true: *God is distinguished from God*, or *he generated another God*. If you say that it does not follow, because *to generate* imports distinction as a *mode* but *to be distinguished* or *to be another* [imports it] as a *thing*; against [this]: upon

<!-- page 100 -->

a consequence [taken] as a mode there follows a consecution [taken] as a thing — whence if this is true: *if a man exists, an animal exists*[^3], from the [existing] man there follows the animal. Moreover, it is clear that the distinction of generation is not only on the side of the one understanding it, but also on the side of the thing: therefore to that distinction, as actually exercised, there corresponds a real distinction.

2. Again, the affirmative is false: *God begotten is God begetting*; therefore the negative is true: *God begotten is not God begetting*. But just as the affirmative signifies identity, so the negative signifies diversity: therefore, just as God begetting and [God] begotten can be compared to each other by means of a negation, so too by means of otherness: therefore this is true: *God generated another God*.

3. Again, *the Father — that is, God — generated another*; this is true, it is clear: therefore either *another God*, or *another not-God*; but not *another not-God*: therefore etc.

4. Again, *another* (*alius*) is a term of the masculine gender[^4]; but a term of the masculine gender stands for a person in partitive terms: therefore *another* expresses personal otherness; but this is true: *God generated another God in person*; therefore this is simply true: *God generated another God*.

**Conclusion.**

*In the strict sense of the words, this expression is false:* God generated another God.

**Reply.** I answer that this expression is customarily distinguished: *God generated another God* — because *another* can be taken adjectivally, and thus it places otherness around the form of this term *God*, and in that case the expression is false; or it can also be taken substantively[^5], so as to be substantivized, and then it is an appositive construction, like *animal-man* — and the sense is thus: *God generated another [who is] God*, that is, he generated another who is God; and in this sense the expression is true.

But although this distinction has a place in theological expressions on account of a certain proper mode of speaking, nevertheless, so far as concerns the force[^6] of the discourse, it ought not to be drawn; since an adjective attached to a substantive — as *white man* — is not said to be substantivized, nor is an appositive construction said to obtain there[^7], especially since such [a construction] is less common with respect to what is more common. Whence, since this term *another* is an adjective having a substantive joined to it, in the aforesaid expression it places otherness around it [the substantive] both by reason of supposit and by reason of form.

And therefore, if we wish to proceed artificially[^8] — i.e. by the rules of the [liberal] arts — such an expression is to be judged false. On this account, for understanding the said expression, a common rule is to be noted: **distinction has no place**[^9] **where there is not union from diverse causes.** For example, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are united in the name *God* not from diverse causes, or by reason of diverse [things], but by reason of one deity, i.e. essence. Union from diverse causes obtains, as [when] in "man" Peter and John are united by reason of diverse humanities, since the humanity of Peter is one, and of John another.

And alongside this rule, taken from opposites[^10], another rule is to be received: **total union has no place where, together with union, there is distinction** — as the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are united in one deity or essence, but have distinction by reason of the plurality of persons.

According to this, it is to be noted that in divine [matters] certain terms import distinction only, certain ones total union, and certain ones [stand] in a middle mode. Since, therefore, *God begetting* and *God begotten*, although they are personally distinct, are nonetheless united in deity from the same cause — namely by one deity — therefore terms importing distinction simply are not received[^11]. For this reason this is not admitted: *God is distinguished from God*; and likewise: *God generated another God*. Again, by reason of distinction, terms importing total union in supposit and form are not received: whence this is not received: *God generated himself*. But those [terms] which stand in a middle mode are received — such as the verb *to generate*, because it expresses distinction in person together with[^12] unity of essence. Likewise this is conceded: *the Father generates another himself*. Whence Augustine *to Maximinus*[^13]: "The Father generated another himself"; and likewise on John: "The Father, sending the Son, sent another himself." And from this it is the case that [a thing] does not follow upon a word simply importing distinction; and so the first [objection] is clear.

**Reply to 2.** To the second objection concerning negation, I readily grant that there is otherness; yet it does not follow that otherness can be said to obtain in the essence or form of deity. Whence it does not follow: *the begotten is other than the begetter, therefore*[^14] *he is another God*, because the supposition of this term *God* shifts.

<!-- page 101 -->

**Reply to 3.** To the objection made third — *either another God, or another not-God* — I say that the division is not sufficient, because there is no contradiction unless the negation is taken with respect to the whole. For in this [expression] — *he generated another God* — two things are said, namely that *God*[^15] [generated] *God*, and that [the begotten is] *another* in deity; and therefore, in order that a contradiction may be reached, it is necessary that [the negation] be carried over the whole. Whence, just as — when a black monk who is white by nature is pointed out — this does not hold: *he is either a white monk, or a white not-monk*, since both are false, so is it to be understood in the case at hand. Nor does this hold: *he is God and he is another: therefore he is another God* — indeed, there is an accident [fallacy] there, as here: *he is good and he is a citharist: therefore he is a good citharist*[^16].

**Reply to 4.** To the last objection, it must be said that *another* (*alius*), although it is of the masculine gender, nevertheless — because it places a thing around the substantive[^17] — draws its supposition from it; and therefore it is not taken personally, except insofar as it is substantivized, as is also the term *one*. Whence, just as, if one says *one God*, *one* expresses substantial unity, so if one says *another God*, *another* expresses substantial otherness. And the reason for this comes not only from its being an adjective, but from its being a general [term] which is specified by what is attached [to it].
questions.latinScholion:
I. Distinctionem in principio responsionis positam — quod *alius* hic possit teneri vel adiective vel substantive (nempe ut appositio) — S. Doctor improbat, cum sit regula grammaticorum, quod adiectivum, si immediate sibi coniunctum habet substantivum, non potest accipi ut substantivum sive ut appositio. Si autem *alius* est adiectivum, tunc valet regula logicae, quod *alius*, quando immediate ad suum subiectivum ponitur, importat [alietatem] circa suum substantivum tum ratione suppositi, tum ratione formae. Consequenter in casu nostro hic terminus importaret diversitatem in Deitate.

II. In conclusione et solutione obiectorum principales doctores conveniunt. Alex. Hal., S. p. I, q. 50, m. 3, a. 2, § 2. — Scot., hic q. 1. — S. Thom., hic a. 3; S. I, q. 31, a. 2. — B. Albert., hic a. 8. — Petr. a Tar., hic q. 2, a. 2. — Richard. a Med., hic q. 2.

---
questions.englishScholion:
I. The Holy Doctor rejects the distinction set out at the beginning of the Reply — namely, that *another* here could be taken either adjectivally or substantively (i.e., as an apposition) — since the rule of the grammarians is that an adjective, if it has a substantive immediately joined to it, cannot be taken as a substantive or as an apposition. If, then, *another* is an adjective, the rule of logic holds: *another*, when placed immediately adjacent to its subject, imports [otherness] around its substantive both by reason of supposit and by reason of form. Consequently, in our case this term would import diversity in [the] Deity.

II. On the conclusion and on the solution of the objections, the principal doctors agree: Alexander of Hales, *Summa* pt. I, q. 50, m. 3, a. 2, § 2. — Scotus, here q. 1. — Thomas Aquinas, here a. 3; *Summa theologiae* I, q. 31, a. 2. — Albert the Great, here a. 8. — Peter of Tarentaise, here q. 2, a. 2. — Richard of Mediavilla, here q. 2.

---

apparatus.la: *Cap. 24:* Nam cum dicimus Deum de Deo, Filium de Patre, non alium intelligimus Deum de Deo alio, sed eundem ipsum Deum de eodem ipso Deo. *— Codd. cum Vat. falso ponunt* in Proslogio.
apparatus.en: Ch. 24: "For when we say *God from God, Son from Father*, we do not understand another God [coming] from another God, but the same very God from the same very God." — The codices, along with Vat., wrongly cite [this passage as being] *in the* Proslogion.

apparatus.la: *Nam ut ait Arist., De Anima II, text. 47 (c. 4):* Generat autem nihil ipsum se ipsum. *— De propositione minore Arist., Metaph. XIV, c. 3 (XIII, c. 1):* Alterum (contrarium est) eidem, et aliud ipsi (αὐτῷ). *— In hac propositione minore Vat.* et *loco* sed, *obstantibus mss. et ed. 1.*
apparatus.en: For, as Aristotle says, *On the Soul* II, text 47 (ch. 4): "Nothing generates itself." — On the minor proposition, Aristotle, *Metaphysics* XIV, ch. 3 (XIII, ch. 1): "The *other* (is contrary) to the same, and the *another* [is contrary] to it itself (*autō*)." — In this minor proposition, Vat. reads *et* ("and") in place of *sed* ("but"), against the mss. and ed. 1.

apparatus.la: *Auctoritate mss. et ed. 1 expunximus hic additum* etiam; *cod. 1 autem addit* similiter haec est vera. *Cod. O post* homo est *addit* ergo. *— Plura de hac consequentia vide apud Boeth., de Syllogismo hypothetico.*
apparatus.en: On the authority of the mss. and ed. 1, we have struck out *etiam* ("also") here added; but cod. 1 adds *similiter haec est vera* ("likewise this is true"). Cod. O after *homo est* ("man exists") adds *ergo* ("therefore"). — For more on this consequence, see Boethius, *On the Hypothetical Syllogism*.

apparatus.la: *Vat., obnitentibus antiquioribus mss. et ed. 1, minus bene* qui *loco* sed terminus masculini generis; *et circa finem argumenti* similiter *loco* simpliciter.
apparatus.en: Vat., against the older mss. and ed. 1, less well reads *qui* in place of *sed terminus masculini generis* ("but a term of the masculine gender"); and near the end of the argument, *similiter* ("likewise") in place of *simpliciter* ("simply").

apparatus.la: *Ed. 1* sic ut. *Cod. R* et si substantivetur tunc.
apparatus.en: Ed. 1 reads *sic ut* ("thus, as"). Cod. R reads *et si substantivetur tunc* ("and if it is substantivized, then").

apparatus.la: *Aliqui codd. ut R cc* veritate, *et paulo infra plurimi codd. cum ed. 1 contra Vat.* iunctum *pro* adiunctum.
apparatus.en: Some codices, such as R and cc, read *veritate* ("the truth") [in place of *virtute*, "the force"]; and a little further on, very many codices with ed. 1 — against Vat. — read *iunctum* ("joined") in place of *adiunctum* ("attached").

apparatus.la: *Sensus est: maxime cum appositiva constructio fiat coniunctione termini minus communis cum magis communi.*
apparatus.en: The sense is: especially since an appositive construction comes about through the joining of a less common term with a more common one.

apparatus.la: *Hoc est, stricte secundum regulas artium, scilicet grammaticae et logicae.*
apparatus.en: That is, strictly according to the rules of the [liberal] arts — namely, of grammar and of logic.

apparatus.la: *Codd. cum primis sex edd. omittunt* omnimoda, *quod a Vat. termino* distinctio *praefigitur.*
apparatus.en: The codices, with the first six editions, omit *omnimoda* ("of every kind"), which Vat. prefixes to the term *distinctio* ("distinction").

apparatus.la: *Vat. praeter fidem codd. et ed. 1* opposito.
apparatus.en: Vat., against the fidelity of the codices and ed. 1, reads *opposito* ("from the opposite" — singular).

apparatus.la: *Fide mss. et ed. 1 substituimus* recipiuntur *loco* recipiunt. *Paulo infra multi codd. omittunt* similiter.
apparatus.en: On the fidelity of the mss. and ed. 1, we have substituted *recipiuntur* (passive, "are received") in place of *recipiunt* (active, "they receive"). A little further on, many codices omit *similiter* ("likewise").

apparatus.la: *Cod. X* distinctionem personarum in.
apparatus.en: Cod. X reads *distinctionem personarum in* ("a distinction of persons in").

apparatus.la: *Vide in lit. Magistri, c. 2 in fine; et super Ioannem, c. 3, Tract. 14, n. 11:* Pater mittens Filium se alterum misit.
apparatus.en: See the text of the Master [Peter Lombard], ch. 2 at the end; and [Augustine] *on John*, ch. 3, Tractate 14, n. 11: "The Father, sending the Son, sent himself as another."

apparatus.la: *Codd. M X addunt* est.
apparatus.en: Codd. M, X add *est* ("is").

apparatus.la: *Cod. R addit* genuit.
apparatus.en: Cod. R adds *genuit* ("[he] generated").

apparatus.la: *Exemplum sumtum est ex Arist., Periherm. II, c. 2 (c. 11), ubi secundum translationem Boethii habetur:* si citharoedus est et bonus, est et citharoedus bonus, *licet aliae translationes ponunt* coriarius (σκυτεύς) *pro* citharoedus. *— De hac fallacia accidentis vide supra d. 2, q. 1 ad 1.*
apparatus.en: The example is taken from Aristotle, *On Interpretation* II, ch. 2 (ch. 11), where according to Boethius's translation it reads: "if he is a citharist and [is] good, he is also a good citharist"; although other translations give *coriarius* ("leather-worker," *skuteus*) in place of *citharoedus* ("citharist"). — On this fallacy of accident, see above, d. 2, q. 1 ad 1.

apparatus.la: *Vat. hic* subiectum *loco* substantivum, *et paulo infra post* substantivatur *ponit* Sicut ergo, cum dicitur unus Deus, hoc nomen unus dicit unitatem, *sed contra antiquiores codd. et ed. 1.*
apparatus.en: Vat. here reads *subiectum* ("subject") in place of *substantivum* ("substantive"); and a little further on, after *substantivatur*, Vat. inserts *Sicut ergo, cum dicitur unus Deus, hoc nomen unus dicit unitatem* ("Just as, therefore, when *one God* is said, this name *one* expresses unity") — but against the older codices and ed. 1. ---

questions.notes:
- **Chunk scope.** This chunk covers Q. II of Art. un. of Distinction IV in its entirety, spanning printed pp. 99–101 (PDF pp. 201–203): the brief opening frame, three *videtur quod* arguments, four *Sed contra* arguments, Conclusio, the long Respondeo (with its rejected grammatical distinction, the two *regulae* on distinction/union in divinis, and the threefold division of vocables) which implicitly answers obj. 1, and explicit *Ad* replies to objs. 2–4. The Scholion block at the top of p. 101 is included. This closes the third (and last) of the confirmed d. 1/d. 4 gaps in the rebuild audit.

- **Key terms** (per project glossary): *generatio* → generation; *generans / genitus* → begetting / begotten; *alius / alietas* → other / otherness; *substantivum / adiectivum* → substantive / adjective; *substantivetur* → "be substantivized" (taken as a substantive); *appositiva constructio* → appositive construction; *suppositum / suppositio* → supposit / supposition; *deitas* → deity; *essentia* → essence; *in divinis* → "in divine [matters]" / "in what pertains to God"; *artificialiter* → artificially (i.e., by the rules of the liberal arts, grammar and logic — Bonaventure's own gloss in fn. 8); *figura dictionis* → figure-of-speech [fallacy]; *fallacia accidentis* → fallacy of the accident; *citharoedus* → citharist (player of the cithara — the Aristotelian example of the accident-fallacy).

- **The question's shape.** This is one of Bonaventure's most concentrated logical-theological questions. The form of the argument: (a) he refuses the standard distinction (*alius* adjective vs. *alius* substantive-appositive) because grammatical rules forbid it when a substantive is immediately joined; (b) he judges the expression false *si velimus artificialiter procedere*; (c) he grounds the ruling in two *regulae* about distinction and union; and (d) he exhibits the threefold division of Trinitarian vocables — those importing distinction only, those importing total union, and those standing in the mean. The mean-term *generat* is the lynchpin, because it expresses *distinctio in persona cum unitate essentiae*.

- **The fallacy-of-accident example in Ad 3.** The *bonus citharoedus* example is drawn straight from Boethius's translation of *Peri Hermeneias* II, ch. 11 — the locus classicus for the *fallacia accidentis* in medieval logic. Fn 16 notes that other translations give *coriarius* (leather-worker, Gk. *skuteus*) for *citharoedus*. The point in Bonaventure's usage is that "*he is good and he is a citharist, therefore he is a good citharist*" is invalid for the same reason that "*he is God and he is another, therefore he is another God*" is invalid.

- **Ad 1 is implicit.** The Respondeo closes with *et sic patet primum* ("and thus the first is clear"), which stands in for an explicit *Ad 1*. This is a common Bonaventuran convention when the long body of the Respondeo has already disposed of the first objection by its own argument. The rendering preserves the implicit structure; no explicit **Ad 1** header is inserted.

- **Scholion I — Bonaventure against the adjective/substantive distinction.** The editors' scholion unpacks Bonaventure's grammatical ruling: the rule of the *grammatici* is that an adjective with substantive immediately joined cannot be read substantively; and the rule of the *logici* is that *alius* so placed imports otherness *ratione suppositi* and *ratione formae*. This is the Peter-of-Spain-style supposition doctrine in the background — the detailed supposition primer appears in the *preceding* question's scholion (fn. raw ~23874–23971), which will live in `bon-sent-I-d4-a1-q1.md` when that chunk is built.

- **Vision transcription status.** First-pass vision re-OCR of printed pp. 99–101 (PDF pp. 201–203), reconciled against `raw/bonaventure_vol1_raw.txt` lines 23974–24227 for body text and 24010–24167, 24283–24294 for the apparatus block. Footnote markers were placed from the raw OCR's marker glyphs and should be considered best-effort for the high-marker-density region on p. 100, where markers fall within a few characters of each other. The Greek in fn. 2 (*αὐτῷ*) and fn. 16 (*σκυτεύς*) was re-keyed from the OCR's Latin transliteration, since the scanner's Greek rendering is unreliable; both should be verified against the print before publication. Apparatus entries should be cross-checked against the Quaracchi Vol. I sigla key (forthcoming in `tools/apparatus-sigla.json`).

questions.english:
DIST. IV. THE SINGLE ARTICLE. QUESTION III. (continued from prior chunk)

3. To the third objection — either another God or another non-God: I say that the division is not exhaustive, because there is no contradiction unless the negation is taken with respect to the whole. For in the expression "He begot another God," two things are said — namely that He begot God, and that the other is another in deity; and therefore for the contradiction to be properly derived, it is necessary that the negation be borne over the whole. Hence just as the following does not hold when pointing to a black-robed monk who is white by nature: "He is either a white monk or not a white monk" — because both are false — similarly this is to be understood in the matter at hand. Nor does this hold: "He is God and He is other: therefore He is another God" — on the contrary, this is a fallacy of accident, as in the inference: "He is good and he is a lute-player: therefore he is a good lute-player."

4. To the last objection: it must be said that "another," although it is of masculine gender, nonetheless — because it posits something with respect to the substantive — draws its supposition from the substantive; and therefore it is not taken personally except insofar as it is substantivized, just as the name "one" — hence just as when "one God" is said, "one" denotes substantial unity, so when "another God" is said, "another" denotes substantial otherness. And the reason for this comes not only from the fact that it is an adjective, but because it is a general term that is specified by what is adjoined.

[Scholion omitted]

QUESTION III.

Whether it can be said grammatically according to the rules of grammar: "several gods."

Third, it is asked whether the name "God" grammatically signifies the plural number — or whether it can properly be said "several gods." And it seems it can:

1. Because according to the Philosopher, concepts are the same for all, even though the words differ; but modes of signifying follow modes of understanding: therefore since among the Hebrews it is properly said *Elohim* — which is equivalent to "gods" — the same can be said among us.

2. Likewise, as the Philosopher holds, what is true presupposes what is grammatically well-formed; hence "of Cato it is or it is not" signifies neither truth nor falsehood; but this is true: "there are not several gods": therefore it is grammatically well-formed: therefore so is this: "several gods exist" — because negation does not remove ill-formedness.

3. Likewise, just as "God" belongs to one alone, so "principle of creatures" belongs to one alone; but although it is falsely said "several principles," it is nonetheless said in a grammatically well-formed way: therefore by equal reasoning we can say "several gods."

4. Likewise, the name "phoenix" has only one individual; yet it is grammatically well-formed to say "several phoenixes." If you say that the individual is multiplied through succession of time — I raise the same point against you concerning the name "sun," which is multiplied at no time; and yet it is grammatically well-formed to say "several suns": therefore also "several gods."

On the contrary: 1. Every name that has a plural is a common appellative name — for proper names are not pluralized, since one does not say "several Peters" or "several Johns"; but the name "God" is not an appellative name, because it does not signify a multipliable form: therefore, etc.

2. Likewise, the name "God" is properly the proper name of the divine nature; but no such name is pluralized: therefore, etc.

CONCLUSION.

The name "God," properly speaking, does not have a plural.

I respond: For the understanding of what has been said, it must be noted that the name "God" is used in three ways — namely, by titular use, by adoptive use, and by nature. In the first two ways it is pluralized; hence the Apostle in the first letter to the Corinthians eight: "For indeed there are many gods and many lords"; but in the third way it is not, because in this sense the name "God" signifies the divine nature together with conditions, the collection of which it is impossible to find in another; and therefore just as a proper name, according to the rules of the art, does not have a plural, so neither does this name "God."

1. To the objection, therefore, that among the Hebrews it has a plural — namely *Elohim*: it must be said that modes of signifying do not only follow the diverse general modes of understanding, but also modes of expression. And since the Hebrews have articles and modes of expression that are diverse from ours — which we do not have — they therefore can have it, but we cannot.

2. To the objection that what is true presupposes what is grammatically well-formed: it must be said that there are two kinds of grammatical ill-formedness. One arises from a discohesion of accidents — as in "of Cato it is"; the other arises from a discohesion of concepts — as when one says "several Peters." The first ill-formedness removes truth and falsehood; the second ill-formedness has falsity conjoined with it; and therefore, since through negation falsity is removed, and the saints prefer to speak truly rather than to preserve propriety of speech and speak less truly, they therefore deny several gods. It could however be said that although the word "gods" (*dii*) is not a word that signifies according to the rules of the art and according to original imposition, it is nonetheless a word that signifies by accommodation of usage — as *olli* for *illi*; and therefore the affirmative generates a false understanding, and the negative a true one, even if not grammatically.

3. and 4. To the objection that "principle of creatures" belongs to one alone, and similarly "phoenix": it must be said that to belong to one alone is threefold. For either a name is imposed from an unmultipliable form, as in the case of proper names — and in this sense it removes plurality both in reality and in co-signification. Or it is imposed from a form that is naturally suited to be communicated, although it is not communicated because of a particular determination — as when one says "principle of creatures." Or it is imposed from a form limited because of defect of matter — as "phoenix"; and such a term removes plurality according to reality, but not according to co-signification, because such a form can be co-signified as capable of being multiplied through individuals.

[Scholion omitted]

QUESTION IV.

Whether the name "God" supposes for a person or for the nature.

Fourth and finally, a question is asked concerning the supposition of the name "God." And it is asked whether the name "God" of itself supposes for a person or for the nature. And that it supposes for a person seems evident:

1. Through what Ambrose says on the text "May God bless us, our God, may God bless us": Ambrose says "The threefold confession of God indicates the Trinity of persons" — therefore since "God" is there without any addition, it of itself supposes for a person.

2. Likewise, it is objected by reason thus: the name "man" properly supposes for everything in which humanity inheres: therefore by analogy the name "God" likewise properly supposes for everything

[Critical apparatus omitted]

questions.notes:
- **Opening (Q. II replies 3–4):** The chunk opens with the final two replies to the objections of Question II. Reply 3 invokes the logical point that "either another God or another non-God" is not a genuine exhaustive disjunction — the contradiction must bear over the whole composite expression, not over partial elements. The analogy of the "white monk who is black by clothing" illustrates the failure of the disjunction. Reply 4 turns on the grammar of *alius* as an adjective that draws its supposition from the substantive it modifies — hence "another God" (*alius Deus*) imports substantial otherness, not personal otherness.
- **Question III — plural "gods":** A grammatical/logical question about whether "God" (*Deus*) can properly take a plural form. Bonaventure's *Conclusio* distinguishes three senses of "God": (1) titular (*nuncupative*) — pagan gods, false idols; (2) adoptive (*adoptive*) — those who participate in divine grace; (3) by nature (*naturaliter*) — God properly so called. Only the third cannot be pluralized, because it signifies the divine nature together with conditions (simplicity, infinity, aseity, etc.) that are by definition singular and cannot be instantiated in another.
- **Two kinds of grammatical ill-formedness:** A subtle logical distinction in reply 2. *Discohesion of accidents* (as in "of Cato it is") makes an expression neither true nor false — it is simply grammatically ill-formed in a way that removes the truth-functional dimension. *Discohesion of concepts* (as in "several Peters") generates a necessarily false expression — not merely ill-formed. The negation of the first type produces neither truth nor falsehood; but the negation of "several gods" produces truth, because "gods" in the false/improper sense is being denied.
- **"Olli" for "illi":** A technical example from Latin grammar — an archaic or dialectal form used to illustrate that customary usage can give semantic force to a word that is not properly formed according to grammatical rules. The point is that "dii" (*gods*) can be used meaningfully by accommodation, even if it lacks strict grammatical legitimacy in theological discourse.
- **Three types of names that belong to one alone:** A neat logical taxonomy in reply 3–4: (a) unmultipliable form → proper name, removes plurality both really and in co-signification (like "Peter"); (b) multipliable form, contingently uncommunicated → false but grammatically well-formed plural (like "principle of creatures," where there is only one but the form could in principle be communicated); (c) multipliable form, limited by defect of matter → removes real plurality but not co-signification (like "phoenix" or "sun," whose form could in principle be multiplied). "God" in the proper sense falls under (a).
- **Question IV begins:** The fourth and final question of the article — whether "God" supposes for a person or for the nature — opens. The chunk ends after the statement of objection 2. This question is crucial for Trinitarian predication: if "God" supposes for the essence, then "God generates" would be false (as "Essence generates" is false); if for a person, then the affirmations of prior questions are well-founded. Bonaventure's answer (not yet in this chunk) will be that "God" supposes for the person by its primary mode of supposition, though it signifies the essence — a distinction parallel to the abstract/concrete analysis of Question I.

3. Likewise, the name "God" signifies deity in concrete form; but only in concrete form with respect to a supposit, which is a person; but a concrete term properly supposes for that with respect to which it imports a form — as "white" more properly supposes for the white thing than for the form: therefore, etc.

On the contrary: 1. A pronoun refers back to a thing for its proper supposit; but when it is said "May God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear Him" — the pronoun "Him" refers back to the nature, not to the person: therefore, etc.

2. Likewise, because the term "man" properly supposes for an individual, the expression "man is Socrates and Plato" is false — because the same individual does not accept that predication; but "God is the Trinity" or "God is Father and Son" is true: therefore, since that predicate does not belong to one person, it is clear, etc.

3. Likewise, a term that properly supposes for a person, when a partitive term is added to it, stands only for one — as when it is said "one man runs": therefore similarly, when "one God" is said — therefore this is simply false: "one God is Father and Son."

CONCLUSION.

The name "God," since it has the nature both of a common term and of a singular term, can properly suppose both for the nature and for the person.

I respond: It must be said that there are customarily two opinions on this matter.

One holds that the name "God" properly signifies the nature and supposes for the person — sometimes for one, as when it is said "God generates"; sometimes for two, as when it is said "God spirates"; sometimes for three, as when it is said "God is the Trinity." And the account given for this is that since it has many supposits, it has the nature of a common term; but a common term properly supposes for an individual, and not properly for the nature or form, unless it is drawn there — as when one says "man is a species." They say the same in the matter at hand. They further say that because all the supposits are in a unique supposition in that name, it can therefore suppose simultaneously for many persons — although this cannot be done by the term "man" or another common term; and in this way they resolve the objections.

The other opinion is that it properly supposes for the nature, as it signifies, and does not suppose for a person unless drawn by another — as when it is said "God generates"; and those who hold this say that when it is said "God is the Trinity," it there stands for the nature, not for the person; and one nature is three persons — therefore the expression is true. And the account of this position is that the name "God" has the nature of a discrete term, since it does not have a plural; therefore it signifies and properly supposes the same thing; since therefore it signifies the nature, it properly supposes for the nature.

But it is better to say both — because it has the nature of a common term and of a discrete term: of a common term by reason of the plurality of supposits, of a discrete term by reason of the non-multipliable form — and that it properly supposes both for the nature and for the person. Yet the arguments for each side conclude correctly in their respective way. But this cannot be found in any other term, and therefore neither can a similar mode of suppositing.

DOUBTS CONCERNING THE MASTER'S TEXT.

DOUBT I.

In this part a question arises concerning what he says: "God from God, Light from Light" — because since the preposition "from" (*de*) denotes transition and thus diversity and distinction, it seems that by equal reasoning and from equivalent terms the following are true: "God is other than God," "God is distinguished from God."

I respond: It must be said that there are two ways of importing distinction or diversity — namely as a mode, or as a thing; or as exercised, or as conceived. Since therefore prepositions import distinction as exercised, and distinction exists in divine things with respect to supposits, "from" (*de*) causes the term to stand for diverse supposits. Since therefore it posits the mode around that in which it exercises distinction — and such are the persons — the expression is true. But since the name "another" imports distinction as conceived, and similarly the verb "to distinguish" — these therefore simply posit distinction with respect to the term by reason of its form, and therefore they are false.

DOUBT II.

Likewise, a question is raised concerning the response that the Master gives at: "But what is further added — therefore He begot Himself as God, etc." — because the Master resolves it by denying the conclusion, and he seems to resolve it incorrectly. For since "same" and "diverse" sufficiently divide being, it seems to follow necessarily: He begot God — therefore either Himself or another.

I respond: It must be said that the Master, by upholding the first premise and denying the conclusion, indicates that the conclusion does not follow from the premises: and that it does not follow, he shows by adducing a counter-instance against that disjunction.

To the objection that "same" and "diverse" sufficiently divide being: it must be said that this is simply false. For a part is neither altogether the same as the whole nor simply diverse from it. Yet it has truth according to the same respect. Hence "if not the same as another, then diverse" is true according to that respect according to which it is not the same. But the Son is not the same as the Father in person, and therefore He is another in person; yet it does not follow that He is "another God" — because otherness in essence would be signified.

DOUBT III.

Likewise, a question is raised concerning the distinction that the Master makes regarding the predicate "God the Father" — namely that it can be either an appositional and immediate construction, or a mediate one. For first it seems that this distinction is unintelligible, since what is constructed intransitively from the same side seems to be constructed only immediately. questions.notes:
- **Question IV conclusion — "God" supposes both for nature and person:** Bonaventure surveys two standard scholastic positions and proposes a third as superior. Position 1 (common in his tradition): "God" signifies nature, supposes for person(s) — with the unique feature that it can suppose simultaneously for multiple divine persons because all share a single supposition. Position 2: "God" properly supposes nature (because it lacks a plural, behaving like a discrete/singular term). Bonaventure's *via media*: "God" uniquely partakes of both modes — it is like a common term (multiple supposits) and like a singular term (non-multipliable form). Therefore it can properly suppose both for the nature and for one or more persons. This explains both "God generates" (for the Father) and "God is the Trinity" (for the nature or all three persons simultaneously) without requiring either position alone to carry all the cases.
- **"Unique supposition":** The phrase *in unica suppositione* in Position 1 expresses the point that the three persons, though numerically distinct, do not stand to the name "God" as three separate instances of a common form (as Peter, Paul, and John stand to "man"), but share one numerically identical deity. This is what allows "God" to suppose for all three simultaneously — something impossible for "man" (which cannot suppose for both Peter and Paul at once).
- **Doubt I — prepositions vs. nouns in importing distinction:** A key semantic distinction that resolves apparent inconsistencies in Trinitarian language. Prepositions like "from" (*de*, *ex*, *a*) import distinction *as exercised* — they simply operate within the real relational structure of divine persons without explicitly predicating otherness as a conceptual content. Names like *alius* ("another") and verbs like *distinguitur* ("is distinguished") import distinction *as conceived* — they place it explicitly as the signified content, thereby predicating otherness of the form (essence), which is false. Hence "God from God" is true while "God is other than God" is false.
- **Doubt II — "same and diverse" as exhaustive:** Bonaventure's elegant rebuttal of the disjunction argument (*se vel alium*): the Aristotelian principle that every being is either same or diverse (*Metaphysics* X) holds *within a given respect*, not absolutely. The Son is other than the Father in person, not in essence — so "other" holds in one respect and does not hold in another. This is not a violation of the exhaustive division but its proper application: otherness is always relative to a respect.
- **Doubt III — appositional and mediate construction (Priscian):** The Master's distinction — that "God the Father" can be read either appositionally/immediately (where "Father" qualifies "God" as one compound term, yielding "the Father-God") or mediately (where "God" and "is Father" are separate predications) — is here defended by appeal to Priscian's grammar of the understood copula. The text ends mid-argument as the application of the Priscianic rule is being developed.

DIST. IV. DOUBTS. (continued)

between a substantive and an adjective there is understood a middle copula — *ens* or *quod est ens*. And since what it is — namely *ens* or *who is the Father* — can be taken implicatively: and in this sense it is restricted and takes the place of an appositional construction and is equivalent to one term; it is therefore said that it can be taken or construed immediately — and so "God the Father" is nothing other than the Father Himself. Or the relative can be understood relatively, and so in a certain separation; and then it is not restricted, and the sense is: "God the Father" — that is, God, who is the Father; which amounts to: it is God, and that one is the Father. This solution of the Master indeed resolves the sophism with respect to one deception, and therefore it is good. But another deception concerning the relative immediately arises — and therefore it must still be resolved, not with respect to that deception, but with respect to the other. Therefore Praepositivus resolves this argument in another way: "either the God who is the Father or who is not the Father" — and he says that the inference does not follow, nor are they contradictories, because the supposition of this relative is not the same. For in the affirmative it supposes for the begotten God, because it is not confused; in the negative, however, it supposes simply. Hence just as these are not contradictories but are both false — "no man is Peter," "John is Peter" — so he says in the matter at hand, because the negation confuses. Hence both of these are false: "God the Son is the Father," "God is not the Father." — But although the solution of Praepositivus has its place in the matter at hand — because it makes no difference to place the negation before or after the term "God" — it does not have its place in other contexts. For a negation placed after a relative does not confuse the relative.

And therefore moderns resolve it differently, by distinguishing that this relative "who" can make a simple or a personal relation. If simple, the affirmative is true and the negative false; if personal, conversely the negative is true and the affirmative false. This is clear because this is false: "the person of the Son is the Father," and this is true: "the person of the Son is not the Father."

DOUBT IV.

Likewise, a question is raised concerning what he says: "one God is three persons." But on the contrary: whatever is predicated of one and the same thing is predicated of one another: therefore if one God is Father and Son, then the Father is the Son. If you say this is true when things are predicated of one singular, but not when predicated of one common term — on the contrary: nothing is subjected to two things in a unique supposition, even if it is common to them. Hence this is false: "a man is Socrates and Plato": therefore similarly in the matter at hand.

I respond: It must be said that, as is clear, the supposition of the name "God" is otherwise than the supposition of any other term. For since it has the nature of a common term and of a discrete term, it stands simultaneously for many as for one: and therefore it does not follow: "God is Father and Son, therefore God the Father is the Son" or conversely. Similarly, neither is it permissible to infer from this that the Father is the Son. And it must be noted that such predication is by identity: therefore the supposit is truly predicated of the formal term.

DOUBT V.

Likewise, a question is raised concerning what the Master says: "one and only true God is the Trinity" — because this seems to contradict what he says below, namely that "Trinity" is a collective name and "one and only" are partitive and discretive names: therefore just as this is false: "one and only man is every man," so is this.

I respond: It must be said that the name "Trinity" is collective of persons; but "one and only," added to the term "God," do not denote the discretion of a person, but of the nature from others. Hence "one and only God" denotes one and only nature; and since in divine things nature and the thing of the nature or supposit are the same, the Trinity is therefore predicated of God by predication of identity. Nor is it similar in the case of "every man" and "one and only man." For the term "man" is a term that can be confused and multiplied, and therefore this is true: "every man is a man" — nor does it stand simultaneously for many unless confused; and therefore this is false: "a man is every man," because it is true neither by reason of supposition nor by identity, nor is nature and the thing of nature the same in a human being.

DOUBT VI.

Likewise, a question is raised concerning what he says: "It is enough for a Christian to believe," etc. For he seems to say something false, because either he means "enough" with respect to faith — and in that case it is false, because many other things must be believed; or "enough" with respect to knowledge — and that similarly is false, because from this one never sufficiently knows the cause of a thing.

I respond: It must be said that "enough" is understood with respect to knowledge — not just any knowledge, but that necessary for salvation.

DOUBT VII.

Likewise, a question is raised concerning what he says: "The Father begot another self." For it seems to combine those two poorly, because "self" denotes complete identity and "another" denotes diversity — and so they are opposed, and so they mutually imply opposites. If you say that one diminishes from the other — I ask: what, and from what?

I respond: It must be said that direct opposition is always understood with respect to the same thing. Since therefore in divine things there is simultaneously identity in nature and otherness in supposit, and this without opposition — the name of identity and the name of otherness are joined in speech without opposition — indeed, for the expression of a singular mode.

DOUBT VIII.

Likewise, a question is raised concerning what he says: "The Father, in order to have a Son, did not diminish Himself" — because this seems to say something false; for the following argument holds: whoever generates one son such that he cannot generate further diminishes his power; but this is so in the Father: therefore, etc.

I respond: That is true if generating another were a matter of power; but that, once one has been begotten, He could generate another — this denotes imperfection of the power in generating, because from this it would be shown that He did not give everything to the one.

DOUBT IX.

Likewise, a question is raised concerning what he says: "He begot from Himself another self, but not another god, but another person" — whether "other" (*alterum*) or "another" (*alium*) is said more properly; and it seems "other" (*alterum*), because it denotes a lesser diversity — for Socrates is called "other" from himself; but in divine things the diversity is minimal. But on the contrary: accidental differences cause something to be called "other" (*alterum*); but in divine things there is no accident: therefore it ought not to be called "other."

Likewise, it seems that neither is well said. For if substantial differences cause something to be called "another" (*aliud*), and accidental ones "other" (*alterum*), since neither obtains in divine things, neither seems to be properly said.

I respond: It must be said that since the Father differs from the Son both in supposit and in property, He can be called "another" (*alius*) and He can be called "other" (*alter*). But since that property does not accrue accidentally to the person, it is more properly said "another" (*alius*). And because "another" (*alius*) refers to the supposit and "another thing" (*aliud*) to the essence: therefore, even if "another" (*alius*) in the masculine is admitted there, nevertheless "another" (*aliud*) in the neuter is not.

DISTINCTION V.

Whether the divine essence begot the Son, or was begotten by the Father, or whether the Son was born from it, or the Holy Spirit proceeded from it.

After these things it is asked whether it must be conceded that the Father begot the divine essence, or that the divine essence begot the Son, or that essence begot essence, or whether the divine essence neither begot nor was begotten at all.

To which, agreeing with the Catholic writers, we say that neither did the Father beget the divine essence, nor did the divine essence beget the Son, nor did the divine essence beget essence. By "essence" here we understand the divine nature, which is common to three persons and wholly in each individually. Therefore it must not be said that:

1. The Father begot the divine essence — because if the Father were said to have begotten the divine essence, the divine essence would be said relatively toward the Father or would be placed for a relative term. But if it were said relatively or placed for a relative term, it would not indicate essence. For as Augustine says in the fifth book On the Trinity: "What is said relatively does not indicate substance."

Likewise, since God the Father is the divine essence, if He were its begetter, He would be the begetter of the very thing that He Himself is; and so the same thing would have begotten itself — which Augustine denies, as we showed above.

Likewise, if the Father is the begetter of the divine essence, since He Himself is the divine essence and is God — therefore by the act of generating He both is and is God. Thus it would not be through the thing generated that the Father is God, but through the act of generating that the Father both is and is God. And if this is so, not the begotten gives the begetter the cause of being and being God, but the begetter gives the begotten this cause. By similar reasoning Augustine proves in the seventh book On the Trinity "that the Father is not wise through the wisdom He begot — because if He is wise through it, He is it; for in that being is the same as being wise. But if being is the same as being wise there, the Father is not wise through the wisdom He begot. For what else do we mean when we say 'being and being wise are the same there,' except that He is through that whereby He is wise? Therefore that which is the cause of His being wise is also the cause of His being. If therefore the wisdom He begot is the cause of His being wise, it is also the cause of His being. But no one would say that the cause of the Father's being is the wisdom begotten by the Father; for what is more insane? So therefore if the Father begot the essence by which He is, the essence He begot would be the cause of His being." Therefore He did not beget the essence by which He is. "For in that simplicity," says Augustine, "since being wise is not other than being, wisdom is the same as essence there"; and therefore what is said of wisdom, the same we say of essence. Therefore just as He did not beget the wisdom by which He is wise, so neither the essence by which He is. For as He is wise through wisdom and powerful through power, so He is through essence; and wisdom and power are the same as essence. It is clear from the foregoing, then, that the Father did not beget the divine essence.

But to this there seems to be contrary what Augustine says in the one book On Faith and the Symbol, chapter three: "God, when He begot the Word, begot that which He Himself is — not from nothing, nor from some already created and fashioned matter, but from Himself that which He Himself is." Likewise: "God begot God" — that is, the same from Himself. And here Augustine in the book On Faith to Peter says: "So believe Christ the Son of God, one person of the Trinity, to be true God, that you do not doubt His divinity to have been born from the nature of the Father." Here he seems to say that the nature of the Son is born from the nature of the Father. The same also in the fifteenth book On the Trinity says: "The Son is said to be counsel from counsel and will from will, just as substance from substance, wisdom from wisdom." And here he seems to say that substance is begotten from substance and wisdom from wisdom. But we determine this thus: "wisdom from wisdom and substance from substance" means the Son, who is wisdom, who is substance, is from the Father, who is the same substance and wisdom; and the Son, who is divinity, is born from the Father who is the divine nature. And to say it more expressly: we say the Son-wisdom is from the Father-wisdom, and we say the Son-substance is begotten from and by the Father-substance. That this is how Augustine must be understood, he shows in the seventh book On the Trinity, saying: "The Father Himself is wisdom; and the Son is called the wisdom of the Father, in the way He is called the Light of the Father — that is, as light from light; and so let wisdom from wisdom be understood; and each is one wisdom and one essence." Likewise: "Therefore Christ is called the power and wisdom of God, because from the Father — who is power and wisdom — He Himself also is power and wisdom, just as He is light from the Father who is light, and He is the fount of life with God the Father who is the fount of life. The Son therefore is wisdom from the Father-wisdom, as the Son is light from the Father-light, and God the Son from God the Father, so that each individually is light and each individually is God and each individually is wisdom, and together one light, one God, one wisdom." Behold, with these words Augustine manifestly discloses from what sense those words and similar ones are to be taken — namely when it is said "substance from substance" or "substance begot substance."

But to this there also seems to be contrary what Hilary says in the fourth book On the Trinity: "The Son has nothing that is not born; and the admiration of the honor of the begotten one is in the honor of the one who begets." Since therefore the Son has essence — for the whole divine essence is in him — it seems that the divine essence itself is born. Likewise in the fifth book he says: "The birth of God cannot fail to hold the nature from which it has proceeded; for what subsists as other than God does not subsist from any other source than God." Behold, here he says that the birth of God proceeded from the nature — and so it seems from these words and the preceding ones that the nature of God both has begotten and has been begotten. What he says more openly in the ninth book On the Trinity: "We profess that the only-begotten God, remaining in the form of God, remained in the nature of the human being, and we do not pour back the unity of the servant form into the nature of the divine unity, nor again do we preach the Father in the Son through corporeal insinuation — but we confess that the nature born of the same genus had in itself naturally the nature of the one begetting it, which nature, remaining in the form of the generating nature, accepted the form of the nature and infirmity of the body. For the nature of God had not failed to exist, but the nature of God — remaining in itself — had assumed the lowliness of earthly birth, exercising the power of its own kind in the manner of the assumed lowliness." Behold, here he openly says that the nature begot, that the nature was begotten, and that the nature assumed a nature — which is denied by most. Likewise in the same work: "Is it an injury to the only-begotten God that the unbegottable God should be His Father, when the only-begotten birth subsists from the unbegottable God in the only-begotten nature?" Behold, here too he speaks of an only-begotten nature.

But since he wishes these words to be understood rightly, he himself says in the fourth book: "The meaning of words is to be taken from the reasons that prompted saying them, because things are not subject to speech, but speech to things." These words therefore can be understood thus: the Son has nothing except what is born — that is, He has nothing as God except what He received by being born; and in being born He had the subsisting nature of the Father in Himself. Hence the same Hilary adds in the fifth book: "The begotten one has the same nature as the one who begat — yet so that the one who is born is not the one who begat (for how could He be the Father, if He were begotten?), but the one who is begotten subsists in those very things in which the one who begot is wholly present; because the one who is begotten is not from any other source. And therefore what subsists in one from one is not referred to another. And so in the generation of the Son, the immutable God generating the immutable God follows, as it were, His own nature; and from the immutable God the perfect birth of the immutable God does not abandon its own nature. Let us therefore understand the nature of God as subsisting in that one, when God is in God; and there is no other God beyond the one who is God, because that God Himself and in Him is God."

The nature of God the Father is therefore taught to be truly present in God the Son, when the God who is God is understood to be in Him. For there is one in one, and one from one.

It is also said, and is frequently read in sacred Scripture, that the Father begot the Son from His own substance. Hence Augustine in the book On Faith to Peter says: "God the Father, born of no God, begot from His own nature, without beginning, God the Son, equal to Himself and coeternal with the same divinity with which He Himself is naturally eternal." Behold, here Augustine says that the Son was begotten from the nature of the Father. But there is one nature of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. If therefore the Son was begotten from the nature of the Father, He was begotten from the nature of the Son and of the Holy Spirit — indeed from the nature of the three persons. The same Augustine also in the fifteenth book On the Trinity says that Christ is the Son of the substance of the Father and begotten from the substance of the Father, explaining that word of the Apostle speaking of God the Father: "Who delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of His love" — "By what is said 'the Son of His love,'" he says, "let nothing else be understood than His beloved Son, than the Son of His substance. For the love of the Father, which is in His ineffably simple nature, is nothing other than that nature and substance itself — as we have often said and do not tire of repeating — and therefore the Son of His love is none other than the one who was begotten from His substance." Behold, here Augustine openly says that the Son was begotten from the substance of the Father and is the Son of the substance of the Father. The same Augustine also in the second book Against the Heretic Maximin asserts that the substance of God begot the Son and that the Son was begotten from the substance of the Father, saying: "Full of carnal thoughts, you do not think that the substance of God begets the Son from itself unless it suffers what the substance of flesh suffers when it begets. You err, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God. For you do not at all conceive of the true Son of God if you deny that He was born from the substance of the Father. For He was not the son of a man and then made the Son of God by God's gift — born of God by grace, not by nature. Or perhaps, even though He was not the son of a man, He was nevertheless already some sort of creature and was converted into the Son of God by God's changing Him? But none of this is so: therefore He was born either from nothing or from some substance. But lest we believe you think the Son of God is from nothing, you affirmed that you do not say that the Son of God is from nothing. From some substance, therefore, He is; and if not from the substance of the Father, tell us from which; but you will not find it. Then let it not weary you to confess with us that the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, is from the substance of the Father." Likewise in the same work: "We both read that we may be in His true Son, Jesus Christ. Tell us therefore whether this true Son of God — distinguished by some property from those who are sons by grace — is from no substance or from some? 'I do not say from none, nor will I say from nothing,' you say: therefore He is from some substance. I ask: from which? If He is not from the substance of the Father, seek another. If you find no other, acknowledge the substance of the Father, and confess the Son to be consubstantial with the Father." Likewise in the same work: "I confess that God the Father begot entirely incorruptibly, but that He begot what He Himself is. I also say what must be said often: either the Son of God was born from some substance or from none; if from none, then from nothing — which you no longer say; if truly from some substance, but not from the substance of the Father, He is not a true Son; if however from the substance of the Father, then Father and Son are of one and the same substance. But you do not want the Son to have been begotten from the substance of the Father; and yet you concede that He is neither from nothing nor from any matter, but from the Father — and you do not see how necessary it is that what is not from nothing nor from any other thing, but from God, cannot be except from the substance of God, and must be that which God is, from whom He is — that is, God born from God; because no other previously existed, but the coeternal nature is from God."

By these words introduced, it seems indicated that the divine substance begot the Son and that the Son was begotten from the substance of the Father and that the coeternal nature is from God and that the Father begot what He Himself is. But what He Himself is, is the divine essence; and so it could be thought that the divine essence begot. These words greatly move us, and how they are to be understood I would rather hear from others than transmit myself. Nevertheless, speaking without prejudging or rashness, from this sense can these words be taken: "the coeternal nature is from God" — that is, the Son who is coeternal with the Father is from the Father, such that He is of the same nature with Him or of the same nature. This sense is confirmed by Augustine, who there subjoins and as if explaining what he had said — for after saying "the coeternal nature is from God," he added: "The Son is not other than that from which He is — that is, the Father and Son are of one and the same substance." Then, more openly, he discloses that such an understanding is to be had from the said words, saying in the same book Against Maximin: "This Trinity is of one and the same substance — because the Son is not from some matter or from nothing, but from the one from whom He was begotten. Likewise the Holy Spirit is not from some matter or from nothing, but is from the one from whom He proceeds." With these words he clearly shows the reason for saying that the Son is from the substance of the Father — namely because He is begotten from the Father, being of the same substance with Him; and the Holy Spirit is from the substance of the Father and of the Son — because He proceeds from both, being of the same substance.

Behold, it is shown from those words that the Son and the Holy Spirit are not from nothing, but from something, yet not from any matter. Hence Hilary also in the twelfth book On the Trinity says: "The only-begotten God, since He was born, testifies the Father as his author; since He was born from one who remains, He was not born from nothing; and since He was born before time, He surpasses all understanding by being born." Here it is openly said that the Son was not born from nothing. Similarly the Holy Spirit is not to be said to be or to proceed from nothing — "because the Son was born from the substance of the Father" — that is, He is from the Father, with whom He is of the same substance and is the same substance. From this sense also must be taken the expression: "The Father begot what He Himself is" — that is, the Son, who is what the Father is. And that this is how it must be understood, Augustine discloses, saying in the first book Against Maximin: "The Father begot what He is; otherwise the Son is not true, if the Son is not what the Father is." Likewise: "the substance of God begot the Son" — that is, the Father who is substance begot the Son, who is the same substance and of the same substance. That this is how it is to be understood, Augustine shows, saying to Maximin: "Just as you say 'Spirit begot Spirit,' so say 'Spirit of the same nature or substance begot Spirit.' Likewise, just as you say 'God begot God,' so say 'God of the same nature or substance begot God.' If you believe and say this, you will be accused of nothing further in this matter." For with these words he discloses how the aforesaid are to be understood. Similarly: "The Son was born from the substance of the Father, or the Father begot the Son from His own nature or essence" — that is, from Himself by nature and essence He begot the Son of the same essence and nature, and who is the same essence and nature. Similarly expound that expression: "The Son of the substance of the Father" — that is, the Son of the Father-substance — that is, who is substance, with whom the Son also is the same substance, because the Son is consubstantial with the Father. And this sense is aided by the words of Augustine, who says in the seventh book On the Trinity: "We say three persons of the same essence, or we say three persons are one essence. But we do not say three persons from the same essence, as if what is essence were one thing and what is person were another." With these words he shows that it is not to be said that a person is from essence, except in the aforesaid sense. This sense is also confirmed from what the same author says in the fifteenth book On the Trinity: "As our knowledge is to the knowledge of God, so also our word — which is born from our knowledge — is unlike that Word of God which was born from the essence of the Father. And this is as if one were to say: from the knowledge of the Father, from the wisdom of the Father, or — which is more expressive — from the Father who is essence, from the Father who is knowledge, from the Father who is wisdom."

CHAPTER III.

Why the Word of the Father is called the natural Son.

Hence it is that the only-begotten of God alone is called the natural Son — because He is of the same nature and is the same nature as the Father. Hence Hilary in the fifth book On the Trinity, speaking of Christ, says: "He is Son by nature, because He has the same nature as the one who begot Him."

COMMENTARY ON DISTINCTION V.

On the comparison of generation to the abstract essential term — which is essence.

"After these things it is asked whether it must be conceded," etc.

DIVISION OF THE TEXT.

In the preceding distinction the Master raised the question about the comparison of generation to the concrete essential term — the name "God." In the present distinction he raises the question about the comparison of generation to the abstract essential term — which is "essence." And this part is divided into two parts.

In the first part he raises the question from the comparison of generation to essence in the account of a term — namely whether essence is generated; in the second, in the account of a principle — whether essence generates, etc., at: "Likewise it is not to be said that the divine essence begot the Son," etc.

Likewise, the first part has four sections. In the first he proposes the problems — namely whether the essence is generated or generates. In the second he adduces three arguments proving that the essence is not generated by the Father, at: "Therefore it is not to be said that the Father begot," etc. In the third he adduces arguments on the contrary side, at: "But to this there seems to be contrary," etc. In the fourth and last he resolves and expounds, at: "To which we respond."

"Likewise it is not to be said." This is the second part of this distinction, in which the Master determines the second part of the question — which is about the comparison of generation to essence in the account of a principle — and this part has three sections. In the first he determines this question, saying that essence does not generate; and he confirms this through an argument leading to the impossible. In the second he adduces authorities that are directly contrary to the aforesaid solution, at: "What appears to be contrary to what has been said." In the third he adduces authorities from which a contrariety can be elicited, at: "It is also said, and frequently," etc.

Likewise, the second part has four sections. In the first it adduces the contrary authorities of Augustine. In the second it expounds the adduced authorities, at: "But we determine this thus." In the third, against the aforesaid expositions, it adduces other authorities of Hilary in which a more express contrariety is noted, at: "But to this there also seems to be contrary." In the fourth it explains those authorities and confirms its explanation through the words of Hilary, at: "But since he wishes these words to be understood rightly."

"It is also said, and frequently in sacred Scripture it is read." This is the third part, in which he objects against the solution through authorities from which the contrariety of the aforesaid solution is elicited — because in these it is not said that the essence generates or is generated, but that from the essence or substance of the Father the Son is generated — and this part has four sections. In the first he adduces the contrary authorities. In the second he expounds those adduced, at: "By these words introduced it seems indicated" — where he resumes the aforesaid exposition. In the third he draws from those opinions a certain corollary, at: "It is also shown from those words," etc. In the fourth and last he returns to his matter and shows his exposition to be good, through the authority of Augustine, at: "And that this is how it must be understood," etc.

TREATMENT OF THE QUESTIONS.

In this part, for the understanding of the two principal parts of this distinction, two things are principally asked.

First, a question is asked concerning the comparison of generation to substance or essence in the account of a principle.

Second, a question is asked concerning the comparison of the same to essence in the account of a term.

And two things are asked with respect to the first, and two with respect to the second. With respect to the first it is asked:

First, whether substance or essence generates.

Second, whether someone is generated from substance.

ARTICLE I.

On the comparison of generation to substance or essence in the account of a principle.

QUESTION I.

Whether substance or essence generates.

Concerning the first — that substance does not generate — it is shown thus:

1. To generate implies a relation: therefore to whatever "to generate" belongs, "to be related" also belongs; but to be related does not belong to the essence: therefore neither does generating.

2. Likewise, to generate implies distinction: therefore to whatever "to generate" belongs, "to be distinguished" also consequently belongs; but the essence, since it is one, is not distinguished: therefore, etc. Or if it generates, there are several essences. And to these two incongruities the Master leads.
