questions.english:
DIST. VI. SOLE ARTICLE, QUESTION II.

---

QUESTION II.

Whether the generation in divine things is according to the account of will.

Second, it is inquired whether the generation of the Son is according to the account of will. And that it is not, is shown first by authorities, second by arguments.

First, it is shown by the authority of Hilary, who says in the book *On the Synods*: "Will brought substance to all creatures, but nature gave it to the Son."

2. Likewise, Augustine in the fifteenth book *On the Trinity* reproves Eunomius, who held that the Son of God is the Son of will: therefore, if he reproves rightly, the generation of the Son is not according to the condition of will.

3. Likewise, it is shown by arguments as follows: Generation, of itself, is a natural procession or one proceeding by the mode of nature; but this is a different mode of producing than by will: therefore, etc.

4. Likewise, the Son is the wisdom of the Father: therefore if he proceeds according to the account of will, then will is prior to wisdom; but this is unfitting, because cognition according to the natural order of understanding precedes affection or will: therefore, etc.

ON THE CONTRARY: 1. In every ordered nature, what is posited naturally is subject to the will, or at least conformed to the will, as is evident in the first man; but in God the nature is most perfectly ordered: therefore nothing is from nature or through nature that is not also through will: therefore, etc.

2. Likewise, the mode of proceeding in the created image and in the uncreated Trinity is analogous; but in the image, knowledge arises from the mind through the mediation of will: therefore the Son too proceeds from the Father through the mediation of will or by will. The minor premise is shown by Augustine in the ninth book *On the Trinity*: "An appetite precedes the birth of the mind, through which, as we find by seeking what we will to know, the offspring is born, namely knowledge itself."

3. Likewise, where there is greater communication, there is greater liberality; but the Father communicates more to the Son than to all creatures: therefore there is greater liberality there: therefore, since creatures proceed by the mode of liberality, much more so the Son, and so on.

4. Likewise, in creatures in the act of generation, both nature and will move simultaneously, and nothing is thereby detracted from the offspring: therefore if the Father produces according to his whole self more so than a creature does, then much more so through both nature and will.

5. Likewise, for this there is the authority of Hilary in the third book *On the Trinity*: "Before all time the Father begot the Son, imparting to his nativity all that he is as God through love"; if through love: therefore through will.

6. Likewise, Origen, speaking of the divine mind, says: "Bringing forth a shoot of will, he becomes the Father of the Word": therefore it seems that the Son is generated by the Father through will and that he is the Son of will.

---

*The generation of the Son is according to will in the account of approving, but not in the account of producing, except insofar as will is a principle conjoined to nature, and indeed in such a way that nature produces principally, with will accompanying.*

I respond: It must be said that will can be considered in two ways with respect to what is willed: either in the account of approving and loving, and in this way it stands with respect to every good, whether necessary or contingent, whether created or uncreated, whether from another — which is what is meant when some things are said to be from nature and others from will — or as conjoined.

If as a distinct principle, then will is distinguished in two ways, namely as supervening and as antecedent. The supervening will is that by which one passes from not-willing to willing; this is not in God, neither with respect to God nor with respect to creatures. For God has no new will either with respect to himself or with respect to another. The antecedent will precedes the effect in causality and duration; this indeed is in God, but not with respect to God, but only with respect to creatures; for all the divine persons exist simultaneously.

In another way, as will is considered as a principle conjoined to nature, it can be twofold; for then nature and will together are the principle; and either nature is the producing principle principally, with will accompanying, or conversely; for both cannot be the principal principle simultaneously.

If will is the principal principle, with nature accompanying, thus is the procession of the Holy Spirit, who proceeds by the mode of love, yet alike in nature. But if nature is the primary principle, with will accompanying, thus is the generation of the Son, who is produced as wholly alike and by the mode of nature, and nonetheless as beloved; and therefore it is said that the Father is well pleased in him, and in Colossians 1 the Son is called the Son of love.

1. To the objection on the contrary side, that generation is by the mode of will or according to the account of will: it must be said that this is to be understood either of the approving will, as the two authorities of Hilary and Origen show, or of the accompanying will, as the argument placed first indicates.

2. To the objection concerning the likeness of the image: it must be said that in this respect the created image is unlike the uncreated Trinity, as Augustine says in the fifteenth book *On the Trinity*, because there the word is not born through inquiry, as it can be born in us; whence this argument tends rather to the opposite of what is proposed than to the proposed conclusion.

3. To the objection that there is greater communication in the generation of the Son, etc.: it must be said that greater or lesser communication does not make the mode of emanating be according to liberality or according to the mode of will, but rather the mode or ground of communicating does. And because the Father communicates to creatures through will, such that his will is the producing cause, but to the Son through the fecundity of nature: therefore the Son is not said to be produced through will in the same manner as creatures.

4. To the objection that in human generation nature and will move simultaneously: it must be said that this is owing to a deficiency rather than to completeness; because a father cannot generate by himself, but only through conjunction with another who is distant, which comes about at the command of the will; but God has no need of the assistance of another; and therefore the cases are not parallel.

[Scholion omitted]

---
questions.notes:
- **Structural position**: This question is the second of three in the Sole Article of Distinction 6, following the question on necessity (Q.1) and preceding the question on exemplarity (Q.3). The chunk opens with cross-references to other doctors (Alexander of Hales, Scotus, Thomas, Albert, etc.) that belong to the scholion of Q.1; these have been omitted as critical apparatus.

- **"approving will" vs. "accompanying will" (*voluntas approbans* / *voluntas concomitans*)**: The *Conclusio* turns on this distinction. The will approves and loves every good (necessary or contingent); the will accompanies but does not principally cause the generation of the Son. This is distinguished from will as the *principal* productive principle, which would assimilate the Son's procession to that of creatures or of the Spirit.

- **"supervening will" (*voluntas accedens*)**: The will *de novo* arising, passing from non-willing to willing — categorically excluded from God due to divine immutability. Rendered "supervening" to capture the technical sense of *accedens* (something newly added or coming upon).

- **"antecedent will" (*voluntas antecedens*)**: Precedes the effect in causality and duration. Present in God but only with respect to creatures, not with respect to the divine persons themselves (who are simultaneous). The anecdotal disputed question quoted in the Scholion adds "accompanying and accepting will" (*voluntas concomitans et acceptans*) as the third mode, explicitly applicable to God with respect to both himself and creatures.

- **Holy Spirit vs. Son — mode of procession**: The *Respondeo* articulates a formal distinction that will be treated at length in D.10–11 and D.26: the Spirit proceeds *per modum amoris* (will as principal principle, nature accompanying), the Son *per modum naturae* (nature as principal principle, will accompanying). This asymmetry is foundational to Bonaventure's Trinitarian theology.

- **Colossians 1 reference**: "Son of love" (*Filius caritatis*) — Col. 1:13 (*in regnum Filii caritatis suae*). Rendered "Son of love" to match the Vulgate phrasing and Bonaventure's usage.

- **Reply to argument 2 (the image analogy)**: Bonaventure's response is notable: the Augustinian analogy of the mind producing knowledge through desire (cited in the *sed contra*) actually cuts *against* applying a will-mediated model to the Son's generation, because in God there is no discursive inquiry. The direction of the argument is inverted.

- **OCR artifacts**: The chunk opening contains heavily garbled cross-reference strings (*a. I ; S. p. I. tr. 7. q. 30. ni. 3. a. 2.* etc.) that are clearly the tail end of the Q.1 scholion apparatus; these have been omitted. Minor OCR noise (*soimio* for *solutio*, *homine* for *hominibus* in context) corrected silently.

DIST. VI. SOLE ARTICLE, QUESTION III.

---

QUESTION III.

Whether the generation of the Son is according to the account of exemplarity.

Finally, it is inquired whether the generation of the Son from the Father is according to the account of exemplarity. And that it is, seems to be shown in the following manner.

1. On the text of the Psalm, *God has spoken once*, the Gloss for Augustine says: "that is, he begot the Son, in whom he disposed all things"; but the eternal disposition expresses the account of an exemplar: therefore if the Son proceeds as the Word, he proceeds by the mode of exemplarity.

2. Likewise, the generation of the Son from the Father is analogous to the production of knowledge from the mind; but knowledge proceeds from the mind according to the account of an exemplar, because the exemplar is the ground of knowing: therefore, etc.

3. Likewise, what is image in the product corresponds to exemplar in the producer; for when the product expressly represents, it is called an image. Similarly, when the producer expressly represents, it is called an exemplar: therefore, since the Son proceeds as image, by the same account he proceeds by the mode of exemplarity.

4. Likewise, every cognitive principle of a thing to be produced produces according to the account of exemplifying; but the Father is the cognitive principle of the Son: therefore he produces the Son according to the account of an exemplar. If you say that this does not suffice, and that it is further necessary that the exemplar and the exemplified differ in form and nature: this amounts to nothing, because if a man, in generating a man, could generate such a one as he conceives, then that generation would be not only according to nature but also according to an exemplar. But the Father produced the Son wholly as he knew and willed: therefore, etc. If you say that even this does not suffice, but that it is further necessary that the exemplar precede: it is objected that if God had created the world from eternity — per impossibile — the world would nonetheless have been produced according to the account of exemplarity.

ON THE CONTRARY: 1. Among lower things, agents acting by nature and agents acting by an exemplar are divided as opposites, just as nature and intellect are: therefore what is produced according to nature is not produced according to the account of an exemplar; but the Son is produced by the Father according to nature: therefore, etc.

2. Likewise, everything that produces something according to the account of exemplarity produces according to the account of will; but the Father, as has been shown above, does not produce the Son through will: therefore, etc.

3. Likewise, there is no form of a form, and therefore no exemplar of an exemplar; but the Son is the art and exemplar of all things: therefore he has no exemplar in the Father: therefore he does not proceed according to the account of exemplarity.

4. Likewise, what is in another according to truth is not in that other according to an exemplar; but the Son is in the Father according to truth: therefore not according to an exemplar; but what is not in another according to an exemplar does not proceed according to the account of an exemplar: therefore, etc.

---

*The Son proceeds from the Father as the ground of exemplifying, not as an exemplified thing from an exemplar.*

I respond: It must be said that, just as to proceed by the mode of will and liberality is twofold — for in one way that which is not liberality itself but which is made or given from liberality proceeds by the mode of liberality, and thus creatures proceed from God; and in another way that which is the ground of liberality, such as love, proceeds by this mode, and thus the Holy Spirit proceeds as love, which is the gift in which all gifts are given — so likewise to proceed by the mode of exemplarity is twofold. In one way, as an exemplified thing properly speaking; and thus the creature proceeds from God as an exemplified thing from an exemplar, and in this way the exemplar imports formal causality with respect to the exemplified. In the other way, something is said to proceed by the mode of exemplarity as the ground of exemplifying. And it is in this latter way that the Son himself appears to proceed, who is called the Word of the Father, through whom the Father not only speaks himself but also disposes all other things. Hence the Son is called by Augustine in the sixth book *On the Trinity* "the art full of all living reasons." And from this arises what is customarily said: that one who denies that ideas exist denies that the Son of God exists. And this mode of proceeding according to exemplarity is not repugnant to natural procession; on the contrary, it cannot but be natural. The other mode, however, is repugnant to natural procession; for it proceeds according to the command of the will, such that the producer and the produced differ as cause and caused, and the one is not in the other according to truth.

Hence the arguments adduced in support of this side proceed according to this way and conclude truly according to it; but according to the other way none of them concludes — indeed, all of them are to be answered by denial.

Those arguments, however, that are objected on the contrary side all proceed according to the other way, because they speak of proceeding by the mode of exemplarity in the sense of being an exemplified thing; which is evident, because they are drawn from the account of eternal disposition, of cognition, and of image. The last argument, however, does conclude that it proceeds by the mode of exemplarity as an exemplified thing, and for that reason it is to be answered by denial.

4. To the objection that every principle of a thing to be produced, if it has cognition, produces through an exemplar: it must be said that this is false, unless the account of cognition precedes in such a way that it has pre-cognition at least according to the account of cause with respect to effect; and this ordering requires essential or substantial diversity. For the exemplified, precisely as exemplified, is not in the exemplifying agent according to truth, but according to likeness — which likeness, since it is the ground of knowing and of exemplifying, is called an exemplar. The Son therefore proceeds according to the account of exemplarity, not as an exemplified thing through an exemplar, but as the very exemplar or ground of exemplifying all other things. And if you object that the exemplar is common to the whole Trinity, the Master of Auxerre responds to this in his question on the archetypal world or on ideas, that the idea or archetypal world is not merely appropriated to the Son, but is also proper to him.

Or alternatively it can be said that insofar as exemplar expresses the account of knowing, it is in this way common to the whole Trinity and appropriated to the Son, as wisdom is. But insofar as it further expresses the account of emanating, it is in this way proper to the Son; and it is in this sense that it is imported by the name Word, as will be more fully apparent below.

questions.notes:
- **"ground of exemplifying" (*ratio exemplandi*)**: The *Conclusio* hinges on the distinction between the Son as *exemplatum* (exemplified thing, as creatures are relative to God) and the Son as *ratio exemplandi* (the very ground or principle by which other things are exemplified). The Son is not a copy of a prior divine idea; he *is* the living art through which the Father conceives and disposes all things. *Ratio* here carries its full scholastic sense of formal ground or principle; "ground of exemplifying" is preferred over "reason for exemplifying" to capture the ontological rather than merely logical force.

- **"the art full of all living reasons" (*ars plena omnium rationum viventium*)**: Augustine, *De Trinitate* VI.10.11. The phrase is a touchstone for Bonaventure's exemplarism throughout the *Commentary*. "Art" (*ars*) here means the divine intellect as the seat of the eternal ideas (*rationes*) of all created things; the Son as Word is identified with this art.

- **"one who denies that ideas exist denies that the Son of God exists"**: A formula recurring in Bonaventurian and Franciscan theology, expressing the intimate link between the doctrine of divine exemplar ideas and the eternal generation of the Son. It is not directly quoted from a source here but treated as a *consuetum dici* (customary saying).

- **"Master of Auxerre" (*Altissiodorensis*)**: William of Auxerre (d. 1231), author of the *Summa Aurea*. The Quaracchi editors note the reference is to a passage in *Summa* I treating the archetypal world and ideas, distinguishing what is *appropriated* to the Son (insofar as it pertains to wisdom) from what is *proper* to him (insofar as he is Image and Word). The alternative solution at the end of the *Respondeo* (appropriation vs. proper predication of exemplar) reflects this distinction.

- **"per impossibile"**: Technical scholastic phrase for a counterfactual hypothesis introduced for the sake of argument; retained in Latin as is conventional in English philosophical writing, or rendered "per impossibile" without translation.

- **"denial" (*interemptio*)**: A technical term in scholastic disputation for the move of simply denying the premise of an opposing argument (as opposed to distinguishing or conceding it). Rendered "denial" consistently; the Latin *interemptio* (literally "cutting off") carries the sense of a direct refutation that removes the argument at its root.

- **Doubt I**: The chunk ends mid-sentence in Doubt I, which concerns Augustine's statement that the Father generates neither by will nor by necessity — a division that appears insufficiently exhaustive (why not "naturally / necessarily"?). The resolution will appear in the next chunk.

- **OCR artifacts**: *soimio* (for *solutio*) corrected at two points. The cross-reference apparatus at the opening (Peter of Tarantaise, Richard of Mediavilla, Aegidius Romanus, Dionysius Carthusianus) belongs to the Q.2 scholion and has been omitted.

DIST. VI. DOUBTS.

---

*[Continuation of Doubt I, begun in the preceding chunk:]*

— one who responds to a manifold statement by simply affirming or denying, responds badly, as the Philosopher says: therefore, etc.

I respond: It must be said that Augustine responds according to the heretic's intended sense. Although the statement is in itself manifold, nevertheless, because the heretic accepts it in one sense, that multiplicity would not bear on the resolution, since the argument does not proceed according to that multiplicity. But the distinction of a manifold proposition, when the deception does not turn on that multiplicity, pertains more to ostentation than to a genuine response.

---

DOUBT II.

Likewise there is a question concerning the statement: *Let us say that the Word of God is the Son of God by nature, not by will.* For this seems to speak rightly, because the Father is God by one thing and Father by another, since he is God by deity and Father by paternity, as Augustine says. But the Son is God by the nature of deity: therefore he will not be called Son by that, but by sonship itself.

I respond: It must be said that the ablative in question can be construed formally; and in that case the statement is false, because formally the Son is God by one thing, namely nature, and Son by another. It can again be construed originally and in the account of a principle; and in that case it is true, and the sense is that the Son has his origin from the Father naturally.

---

DOUBT III.

Likewise there is a question concerning the statement: *Some one shrewdly replied* — since Augustine commends this solution, which ought not to be commended, because to multiply an inconvenience is not to resolve it.

I respond: It must be said that there is a solution *ad hominem* and a solution addressed to the statement itself; and sometimes it is better and more useful to resolve *ad hominem* than to address the statement directly, for instance when the respondent is contentious and refuses to understand the truth, and when the bystanders are simple and cannot grasp the truth and its subtlety. Therefore, because the heretic was rejecting and opposing the truth, it was necessary to oppose the opponent, and in such a way that he would be most deprived of glory and the bystanders of his fallacy. Therefore Augustine commends this response, because he plainly bound the objector with his own question. The Lord taught this mode of responding in Matthew 21, where he said: *The baptism of John — was it from heaven, or from men?* etc.

Likewise it is asked, since the statement has not been answered directly, how it ought to be answered. For the heretic's division seems to be through immediates, since willing and not-willing are opposed contradictorily, between which no middle term falls. And to this it must be said that the heretic asks concerning the supervening or antecedent will; and then neither part is true, nor are the members opposed contradictorily but contrarily. For not-willing and willing express contrary acts of will, between which a middle term falls. For there is something with respect to which the will has neither the account of cause nor of repugnance; and thus the matter is clarified.

---

DOUBT IV.

Likewise there is a question concerning the Master's solution, where he seems to say something false when he says: *The knowledge and foreknowledge of God is concerning both good and evil things.* For the Gloss on the Psalm text *What I knew not, they asked of me*, says: "Art knows no vice"; but in God there is the art of arts: therefore, etc. If you say that he does not know it in a practical mode but only in a speculative mode: *on the contrary*, only that which shines forth in a thing is known in this way by it; but evil things do not shine forth in God: therefore, etc.

Likewise, the Master does not seem to answer the argument; for to multiply an inconvenience is not to resolve it.

I respond: It must be said that, as will be stated below, God knows evil things through himself, just as the straight judges the crooked and light judges darkness; nor is it necessary that evil shine forth in God, but it suffices that the opposite of evil shine forth in him.

---

DOUBT V.

Likewise there is a question concerning what is said in the note: that the holy Church anathematizes those who say that God did not generate by counsel. For this seems to contradict what Damascene says, that in God there is no counsel, because counsel is of an ignorant nature.

I respond: It must be said that "counsel" (*consilium*) is used in two ways: in one way it means to take counsel, and in this sense it implies ignorance; likewise *consilium* in this sense is derived from this; in another way *consilere* means to give counsel, and in this sense it implies knowledge, and this can be transferred to divine things. For God in no way takes counsel from another. Hence it must be noted that in counsel there are two elements: there is the cognition of a hidden matter, and there is a firm disposition. Therefore, because in God there is most true cognition of hidden things and immutability, it is rightly said that counsel is in him. Hence Gregory: "God changes his sentence, but not his counsel."

---

DISTINCTION VII.

Whether the Father was able or willed to generate the Son.

Here it is customarily asked by some whether the Father was able or willed to generate the Son. For if, they say, he was able and willed to generate the Son: then he was able to do something and willed something that the Son neither was able nor willed; for the Son neither was able nor willed to generate a Son. To this sophism we respond easily by saying: to be able or to will to generate the Son is not to be able or to will something that is a subject of will or of power. There is nonetheless some power or will, namely the power or will to beget the Son; and therefore the meaning of the word in question must be distinguished: to be able or to will to beget the Son is to be able or to will something. For the generation of the Son is not among those things that are subject to divine power and will, nor is it something among all things or concerning all things, but above all things and before all things. For he did not first will or have the power before he generated; just as he did not first exist before he generated, because from eternity he existed and from eternity he generated. We can also see this from a parallel case. For the Father can be Father and wills to be Father; but the Son neither can nor wills to be Father: therefore the Father can or wills to be something that the Son neither can nor wills to be. This does not follow, because to be Father is not to be something absolutely, but to be toward something, as will be shown in what follows.

But we are considerably moved by what Augustine says in the second book *Against Maximinus*, who asserted that the Father is more powerful than the Son, on the ground that the Father begot the Son as God the Creator, while the Son did not do so; and he said that the Father was able to beget one who was not the Son, and that therefore the Father is more powerful than the Son. In response to this, Augustine appears to say that the Son also was able to beget, wishing to show that the Father is not more powerful than the Son, in these words: "Far be it that the Father be therefore more powerful than the Son, as you think, because the Father begot a Creator while the Son did not; for it was not that he could not, but that it was not fitting." See and carefully attend to these words: *it was not that he could not, but that it was not fitting.* For he seems to say that the Son was able to beget, but it was not fitting; and so he was able to do what was not fitting. But why it was not fitting he adds by saying: "For divine generation would be immoderate if the begotten Son were to beget a grandson for the Father, because even that grandson, unless he were to beget a great-grandson for the grandfather, would according to your remarkable wisdom be called powerless. Likewise even that one, if he were not to beget a grandson for the grandfather and a great-grandson for the great-grandfather, would not be called omnipotent by you; nor would the series of generation be completed if one were always born from another; nor would anyone complete it, if one omnipotent person were not sufficient. Therefore the nature of the Father begot an omnipotent Son; it did not make him."

But this — namely that the Son was able to beget — does not seem to some to be tenable. For if the Son was able to beget, he was able to be a father; and if he was able to be a father, then he was able to be the father either of himself, or of the Father, or of the Holy Spirit —

*[Text continues, resuming after a gap in the OCR:]*

— whether there is in the Father a power that is not in the Son. For if the Father is by nature powerful to generate the Son, and the Son is not, this is evident, etc. And to this question the Master responds that the power in the Father and the Son is entirely the same. But because this was in doubt, he therefore objects against the said solution and determines through a distinction. Second, he responds to the first question by distinguishing whether the Son has the power of generating, where he says: *Likewise, when it is said that the Son does not have*, etc. For if this is understood actively, the meaning is false, namely that the Son is able to generate. But if it is understood passively, namely that he has the power by which he can be generated, it is true. And this distinction is grounded by some on the fact that the gerund *generandi* can be understood in a passive or active sense. If in a passive sense, then it is true; and the meaning is: the Son has the power of generating, that is, the power by which he is generated. If in an active sense, this can be twofold, because it can be the gerund of a personal verb, and then it has a determinate subject and is false; for the meaning is: the Son has, etc., that is, the Son has the power by which the Son himself generates; or it can be the gerund of an impersonal verb, and then it has no fixed subject and the statement is true; for the meaning is: the Son has the power of generating, that is, he has the power by which someone generates — though this sense the Master does not posit.

---

TREATMENT OF THE QUESTIONS.

For the understanding of what the Master says concerning the power of generating, four things are inquired.

First, it is inquired whether the power to generate in divine things expresses something absolute or something relative.

Second, whether the Father communicates to the Son the power of generating, that is, whether the power of generating is in the Son.

Third, whether the power to generate and the power to create are one single power or not.

Fourth, whether the power to be generated and the power to be created are univocal powers.

---

QUESTION I.

Whether the power of generating expresses something absolute or something relative.

Concerning the first point, that the power to generate expresses something absolute, it is shown:

1. First, by the authority of the Master in the text: "The Father is powerful only through nature, and his power is nature itself or essence"; but nature and power express something absolute, not something relative: therefore so too does the power of generating.

2. Likewise, it is shown by argument as follows: to generate is to produce something alike in nature; but according to the Philosopher "nature is a force implanted in things, producing like from like": therefore the force of generating regards nature or essence as such, not the person; but everything of this kind expresses something absolute: therefore, etc.

3. Likewise, "in perpetual things, to be and to be able are not different": therefore much more so in eternal things; therefore being and being-able are the same, and so too potency and essence; but being and essence in divine things express something absolute, not something relative, whether said by itself or with something added; hence the essence of the Father expresses something absolute: therefore by the same account the power of generating.

4. Likewise, in divine things the power to know and to will are the same in reality; but in divine things there is no knowledge that is proper or relative — rather, knowledge expresses something absolute and belongs to the three persons, and likewise will: therefore the power of generating expresses something absolute, i.e., the essence.

ON THE CONTRARY: 1. The Master says in the text, and it seems from the first chapter: the power to generate is not the power to do something absolute; therefore it does not express something absolute; and it expresses either something absolute or something relative: therefore, etc.

2. Likewise, it is shown by argument: powers are distinguished by their acts: therefore if the act of a power expresses something absolute, so does the power; and if it expresses something relative, then so does the power likewise. But it is clear that to generate in divine things does not express something absolute but something relative: therefore neither does the power to generate.

3. Likewise, although in creatures force and operation differ, yet in God they are the same, as Dionysius holds: therefore in God the power to generate and generating are the same; but to generate in divine things expresses something relative and not something absolute: therefore likewise the power to generate.

4. Likewise, the Father generates and is able to generate: either, then, he is able because he generates, or he generates because he is able. It is clear that he is not able to generate because he generates: therefore he generates because he is able to generate. If therefore the account of what is proper ought itself to be proper, then the power of generating ought to be proper; and nothing is proper in divine things except what expresses something relative: therefore, etc.

5. Likewise, every active power that inheres in a creature inheres by reason of some conditions or properties, as is evident. For the power to illuminate inheres in a luminous thing through light, and the power to heat in a hot thing through heat. Although the power of generating is not active, it is nonetheless analogous to an active power: therefore, since it inheres in the Father, it inheres through some property; and that property either expresses something absolute or something relative. If something absolute: then it inheres in all persons, and therefore the power to generate does also, which the Master explicitly denies: therefore it expresses something relative; and therefore so does the power that inheres according to it: therefore, etc.

---

CONCLUSION.

Among the three opinions on this matter, the more probable seems to be the one that holds that the power of generating signifies both relation and substance, but relation in the primary sense.

I respond: It must be said that concerning this problem there have been three positions.

There were some who distinguished the power of generating, saying that the power of generating can be called a bare power or a disposed power. If called a bare power, they wished to say that it expresses something absolute and is in all three persons, since this power so understood follows upon nature; hence, since nature is in each person, so likewise is a power of this kind. But as it expresses a disposed power — because it has no disposition or fitness to issue in the act of generation except in the sole person of the Father — they wished to say that it expresses something relative.

But the words of this position do not seem true or sound. Not true, I say, because that whose power is bare is naturally fit to be disposed in like manner; if therefore the power of generating, as bare power, belongs to the three persons, likewise the disposed power; and thus each person could generate. Furthermore it does not seem sound: for to posit a bare power that stands indifferently to being and not-being with respect to generation — which is altogether necessary — does not seem to be said soundly or properly.

There were also others who said that since in divine things the power to be and being are the same, and potency and essence are the same, just as potency and essence express something absolute, so too being and power to be. And just as when I say the essence of the Father and the essence of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, or the being of the Father, the being of the Son, the being of the Holy Spirit, I do not say a different essence or a different being, but of one and another — so when I say the power of the Father, or that the Father is able to generate and the Son is able —

- **Chunk structure**: This chunk is unusually large and covers two distinct sections: (1) Doubts I–V on Distinction VI, and (2) the opening of Distinction VII, including the Lombard's base text on *potentia generandi* and the opening of Question I of that Distinction's questions. The *Tractatio Quaestionum* header and Q.I structure that appear near the end belong to Distinction VII, not Distinction VI.

- **Doubt I (completion)**: The resolution clarifies why Bonaventure does not fault Augustine for failing to distinguish the proposition explicitly: when the heretic argues from only one of its senses, the multiplicity of the proposition is simply not in play, and distinguishing it would be pedantic rather than genuinely responsive. The reference is to *Sophistici Elenchi* II (Boethius translation): one who responds simply to an equivocal statement responds badly.

- **Doubt II — ablative construal (*formaliter* vs. *originaliter*)**: A characteristic grammatical-theological move. The ablative "by nature" (*natura*) can be read as expressing the formal constituent of sonship (false — sonship is constituted by filiation, not nature) or as expressing the principle of origin (true — the Son originates from the Father naturally). This distinction recurs in several prior chunks on *esse* and *essentia*.

- **Doubt III — *ad hominem* vs. *ad orationem***: Bonaventure defends Augustine's strategy of *refutatio ad hominem* (binding the heretic with his own question, as Christ did with the Pharisees in Matt. 21:25) as sometimes superior to formal logical response. The second sub-question then provides the direct logical answer: the heretic's dichotomy (willing / not-willing) is contrary, not contradictory, so a middle term is available — God's relation to the generation of the Son falls outside both members.

- **Distinction VII base text (Lombard)**: The passage beginning "Here it is customarily asked…" is the Lombard's own text (*littera Magistri*) for Distinction VII, which Bonaventure translates/expounds as usual. The extensive quotation from Augustine's *Against Maximinus* II is embedded in the Lombard's text and translated accordingly; it concerns the provocative claim that the Son *potuit gignere* (was able to beget) — a claim requiring careful qualification.

- **"something absolute / something relative" (*quid* / *ad aliquid*)**: The central logical distinction of D.VII Q.I. In Aristotelian-scholastic usage, *quid* (literally "what") refers to substance or essence-predicates; *ad aliquid* (literally "toward something") refers to relational predicates. The question is whether *potentia generandi* is a proper relational predicate (belonging to the Father alone) or an absolute one (common to the divine essence and all three persons). The *Conclusio* holds the former.

- **Three opinions on *potentia generandi***: (1) bare vs. disposed power — refuted as unsound; (2) identity of *posse* and *esse* — begins to be stated but is cut off at chunk end; (3) the preferred position (*Conclusio*): the power signifies both relation and substance, but relation in the primary sense (*in recto*). The full articulation of position 2 and the *Conclusio*'s development will continue in the next chunk.

- **OCR lacuna**: There is a significant gap in the OCR between lines 193 and 292 (approximately 100 lines), corresponding to the continuation of the argument about whether the Son *potuit gignere* and its resolution. The text resumes mid-discussion with the Master's response distinguishing active and passive senses of *generandi*. The lacuna has been flagged with a bracketed note; the missing material should be recovered from the source PDF before finalizing this chunk's translation.

- **"gerund of a personal vs. impersonal verb"**: A technical grammatical distinction used to parse the ambiguity of *potentiam generandi*. The gerund of a personal verb implies a fixed subject (the Son generates); the gerund of an impersonal verb leaves the subject indeterminate (someone generates). The Master accepts only the passive reading and does not posit the impersonal active reading.

DIST. VII. SOLE ARTICLE, QUESTION I.

---

*[Continuation of the response to Question I, begun in the preceding chunk:]*

— a relation toward origin, and therefore it can express a proper relation of person to person. Hence the Master's analogy does not hold according to this position, namely that just as there is one will by which the Father wills to be Father and does not will to be Son, and conversely, so likewise there is one power, as it seems.

But if someone wishes to maintain the Master's position, he can easily respond to all the arguments on the other side.

1. For no argument proves that power as such expresses something proper, but only that the power of generating taken actively — or the power to generate — expresses, by reason of what is added to it, a relation toward the person, and thus expresses something relative; but this is only by reason of what is added. Hence it must be noted that there are four kinds of names in divine things. Some are essential names expressed essentially, such as deity and majesty; some are essential names expressed personally, such as the power of generating; some are personal names expressed personally, such as generating and generated; and some are personal names expressed essentially, such as sent, incarnate, and the like, which express a relation to a person and are therefore personal, and an effect in a creature, and are therefore expressed essentially.

2. To the two following arguments it is easy to respond, because that principle does not hold true except when an act encompasses the whole power; this is not so with the power of God, because in God the power to beget and the power to be begotten are the same.

3. To the objection that the power to generate and generating are the same: it must be said that this does not follow. For although the Father and substance are the same, it does not therefore follow that if "Father" is said relatively, so too is "substance," as will be more fully apparent below.

4–5. To the last two arguments it is difficult to respond well; yet one can say that those arguments do not conclude that power expresses something relative of itself, but only by reason of what is added, namely generating; and thus the rest is clear.

[Scholion omitted]

---

QUESTION II.

Whether the power of generating is in the Son.

Second, it is inquired whether the power of generating is in the Son; and that it is, seems to be shown by authorities and by arguments.

1. First, as follows: Hilary says in the ninth book *On the Trinity*: "The Son has in himself by nature a nature fitted to beget": therefore the nature in the Son is naturally disposed to generate.

2. Likewise, Augustine in the book *Against Maximinus*: "For it was not that the Son could not generate"; but two negations are equivalent to one affirmation: therefore he was able to generate.

3. Likewise, it is shown by arguments as follows: to generate is more ordered toward the power of generating than toward the power of spirating; but the Father, in generating the Son, communicates to him the power of spirating: therefore, much more so, the power of generating.

4. Likewise, the Son is the most express image of the Father: therefore he imitates the Father to such a degree that no more similar image can be conceived; but if the Son is conceived as generating, he is conceived as imitating more fully: therefore if he imitates more than anyone can conceive, he does so also in the act of generating.

5. Likewise, a parallel case seems to show this: there is greater communication and diffusion in eternal light than in created light; but created light gives to its radiance the power of producing another, and so proceeding; and if it were of infinite power, it would produce infinite radiances: therefore, etc.

6. Likewise, in carnal generation a father is not said to have perfectly generated a son unless he gives him the power of generating: therefore by the same account, and indeed much more so, the Son will not be perfect unless he has the power for that which the Father is able to do; therefore the power to generate. Or if it is not so in divine things, then I ask the reason why, in the perfection of eternal generation, there is no communication of the power of generating such as there is in created generation.

ON THE CONTRARY: 1. Augustine, in *Against Maximinus*, says "that it was not fitting for the Son to generate"; but if it was not fitting, neither was it appropriate; but everything unfitting in God is impossible: therefore it was impossible for the Son to generate: therefore the Son cannot generate: therefore he does not have the power of generating, because whoever has a power is powerful with respect to that power: therefore, etc.

2. Likewise, Anselm in the *Proslogion*: "One who can do what does not befit him — the more he is able to do it, the more adversity and perversity can prevail against him": therefore, since it does not befit the Son to generate, if he were able to do so, that power would be in him a misery; but he has no misery: therefore neither does he have the power of generating.

3. Likewise, the same is proven by argument as follows: in everything in which two things are necessarily distinguished, if one necessarily belongs to the one, it is impossible that it ever belong to the other, as is evident — if Peter and John are necessarily distinguished by whiteness, and whiteness belongs to Peter, it is impossible that it belong to John; but the Father and the Son are personally distinct in such a way that they must necessarily be distinct, and there is no —

questions.notes:
- **Chunk structure**: This chunk opens with the tail of Q.I's reply to objections (the four-fold taxonomy of divine names and the final responses) and then begins Q.II in full. Q.II asks the more pointed question arising from Q.I: even if the power of generating is a relational predicate proper to the Father, does the Son nonetheless possess it in some sense? The chunk ends mid-argument in the *sed contra* of Q.II.

- **Four-fold taxonomy of divine names**: A compact but important classificatory scheme —
  (1) *essentialia essentialiter dicta* (e.g., deity, majesty): absolutely common to all three persons;
  (2) *essentialia personaliter dicta* (e.g., power of generating): essentially grounded but personally expressed — this is Bonaventure's preferred characterization of *potentia generandi*;
  (3) *personalia personaliter dicta* (e.g., generating, generated): relational and proper;
  (4) *personalia essentialiter dicta* (e.g., sent, incarnate): personal in reference but expressed through an essential effect in the creature.
  This taxonomy resolves the apparent tension between Q.I's *Conclusio* (power of generating signifies relation *in recto*) and the Master's position (it signifies substance): both capture something true, depending on whether the compound phrase *potentia generandi* is read as a single term or analyzed into its components.

- **"the power to beget and the power to be begotten are the same in God"**: Response to arguments 2–3 of the *sed contra* in Q.I. The identity of active and passive potency in God blocks the inference from act to power that would work in creaturely contexts. This is an unusual claim that requires the context of divine simplicity and the identity of essence with all divine attributes.

- **Q.II argument 3 (*spirating* vs. *generating*)**: The argument draws on a common scholastic intuition: if the Father communicates the power of spirating (which belongs to Father and Son jointly) to the Son in the very act of generating him, why not also the power of generating? Bonaventure will need to show why the two powers are asymmetric.

- **Q.II argument 6 (perfect generation)**: A forceful argument from the logic of perfect communication: in creaturely generation, a father who does not give his son the capacity to reproduce has not fully communicated his nature. The challenge to the opposing view is explicit — Bonaventure anticipates a *quaero rationem* (I ask the reason) if the analogy is simply denied.

- **Anselm, *Proslogion***: The citation is to the chapter on divine omnipotence (*Proslogion* 7), where Anselm distinguishes genuine power from the power to do what is unfitting, which is actually a form of weakness or liability. The argument is used here against the Son's possession of the power of generating: if the Son had it but it was unfitting to exercise it, this would be a deficiency rather than a perfection.

- **OCR**: The opening of the chunk is a direct continuation of the *Respondeo* from D.VII Q.I that was cut off in the previous chunk (the second of the three opinions and the *Conclusio*'s defense). The transition is seamless in the translation. Cross-reference apparatus at the scholion boundary has been omitted.

DIST. VII. SOLE ARTICLE, QUESTION II.

---

*[Continuation of the sed contra of Question II, begun in the preceding chunk:]*

— are distinguished except in this, that the one is generating and the other generated: therefore, since generating belongs to the Father, it is impossible that it belong to the Son: therefore the Son cannot generate: therefore he does not have the power of generating.

4. Likewise, the generation of the Son from the Father is expressly analogous to the generation of the word from the mind; but the generated word does not have the power of generating another word — on the contrary, every word must proceed immediately from the mind: therefore if the uncreated Word is rightly analogous, he does not have the power of generating, but the power of generating is in the Father alone.

5. Likewise, let the argument of Augustine be made, leading to an impossibility. If the Son has the power or ability to generate, suppose that he does generate; I ask the same of the second likewise; and if there is no stopping at the first, it is necessary to posit infinite sons, because by the same account that one does not stop at the first, neither does one stop at any: therefore, if there is a stopping point — since the contrary is repugnant to divine completeness — but by the same account that one stops at any point, one stops at the first: therefore the first does not have the power of generating.

6. Likewise, let the argument of Richard be made: if the Son were to generate another son, then since a begotten son is more closely related to the father than to the grandfather, accordingly there would not be there a supreme and equal connection: therefore neither a supreme and equal love: therefore neither perfect blessedness — all of which pious faith rejects as supremely impossible.

---

CONCLUSION.

*The Father does not communicate the power of generating to the Son, which is proven by two arguments.*

I respond: The opinion of some is that in the Son there is the power of generating, but he does not generate — and this not because he cannot, but because it does not befit him. And they posit a parallel in the production or creation of creatures. God is able to produce infinite creatures; but that he does not produce them is not owing to powerlessness but because it does not befit him; and so likewise in the matter at hand.

But on the contrary: suppose then that the power which is in the Son for generating is actualized; it is clear that the Son will generate an eternal God: therefore something will be able to begin to have being and to have eternal being; but this is impossible and unintelligible.

Therefore it must be said that the Father does not communicate to the Son the power to generate, for two reasons. One is that he cannot; the other is that he ought not.

The reason why he cannot is this: the fecundity for generating is in the Father because he is the principle, and he is the principle because he is the first. But it is impossible that what is first communicate its primacy to another. For there is a contradiction in terms in saying that a produced person is first. Therefore, since the fecundity for generating inhered in the Father by reason of his primacy, he cannot communicate it to the Son; and I believe this to be the proper reason for this, as will be apparent below in Distinction Twenty-Seven, where it will be treated why the Father generates.

Likewise, he ought not communicate it, because in the emanation of the divine persons there must be attended to both original distinction and most full communication: original distinction, because it is necessary that things which communicate in nature be distinguished either through matter or through origin. To be distinguished through matter is impossible for the persons; because where there is this mode of distinguishing, there is composition and variation and multiplication of forms, all of which are repugnant to God, who is simple and invariable and truly one. And therefore it is necessary that they be distinguished through origin or relation: therefore through generating and being generated: therefore if the Son is able to generate, he can also fail to be distinguished. If you say that there is still a distinction, because one is only Father, another only Son, and another Father and Son: then I object to you that the second son could generate by the same account as the first; and then there would be two of whom each would be both father and son.

Likewise, by reason of most full communication —

*[brief lacuna in OCR]*

— that he would communicate that power to the Son: and therefore it was impossible, because whatever is unfitting in divine things is impossible.

1. To the objection on the contrary side from the authority of Hilary, that the Son has in himself a nature fitted to beget: it must be said that this expression is improper, and one must not argue from improper expressions but rather explain their impropriety, as the Master explained above. For the sense is: he has in himself the nature of the one who begets, that is, the nature of the Father.

2. To the objection that "it was not that he could not": it must be said that the Master explains this well, namely that it means he was not thereby powerless. Hence, according to the art, a distinction must be made when it is said that the Son could not generate: for this can be taken privatively, and then the sense is that he could not, that is, he was powerless; and then power is denied while aptitude is left, as it is said of one who has been maimed that he cannot walk, because he is by nature apt for walking yet cannot walk — this cannot be said of the Son in this mode, because he has no such aptitude for this. And it is in this sense that Augustine speaks. In another way, "not to be able" is taken negatively; and in this sense it must be conceded that the Son could not generate.

3. To the objection that the Father communicates to the Son the spirative power: the response is clear, because since the Son is generated, he cannot have primacy with respect to generation; but since he is not spirated, he is inspiratable; and therefore he was able to have primacy and fecundity with respect to that; and thus it is clear that the argument does not hold.

4. To the objection that the Son is the most express image, etc.: it must be said that the Son is called the most express image because he represents in all those things in which an image is naturally fitted to represent; but an image is so fitted to represent that it is nonetheless not itself the thing imaged — otherwise it would not be an image. But if the Son were to represent in the act of generating, he would already be the Father: and therefore it is neither intelligible nor possible for the Son to generate or to imitate the Father in generating.

5. To the objection concerning light and radiance: it must be said that the cases are not parallel, because light does not perfectly multiply itself in the first radiance, and therefore in many it accomplishes what it cannot in one.

6. Likewise in the case of a carnal son: hence one father generates several sons. Yet this argument is not the principal one, but rather the one stated above, because in lower things fecundity is not by reason of primacy but by reason of perfection. In God, however, because he is most perfect and first, it is not merely by reason of perfection — for then it would be in all persons and there could be no stopping point — but by reason of primacy. Likewise these arguments do not proceed by analogy but rather more by disanalogy.

---
questions.notes:
- **Chunk structure**: This chunk completes the *sed contra* of Q.II (arguments 3–6) and then gives the full *Respondeo* and replies. The *Conclusio* ("the Father does not communicate the power of generating to the Son") is established by two independent reasons: (1) he *cannot* — grounded in the logic of primacy; (2) he *ought not* — grounded in the requirements of original distinction and full communication. Only the first reason is fully articulated before the OCR lacuna; the conclusion of the second reason picks up at "that he would communicate that power."

- **"primacy" (*primitas*)**: A key technical term in Bonaventure's Trinitarian theology. The Father's fecundity for generating is inseparable from his being the *primum* — the unoriginated principle. Primacy cannot be communicated because the very notion of a "produced first" is self-contradictory (*oppositio in adiecto*). This ground is called the "proper reason" for why the Father alone generates, to be developed fully in D.27. Rendered "primacy" throughout rather than "being-first" to preserve the nominal form.

- **"original distinction" (*originalis distinctio*)**: The technical principle that divine persons must be distinguished by their relations of origin (generation, spiration), since material or formal distinction is inapplicable to a simple, invariable being. This is contrasted with "most full communication" (*plenissima communicatio*) — the two requirements must both be satisfied, and communicating the power of generating would violate the first.

- **"inspiratable" (*inspirabilis*)**: A coined scholastic term meaning "capable of being spirated" — i.e., able to be the terminus *a quo* of spiration rather than its product. Since the Son is not spirated (unlike the Holy Spirit), he can be a principle of spiration together with the Father. The argument is: the Son's position in the order of origin permits fecundity with respect to spiration but not with respect to generation, precisely because he is himself generated.

- **Privative vs. negative "cannot" (*non posse privative / negative*)**: A standard logical distinction applied here with theological precision. Taken *privatively*, "the Son cannot generate" would imply that the Son is *deprived* of a capacity he ought to have — which would be a deficiency. Taken *negatively*, it simply denies the capacity without implying any lack or imperfection. Bonaventure grants only the negative sense; Augustine's statement in *Against Maximinus* is read in the privative sense and reinterpreted.

- **Reply to argument 4 (image)**: The resolution draws on the formal definition of image: an image represents its original *without being identical to it*. If the Son generated, he would become a second Father, collapsing the distinction between image and original. The argument shows why the analogical structure of image-and-original actually *excludes* the Son from generating, contrary to what argument 4 claimed.

- **Reply to argument 6 (carnal generation)**: Bonaventure notes that the analogy from carnal generation fails in an important respect — in lower beings, fecundity is grounded in *perfection* (a sufficiently developed nature), not in *primacy*. Since in God the two coincide only in the Father (who is both most perfect and first), the analogy cannot be straightforwardly extended. The reply also notes that a father in created generation does generate multiple sons, which shows the analogy breaks down structurally.

- **OCR lacuna**: A brief gap appears in the text between the second reason's development and the conclusion "that he would communicate that power to the Son." The transition is recoverable in sense — the missing material likely completed the argument from *plenissima communicatio* — but should be verified against the source PDF.

DIST. VII. SOLE ARTICLE, QUESTION III.

---

QUESTION III.

Whether the power of generating and the power of creating are one single power.

Third, it is inquired whether the power to generate and the power to create are one single power; and that they are not one, seems to be shown as follows.

1. Augustine: "The Father is Father by one thing and God by another": therefore he is generating by one thing and creating by another; but the power of generating is that by which he generates, and the power of creating is that by which he creates: therefore, etc.

2. Likewise, powers are distinguished by their acts and acts by their objects; therefore if generation is terminated at God and creation at a creature, and these are altogether different: therefore, etc.

3. Likewise, powers are multiplied according to subjects, since in many powerful agents there are many powers; but the power of creating — or the power to create — is in the Son, whereas the power to generate is not in him: therefore they are not one single power.

4. Likewise, whatever things are such that one can be understood without the other being understood, and conversely, are not one; but the power to generate can be understood while the power to create is set aside, and conversely the power to create while the power to generate is set aside: therefore, etc.

ON THE CONTRARY: 1. Of one altogether simple powerful agent, there is only one single power; but the Father is altogether simple: therefore he has only one single power; but he has the power to generate and the power to create: therefore these two are one single power.

2. Likewise, if the power to generate and the power to create were different, since the power to generate regards a person and the power to create regards nature: therefore nature and person would be two distinct things: therefore neither would nature be predicated of person nor conversely, which is altogether false.

3. Likewise, if there is a distinction between the power to generate and the power to create, there is an order between them. I ask, therefore, what is prior according to the account of understanding. And that the power of generating is prior seems to follow, because it is with respect to the eternal, and the eternal is before the temporal. But on the contrary: the understanding of what is common is prior to the understanding of what is proper; but the power of creating expresses what is common to the three persons, while the power of generating expresses what is proper to the Father: therefore, etc.

---

*The power of generating and the power of creating differ not in reality but only according to the account of understanding.*

I respond: It must be said that the power to generate and the power to create are one single power, yet expressed in two ways. For it is one being in reality to be Father and to be God, yet differing according to the account of understanding; because the latter is absolute, when I say "to be God," and the former is relative, when I say "to be Father." And the same is to be understood concerning power. Hence, just as essence and person are one in reality, yet there is a difference of account in understanding and in expression, so likewise must it be said of the power of generating and the power of creating.

And just as there is there a difference not in reality but according to account, so too there is there an order according to the account of understanding. Hence they have one order and another according to different comparisons. For comparing the power to create and the power to generate to that of which they are powers: since the power to create belongs to nature and the power to generate belongs to the person, and the understanding of what is common is prior to the understanding of what is proper, thus without dispute the power of creating is prior according to the account of understanding. But comparing them to that at which they are terminated: since the power of creating regards the temporal and the power of generating regards the eternal, the power of generating is prior according to the account of understanding relative to the power of creating. And thus the objections concerning order are answered.

Therefore the arguments showing that the power to generate and the power to create do not differ in reality or in essence are to be conceded.

1. To the objection that the Father is Father by one thing and God by another: [*response not present in this OCR chunk — apparent lacuna*]

3. To the objection that powers are multiplied according to subjects: it must be said that this is true of the proper subject; but the Son, as Son, is not the subject of the power of creating — rather, as God he is. And it is clear that the divine nature does not constitute a numerical plurality with the Father; and so neither does the power that regards nature do so with the power of the Father.

4. To the final objection, that one can be understood without the other and conversely: it must be said that you are speaking either with respect to what is signified or with respect to what is connoted. If with respect to what is connoted, you say truly that a creature can be understood without understanding the person of the Son, and conversely. If with respect to the principal signification, you say what is false; for it is impossible to understand the power of generating without the power of creating, just as it is impossible to understand person without essence.

[Scholion omitted]

---

Whether the power to be generated and the power to be created are univocal powers.

Fourth, it is inquired whether the power to be generated and the power to be created are univocal powers —

*[Arguments for the negative position:]*

2. Likewise, creation expresses egress and change, whereas generation excludes all change: therefore, since the power to be created imports the potency of being transmuted, and the power to be generated does not, and since powers differ in their generality with respect to the potency of being transmuted, and do not agree in this: therefore they agree in nothing.

3. Likewise, "omnipotent" distributes its term for all things that are univocal or analogous under it; but when I say "omnipotent," distribution is not made for that which can generate, because then the Son would not be omnipotent: therefore it is manifest that neither power is univocal or analogous to the other; otherwise omnipotence would not belong to the Son.

questions.notes:
- **Chunk structure**: Q.III is complete except for a lacuna in reply to objection 1 (the reply to "alio est Pater, alio est Deus" is missing from the OCR — the text jumps from the concession statement directly to reply 3). Q.IV begins but its *sed contra* is cut off at the end of the chunk; the opening arguments for the negative position also appear to be missing their first item (the OCR begins at argument 2).

- **One power, two expressions (*unum posse, dupliciter dictum*)**: The *Conclusio* applies the standard essence/person distinction to the domain of power: just as being Father and being God are one reality expressed under two accounts (*rationes*), so generating and creating are one power considered under a personal and an essential description respectively. This is a direct application of the principle established in Q.I.

- **Order of the two powers**: Bonaventure's resolution of the third *sed contra* argument (which asks which power is prior) is elegant: the answer depends on the direction of comparison. Relative to their *subjects* (nature vs. person), the power of creating is conceptually prior because the common (essence) is understood before the proper (paternity). Relative to their *termini* (temporal vs. eternal), the power of generating is conceptually prior because the eternal precedes the temporal. Neither order is real; both are *secundum rationem intelligendi*.

- **Q.III reply 3 — proper vs. improper subject**: The Scholion elaborates this reply: the *proximate and adequate subject* of the creative power is the divine essence alone; the divine persons are only *remote* subjects. Therefore the axiom "powers are multiplied by subjects" does not apply here.

- **Q.III reply 4 — signified vs. connoted (*significatum / connotatum*)**: A standard logical distinction. What is *connoted* (the object or terminus — creature vs. divine person) can be understood separately; but the *principal signification* (the single divine power as such) cannot be split, any more than person can be understood in isolation from essence.

- **Q.IV context**: The question shifts from active to passive power — not "can the Father generate?" but "is the capacity *to be generated* and the capacity *to be created* the same kind of capacity?" This is a more abstract question about whether passive potency is univocal across the Trinitarian and creaturely orders. The *sed contra* argument from *res* (common to *fruibile* and *utibile*) draws on the Bonaventurian teaching from D.1 on the enjoyment/use distinction.

- **OCR issues**: Argument 1 of the negative side in Q.IV is missing. The heading "DIST. V([." at the top of the chunk is an OCR misread of "DIST. VII." The lacuna in Q.III reply 1 (text jumps from the concession to reply 3, skipping reply 1 and apparently reply 2 as well) should be flagged for recovery from the source PDF.

DIST. VII. SOLE ARTICLE, QUESTION IV.

---

*[Continuation of the sed contra of Question IV, begun in the preceding chunk:]*

— nor diversity: therefore, since the power to be created and the power to be generated existed from eternity before the establishment of creatures, they do not have multiplication in the power itself.

3. Likewise, when I say "a creature is able to be created," I am not saying anything created; because that is truly said of what is altogether nothing, as of the soul of the Antichrist: therefore I am only expressing the power of the agent; but the power of God is single, having no multiplicity whatsoever: therefore his power is univocal with respect to the power to be created and the power to be generated.

---

*The power to be generated and the power to be created are in reality the same with respect to their principal signification and are said univocally; but with respect to what they connote, they are said analogically.*

I respond: It must be said that when I say "the power to be created" and "the power to be generated," I express both a principal signification and a connotation. With respect to the principal signification, I say that the power to be created expresses in reality the same thing as the power to create, differing only in mode of expression: because what is expressed by way of action through "the power to create" is expressed by way of passion through "the power to be created." But with respect to what is connoted, it expresses an effect in the creature.

When therefore the power to be created and the power to be generated are compared, if they are compared by reason of the principal signification, I say that they are not merely univocal but indeed identical, as has been seen, yet understood and expressed in different ways — just as the power to generate and the power to create are. But if they are compared by reason of what is connoted, then I concede that they are analogical, just as the name *res* is with respect to what is enjoyable and what is useful. For although Creator and creature have no univocal common term, they nonetheless have an analogical one.

It must be noted, however, that analogy is twofold. One is by reduction to a unity of nature according to prior and posterior; and this can obtain in comparing creature to creature, and in this case a sign distributes for all things contained under it, unless the distribution is restricted by an addition or by usage or by mode of expression — as in the case of what is called an accommodated distribution, as when it is said "the heavens cover all things." The other is analogy by reduction to a unity of proportional likeness, not of nature; and what is analogized in this way is not among other things but above them. Hence a sign does not properly distribute for it unless it is extended. Thus God is not a being among all things but above all things.

And from this it follows that "omnipotent" does not in a proper distribution distribute for the power of generating — unless a certain extension is made, and from that extension a certain appropriation follows with respect to the supposit. Hence "omnipotent" properly belongs to the three persons, because it does not distribute for the power of generating; but by appropriation, according as an ampliation is made on the part of the sign, it belongs to the Father alone.

From these considerations all the objections are answered; for they proceed along different lines, as is evident to one who examines them.

---
questions.notes:
- **Chunk structure**: This chunk completes Q.IV, which is the final question of Distinction VII's sole article. The *sed contra* arguments 2–3 from the preceding chunk are here resolved, and the full *Respondeo* with its two *Conclusiones* is given. There are no individual numbered replies; the final sentence ("from these considerations all the objections are answered") serves as a collective dismissal.

- **"principal signification" vs. "connotation" (*principale significatum* / *connotatum*)**: The same distinction deployed in Q.III reply 4 is here applied to the passive sense. The *principale significatum* of "the power to be created" is simply the divine power itself (identical for all divine operations); the *connotatum* is the creaturely effect or terminus, which introduces the analogical difference.

- **"the power to be created expresses in reality the same as the power to create"**: A striking claim: the active and passive formulations refer to identically the same divine power, differing only grammatically (action vs. passion). This follows from divine simplicity — there is no real passive potency in God, only the one omnipotence expressed from different vantage points.

- **"soul of the Antichrist"**: A standard scholastic example for something that is genuinely nothing yet can be spoken of as a possible object of divine power. When one says "the Antichrist's soul can be created," nothing actual is being referred to; the statement concerns only the divine power as its ground. This supports the claim that "the power to be created" signifies primarily the agent's power, not any property of the recipient.

- **Two kinds of analogy**: Bonaventure here articulates a distinction between:
  (1) *Analogy of prior and posterior* (*per reductionem ad unitatem naturae*): applies within creaturely or categorical comparisons; the analogized term distributes normally for all instances, subject to contextual restriction. Example: "healthy" predicated of organism, urine, diet.
  (2) *Analogy of proportional likeness* (*per reductionem ad unitatem similitudinis proportionalis*): applies when one term is not *among* but *above* the others; proper distribution does not extend to it without explicit extension. Example: God as "being" — he is not a being among beings but above being.
  This twofold distinction anticipates the more developed treatments of analogy in later scholasticism (Cajetan's *analogia proportionis* vs. *analogia attributionis*), though Bonaventure's formulation is his own.

- **"omnipotent" and appropriation**: "Omnipotent" properly distributes over the three persons equally (since it regards the common essence), but does not in a *proper* distribution include the power of generating (which is personal and proper to the Father). Only by *extensio* — an ampliation of the term's range — and subsequent *appropriatio* does "omnipotent Father" come to connote the power of generating specifically. This resolves Q.IV's third negative argument, which claimed that if "omnipotent" does not distribute for the power to generate, then the Son (who lacks that power) cannot be omnipotent — a false inference, since "omnipotent" does not include the personal power of generating in its proper distribution at all.

- **"accommodated distribution" (*distributio accommoda*)**: A technical term from medieval logic for a distribution that is contextually or idiomatically restricted, not reflecting the term's full logical extension. Example: "the heavens cover all things" — "all things" is accommodated to terrestrial objects, not a universal quantification. Rendered with the technical term retained.

- **Conclusion of Distinction VII**: With Q.IV, the Sole Article of Distinction VII is complete. The four questions have treated: (1) whether *potentia generandi* is absolute or relative; (2) whether it is in the Son; (3) whether it is identical with the power to create; (4) whether the power to be generated and the power to be created are univocal. Distinction VIII will take up the next topic in the Lombard's sequence.
