— nor diversity: therefore, since the power to be created and the power to be generated existed from eternity before the establishment of creatures, they do not have multiplication in the power itself.

3. Likewise, when I say "a creature is able to be created," I am not saying anything created; because that is truly said of what is altogether nothing, as of the soul of the Antichrist: therefore I am only expressing the power of the agent; but the power of God is single, having no multiplicity whatsoever: therefore his power is univocal with respect to the power to be created and the power to be generated.

---

*The power to be generated and the power to be created are in reality the same with respect to their principal signification and are said univocally; but with respect to what they connote, they are said analogically.*

I respond: It must be said that when I say "the power to be created" and "the power to be generated," I express both a principal signification and a connotation. With respect to the principal signification, I say that the power to be created expresses in reality the same thing as the power to create, differing only in mode of expression: because what is expressed by way of action through "the power to create" is expressed by way of passion through "the power to be created." But with respect to what is connoted, it expresses an effect in the creature.

When therefore the power to be created and the power to be generated are compared, if they are compared by reason of the principal signification, I say that they are not merely univocal but indeed identical, as has been seen, yet understood and expressed in different ways — just as the power to generate and the power to create are. But if they are compared by reason of what is connoted, then I concede that they are analogical, just as the name *res* is with respect to what is enjoyable and what is useful. For although Creator and creature have no univocal common term, they nonetheless have an analogical one.

It must be noted, however, that analogy is twofold. One is by reduction to a unity of nature according to prior and posterior; and this can obtain in comparing creature to creature, and in this case a sign distributes for all things contained under it, unless the distribution is restricted by an addition or by usage or by mode of expression — as in the case of what is called an accommodated distribution, as when it is said "the heavens cover all things." The other is analogy by reduction to a unity of proportional likeness, not of nature; and what is analogized in this way is not among other things but above them. Hence a sign does not properly distribute for it unless it is extended. Thus God is not a being among all things but above all things.

And from this it follows that "omnipotent" does not in a proper distribution distribute for the power of generating — unless a certain extension is made, and from that extension a certain appropriation follows with respect to the supposit. Hence "omnipotent" properly belongs to the three persons, because it does not distribute for the power of generating; but by appropriation, according as an ampliation is made on the part of the sign, it belongs to the Father alone.

From these considerations all the objections are answered; for they proceed along different lines, as is evident to one who examines them.

---
questions.notes:
- **Chunk structure**: This chunk completes Q.IV, which is the final question of Distinction VII's sole article. The *sed contra* arguments 2–3 from the preceding chunk are here resolved, and the full *Respondeo* with its two *Conclusiones* is given. There are no individual numbered replies; the final sentence ("from these considerations all the objections are answered") serves as a collective dismissal.

- **"principal signification" vs. "connotation" (*principale significatum* / *connotatum*)**: The same distinction deployed in Q.III reply 4 is here applied to the passive sense. The *principale significatum* of "the power to be created" is simply the divine power itself (identical for all divine operations); the *connotatum* is the creaturely effect or terminus, which introduces the analogical difference.

- **"the power to be created expresses in reality the same as the power to create"**: A striking claim: the active and passive formulations refer to identically the same divine power, differing only grammatically (action vs. passion). This follows from divine simplicity — there is no real passive potency in God, only the one omnipotence expressed from different vantage points.

- **"soul of the Antichrist"**: A standard scholastic example for something that is genuinely nothing yet can be spoken of as a possible object of divine power. When one says "the Antichrist's soul can be created," nothing actual is being referred to; the statement concerns only the divine power as its ground. This supports the claim that "the power to be created" signifies primarily the agent's power, not any property of the recipient.

- **Two kinds of analogy**: Bonaventure here articulates a distinction between:
  (1) *Analogy of prior and posterior* (*per reductionem ad unitatem naturae*): applies within creaturely or categorical comparisons; the analogized term distributes normally for all instances, subject to contextual restriction. Example: "healthy" predicated of organism, urine, diet.
  (2) *Analogy of proportional likeness* (*per reductionem ad unitatem similitudinis proportionalis*): applies when one term is not *among* but *above* the others; proper distribution does not extend to it without explicit extension. Example: God as "being" — he is not a being among beings but above being.
  This twofold distinction anticipates the more developed treatments of analogy in later scholasticism (Cajetan's *analogia proportionis* vs. *analogia attributionis*), though Bonaventure's formulation is his own.

- **"omnipotent" and appropriation**: "Omnipotent" properly distributes over the three persons equally (since it regards the common essence), but does not in a *proper* distribution include the power of generating (which is personal and proper to the Father). Only by *extensio* — an ampliation of the term's range — and subsequent *appropriatio* does "omnipotent Father" come to connote the power of generating specifically. This resolves Q.IV's third negative argument, which claimed that if "omnipotent" does not distribute for the power to generate, then the Son (who lacks that power) cannot be omnipotent — a false inference, since "omnipotent" does not include the personal power of generating in its proper distribution at all.

- **"accommodated distribution" (*distributio accommoda*)**: A technical term from medieval logic for a distribution that is contextually or idiomatically restricted, not reflecting the term's full logical extension. Example: "the heavens cover all things" — "all things" is accommodated to terrestrial objects, not a universal quantification. Rendered with the technical term retained.

- **Conclusion of Distinction VII**: With Q.IV, the Sole Article of Distinction VII is complete. The four questions have treated: (1) whether *potentia generandi* is absolute or relative; (2) whether it is in the Son; (3) whether it is identical with the power to create; (4) whether the power to be generated and the power to be created are univocal. Distinction VIII will take up the next topic in the Lombard's sequence.

questions.english:
DIST. VII. DOUBTS.

---

*[Continuation of a Doubt begun in the preceding chunk — the question concerns whether the Holy Spirit could be or could have been the Son:]*

— the more a relation differs from a supposit, it can be said that what is similar to another can be dissimilar to it without any change in itself: therefore, since filiation and spiration are relations, by the same account the Son could be the Holy Spirit and conversely, without any change. Likewise, everything mutable is something other than that according to which it is changed, as when what is not white becomes white, it is other than whiteness: therefore if the Holy Spirit is understood to be changed, if he were to be generated, then generation would be one thing in him and the one who is generated would be another; but this is false: therefore, etc.

I respond: The case of relations in creatures and in God is different: because relations in creatures do not give relational things their existence; hence a thing can exist without them and with them. But in divine things relations give the persons their existence; and therefore if it is understood that a property inheres in a hypostasis, the existence of the hypostasis is understood, and likewise if it is understood not to inhere, the non-existence of the hypostasis is understood. Therefore, since the Holy Spirit cannot simultaneously be spirated and generated — because although one person can produce in two ways, one person cannot be produced in more than one way — it follows of necessity: if the Holy Spirit can be or could have been the Son, he can be or could have been not the Holy Spirit, i.e., not spirated; and if he could have been not spirated, he could have not existed; and again if he could have been generated, he could have existed; and thus it would have been possible for him to pass from being to non-being and from non-being to being, and thereby to be changed.

And thus the last point is clarified: he is not said to be changed by reason of a diversification of properties around the same supposit, as occurs in natural change, but by reason of the corruption and inception of that same supposit. Nor does this parallel hold: the Father can generate and spir­ate without any change in himself: therefore the Holy Spirit can be generated and spirated; because it is not unfitting that one principle produce in multiple ways, but it is impossible and incompossible that one thing produced be produced in multiple ways; and thus the matter is clarified.

---

DOUBT V.

Likewise it seems false to say, as is said: "The Father is powerful only through nature; for his power is his essence" — because on this basis generating, which in no way belongs to essence, would in no way belong to power.

I respond: Although power, considered absolutely, is the same as essence, nevertheless power, since it is not a name as abstract as essence, is drawn toward the person. Hence the power of generating does not express the divine nature simply, but the nature as in such a person — namely, the innascible; therefore the name "essence" and the name "power" are not parallel in this respect.

---

DOUBT VI.

Likewise it seems to be said improperly where it says: "You would signify another power, by which the Father is able to beget, etc."; because the sufficient division of power is into active and passive; but the power to beget expresses active power, and the power to be begotten expresses passive power: therefore no other power can be signified. If you say that to generate is not properly speaking to act, and likewise that to be generated is not properly speaking to undergo: it is objected that powers are distinguished by acts; but to beget and to be begotten are different: therefore the power of the one and the power of the other are different.

I respond: The distinction that the Master makes between the power to beget in the active sense and in the passive sense is grounded on this, that power can be considered according to what it is; and in this way it expresses nature, and just as one nature is in the one generating and the one generated, but in one way and another, so the same power. It can again be considered according to that for which it is; and in this way it expresses the mode of nature's existing in a person in relation to another who is either principle or principiated. And in this way, since the modes are different, the properties of the power to generate and the power to be generated are said to be different, and are distinguished according to personal acts; but not in the first way.

---

DOUBT VII.

Likewise there is a question concerning his statement that the Son has the power by which he can be Son or by which he can be begotten. For this seems doubtful or false, because to be begotten belongs entirely to the act of begetting, and begetting belongs to the power of the Father: therefore so too does being begotten.

I respond: Just as the power of begetting in the Father expresses nothing other than nature in a person as naturally fitted to produce another from itself, so the power of begetting in the Son — in the passive sense — expresses nothing other than nature in a person as naturally fitted to be produced by another; for just as it befits the hypostasis of the Father to generate, so it befits the hypostasis of the Son to be generated. Nor does the objection on the other side hold. For everything the Son has, whether essential or personal, he has from the Father. Therefore, although being begotten itself is from the power of the Father, this does not exclude there being a passive power of being begotten in the Son.

---

DISTINCTION VIII.

On the truth and proper character of the divine essence.

Now there must be treated the truth or proper character, and the immutability and simplicity, of the divine nature, or substance, or essence. "God is, as Augustine says in the fifth book *On the Trinity*, without any doubt a substance, or — if that name is better — an essence, which the Greeks call *ousia*. For just as wisdom is named from what it is to be wise, and knowledge from what it is to know, so essence is named from what it is to be. And who exists more truly than he who said to his servant Moses in Exodus 3: *I am who I am*; and you shall say to the sons of Israel: *He who is has sent me to you*?" He truly and properly is called essence, whose essence knows neither past nor future. Hence Jerome, writing to Marcella, says: "God alone, who has no beginning, holds the name of true essence, because in comparison with him who truly is — because he is immutable — things that are mutable are as if they are not. For of what is said 'it was,' it is not; and of what is said 'it will be,' it is not yet. But God alone is, who does not know having been or being about to be. God alone therefore truly is, compared to whose essence our existence is not."

Here it must be carefully noted how those words of Jerome are to be understood: "he does not know having been or being about to be, but only being" — as though it could not be said of God that he was or will be, but only that he is — since we find it frequently written of him: "he was from eternity," "he was always," "he will be for ages," and the like; whence it seems that of God one should say not only that he was, or that he is, or that he will be. For if it were said only that he was, it would be thought that he has ceased to be; if it were said only that he is, it would be thought that he has not always been but that he began to be; if it were said only that he will be, it would be thought that he does not exist now. Let it be said therefore that he always was, is, and will be, so that it is understood that he neither began nor ceased nor ceases nor will cease to be. Concerning this, Augustine on John says: "When 'is' is properly said of an eternal thing, according to our manner of speaking 'was' and 'will be' and 'is' are well said: 'was,' because he never ceased; 'will be,' because he will never be lacking; 'is,' because he always is: he has not passed away as something that does not endure; he does not arise as something that did not exist. Therefore, when our speech varies through tenses, the verbs of every tense are truly said of him who was absent at no time, is not absent, and will not be absent; and therefore it is no wonder if, speaking of the Spirit of truth, the Truth said by way of the future tense: *Whatever he will hear, he will speak* — 'will hear,' namely from him from whom he proceeds. His hearing is his knowing, and it is also his being. From whom, therefore, he has his essence, from him he has his hearing, that is, his knowledge, which is nothing other than his essence. 'He will hear,' therefore, was said of what he heard and hears, that is, of what he always knew, knows, and will know." Behold, Augustine here says that the verbs of every tense are said of God, but that properly speaking "is" is the right one. Therefore what Jerome says is to be understood thus: "he does not know having been or being about to be, but only being" — that is, when it is said of God that he was or will be, it is not to be understood that he has passed away or is yet to come, but that he simply exists without any temporal motion. For although the substantive verbs of various tenses are said of God — was, will be, is, was [imperfect], is [present] — yet they do not then distinguish temporal movements, such as past, future, imperfect past, perfect past, or pluperfect, but —

*[text truncated in OCR; brief continuation lost]*

---

DISTINCTION VIII, PART II.

On the immutability of the same.

The essence of God alone is also properly called immutable, because it neither is changed nor can be changed. Hence Augustine in the fifth book *On the Trinity* says: "Other essences or substances admit accidents, through which change, great or small, is brought about in them; but nothing of this kind can befall God; and therefore the substance or essence alone which is God is immutable, to which certainly it most truly and fully belongs to be. For what is changed does not preserve being itself; and what can be changed, even if it is not changed, can cease to be what it was; and therefore that alone which not only is not changed but also absolutely cannot be changed is most truly said to be" — namely the substance of Father and Son and Holy Spirit. And therefore the Apostle, speaking of God, says: *Who alone has immortality.* For as Augustine says in the first book *On the Trinity*: "Since the soul is said in a certain way to be immortal and is so, the Apostle would not say *God alone has immortality* unless it were because true immortality is immutability, which no creature can have, since it belongs to the Creator alone." Hence James says: *With whom there is no change nor shadow of alteration.* And David: *You will change them and they will be changed; but you are the same.* Therefore Augustine on Genesis says that God is moved neither through places nor through times, while creatures are moved through times and places. And to be moved through times is to be changed through affections; but God can be changed neither by place nor by affection, who says through the Prophet: *I am God and I am not changed* — who alone is immutable. Hence he is rightly said alone to have immortality. "For in every mutable nature," as Augustine says *Against Maximinus*, "there is a certain death in change itself, because it causes something to not be in it that previously was. Hence even the human soul, which is therefore said to be immortal because in its own manner it never ceases to live, nevertheless has its own death; because if it was living justly and sins, it dies to justice; if it was sinful and is justified, it dies to sin — to say nothing of its other changes, about which it would take long to dispute now. And the nature of heavenly creatures could die, because it could sin. For the angels too sinned and became demons, of whom the devil is prince; and those who did not sin could have sinned; and to whatever rational creature it is granted that it cannot sin, this is not from its own nature but from the grace of God. And therefore God alone, as the Apostle says, has immortality, who not by the grace of anyone but by his own nature neither could nor can be changed by any conversion, nor could nor will he ever sin by any change." "Therefore, as Augustine says in the first book *On the Trinity*, to contemplate and know the substance of God — making mutable things without any change in himself and creating temporal things without any temporal motion in himself — though it is difficult, is necessary." Truly therefore and properly immutable is the essence of the Divinity alone, which without any change in itself established all natures.

---

Chapter III.

On the simplicity of the same.

And this same essence alone is properly and truly simple, in which there is no diversity or variation or multiplicity either of parts or of accidents or of any forms whatsoever. But that you may know how that substance is simple, as Augustine teaches you in the sixth book *On the Trinity*, "observe first why every creature is multiple and in no way truly simple — first concerning corporeal, then concerning spiritual creatures. Corporeal creature certainly consists of parts, such that there is one part smaller and another larger, and the whole is greater than any part; and in any given body, magnitude is one thing, color another, and figure another. For with magnitude diminished, the same color and the same figure can remain; and with color changed, the same figure and the same magnitude can remain. And thereby the nature of body is shown to be multiple, but in no way simple."

---

On how corporeal and spiritual creatures are multiple and not simple.

"Spiritual creature too, such as the soul, in comparison with body is indeed simple, but without comparison with body it is multiple and not simple. It is called simple in respect of body because it is not diffused through space by bulk, but in any given body it is whole in the whole and whole in any part of it. And therefore when something occurs in any small particle of a body that the soul may sense, although it does not occur in the whole body, yet the soul senses it wholly, because it does not escape it wholly. Yet even in the soul itself there is no true simplicity" —

---

That God, though simple, is nonetheless spoken of in many ways.

Here it must be carefully noted that, since Augustine says that God alone is truly simple, why he says that the same God is spoken of in many ways. But he does not say this on account of diversity of accidents or parts, but on account of the diversity and multiplicity of names that are said of God; which, though multiple, signify one thing, namely the divine nature. For these names are not accepted, when said of that immutable and eternal substance incomparably simpler than the human mind, in the same way as when they are said of creatures. Hence Augustine in the sixth book *On the Trinity*: "For God, to be is the same as to be strong, or to be wise, or to be just, and whatever of that simple multiplicity or multiple simplicity you may say, by which his substance is signified. But for the human mind, to be is not the same as to be strong, or prudent, or just; for a mind can exist and have none of those virtues."

---

Chapter VI.

That the simplicity of God is subject to none of the categories.

That in the divine nature there is no diversity of accidents and absolutely no mutability but perfect simplicity, Augustine shows in the fifth book *On the Trinity* saying: "Let us understand God, as far as we are able, as good without quality, great without quantity, creator without need, presiding without position, containing all things without habitus, wholly everywhere without place, everlasting without time, making mutable things without any change in himself, and suffering nothing. Whoever thinks of God in this way, even if he cannot yet fully discover what he is, nevertheless piously takes care, as far as he can, not to think of him something that he is not." Behold, if you attend carefully, from these words and what was said before it becomes clear that the categories of the dialectical art are wholly unsuitable to the nature of God, which is subject to no accidents.

---

Chapter VII.

That God is improperly called substance.

Hence "substance" is not even properly predicated of him, as Augustine shows in the seventh book *On the Trinity*: "Just as 'essence' is named from what it is to be, so we call 'substance' from what it is to subsist, if at least it is fitting that God be said to subsist. For this is rightly understood of those things in which inhere what are said to be in some subject, as color or form in a body. For body subsists and is therefore a substance. Mutable things therefore, and non-simple things, are properly called substances. But if God subsists such that he can properly be called substance, then something inheres in him as in a subject, and he is not simple. But it is impious to say that God subsists and is subject to his own goodness, and that goodness is not itself a substance or rather essence, and that God himself is not his own goodness but that it is in him as in a subject. Hence it is manifest that God is called substance improperly, so that by a more common name what is truly and properly called 'essence' may be understood, so that perhaps God alone ought to be called essence. For he alone truly is, because he is immutable."

---

Chapter VIII.

That there is nothing in God that is not God.

The simplicity and purity of this essence is so great that there is nothing in it that is not it itself; but the possessor and what is possessed are the same. Hence Hilary in the seventh book *On the Trinity* says: "God, who is life, does not subsist from things composed; nor is he who is power contained by weak things; nor is he who is light fitted together from dark things; nor is he who is Spirit formed from disparate things: all that is in him is one." The same in the eighth book *On the Trinity*: "God is not in the human manner from composed things, such that in him would be one thing —"

*[Text breaks off; Distinction VIII base text continues into the next chunk]*

questions.notes:
- **Chunk structure**: This unusually large chunk contains three distinct sections: (1) the completion of D.VII Doubts (resuming mid-Doubt IV and adding Doubts V–VII); (2) the full Lombard base text for Distinction VIII (Chapters I–III, with sub-sections on immutability and simplicity, through Chapter VIII); (3) the chunk breaks off mid-sentence in the Hilary citation at the start of Ch. VIII. Bonaventure's own *Divisio Textus* and *Tractatio Quaestionum* for Distinction VIII are not yet present and will follow in subsequent chunks.

- **D.VII Doubt IV (completion)**: The opening resolves a question about whether the Holy Spirit could be the Son. The key move is that in God, relations *constitute* hypostases rather than modifying pre-existing ones (as in creatures). Therefore, if the Holy Spirit's constitutive property (spiration) were replaced by generation, the Holy Spirit would cease to exist and a different person would begin — genuine change in the ontological sense, not mere relational variation.

- **"incompossible" (*incompossibile*)**: Established term from earlier chunks. Here deployed to assert that one principiated thing being produced by two distinct principles of origin is incompossible — the modes of being produced are mutually exclusive for a single divine person.

- **D.VII Doubt V — "power" drawn toward the person**: Bonaventure's resolution clarifies the D.VII Q.I *Conclusio* from a different angle: "power" (*potentia*), unlike "essence" (*essentia*), is not fully abstract and therefore is drawn (*trahitur*) toward the personal mode. Thus *potentia generandi* picks out the nature as it exists in the innascible person. The term "innascible" (*innascibilis*) refers to the Father's incapacity to be generated — his defining personal property.

- **D.VII Doubt VI — active/passive distinction grounded in relational mode**: The Master's distinction between the power to beget (active) and the power to be begotten (passive) is not, Bonaventure clarifies, a distinction in the power *as such* (which is the single divine nature) but in the *mode* of the nature's existing in a person relative to another — whether as principle or as principiated. The distinction is personal, not essential.

- **D.VIII base text**: The Lombard's text for Distinction VIII treats three divine attributes: (1) truth/proper being (*veritas / proprietas*), (2) immutability (*incommutabilitas*), (3) simplicity (*simplicitas*). These are expounded through a dense sequence of Augustine citations (De Trinitate V, VI, VII; Ep. ad Marcellam; In Ioannem; De Genesi; Contra Maximinum), Jerome, Hilary, James, and the Psalms. The translation preserves Bonaventure's full reproduction of the Lombard's text, including embedded patristic quotations, without editorial compression.

- **"essence" vs. "substance"**: Chapter VII contains the Lombard's important Augustinian point that "substance" (*substantia*) is technically improper for God because it implies a subject in which accidents inhere (*subsistit* → *substat*), whereas "essence" (*essentia*) from *esse* is the only fully proper name. This will be theologically significant for Bonaventure's own questions in D.VIII.

- **OCR issues**: The text is truncated at lines 165–171 (a brief passage on the temporal verbs in Ch. I of D.VIII) and again at the end (mid-sentence in Ch. VIII). Both should be recovered from the source PDF. The chapter numbering (Caps. III, VI, VII, VIII) reflects the Lombard's own section divisions; Cap. IV and Cap. V are absent from this OCR and presumably in the lacuna.

DIST. VIII, PART I, ARTICLE I, QUESTION I.

---

*[The chunk opens mid-discussion, within the arguments for the affirmative position of Q.I; the initial arguments and the opening of the question are not present in this OCR section.]*

2. Likewise, the true is equally as common as the good, and in a certain way more so; but goodness is not a property of God: therefore by the same account neither is truth.

3. Likewise, truth is the ground of distinguishing the Creator from creatures and one creature from another; but what is the ground of distinguishing and differentiating is diverse in diverse things: therefore the truth in God is different from the truth in a creature, and the truth in one creature from the truth in another: therefore it is not the exclusive property of God.

4. Likewise, Augustine in the *Soliloquies*: "The true is that which is"; therefore truth is being itself: therefore it is not a property of essence, because if it were, by the same account that it is said "truth is a property of essence," the converse could equally be said — since they are altogether the same.

---

*Truth, insofar as it is opposed to falsity, is found also in creatures according to its threefold relation to the subject it informs, to the principle it represents, and to the intellect it activates; but insofar as it is opposed to admixture, it is the exclusive property of God.*

I respond: It must be said that truth has a threefold relation. For it can be related to the subject it informs, to the principle it represents, and to the intellect it activates. In relation to the subject, truth is called the indivision of act and potency. In relation to the principle, truth is called the representation or imitation of supreme unity. In relation to the intellect, truth is called the ground of discerning.

And in all these relations truth can be taken in two ways: in one way, insofar as it is distinguished against falsity; in another way, insofar as it is distinguished against admixture, according to which the true is called pure and unmixed.

Insofar as truth is divided against falsity — which is the privation of indivision, imitation, and expression — since in a creature there is in some manner both indivision and imitation and expression, truth is in this way found not only in the Creator but also in the creature; and thus in this sense it is not assigned as a property of God.

In the other way, insofar as truth is divided against admixture or impurity, it is in this way in God alone. For in God alone there is pure indivision, unmixed with any diversity; in God alone there is pure imitation and likeness, unmixed with any dissimilitude; and in God alone there is the expression of light unmixed with obscurity. In the creature, by contrast, there is indivision along with a diversity of act and potency, and imitation along with dissimilitude; and further in it there is expression along with obscurity. And therefore in this sense truth is a property of divine being; and it is in this sense that the Master and Augustine and Jerome understand it. For they call that being true which has nothing of potentiality, nothing of vanity, nothing of non-being. And therefore in God there is no past and no future, which are in some manner non-beings.

1, 2, 5, 6. And in this way the first two authorities and arguments on the affirmative side proceed.

3. To the objection that there is no truth other than the eternal truth, since it alone causes understanding: it must be said that just as color is the object of sight and the motive of sight — yet not without the act of light — and differs from light itself; so likewise it must be said that created truth, although it cannot move without uncreated truth, is nonetheless in its own way a motive, and is a different truth from that one.

4. and 7. To the objection from Anselm, that all things are true by the first truth: it must be said that "true," by its original imposition, expresses a relation to the exemplar cause, just as "good" expresses a relation to the final cause. For just as something is called good by reason of order, so something is called true by reason of expression; and the ground of expressing belongs to the exemplar. Therefore, just as when it is said of created goods that they are good by uncreated goodness, "goodness" predicates the end in the ablative, not the form — because God's goodness is not the form of any created thing — so similarly, when it is said that all things are true by uncreated truth, the ablative expresses the exemplar formal cause. For all true things are and are naturally fitted to express themselves through the expression of that supreme light; which, if it were to cease to flow in, all other things would cease to be true. Therefore no created truth is true by essence, but by participation; and from this the last point is clear.

To the objection on the contrary side that truth is not a property: the response is clear, because —

4. To the objection that truth is the same as the divine essence: it must be said that the notion of a property in creatures involves three elements: first, that it belongs to it alone; second, that it is the ground of making it known; third, that it differs from that of which it is the property. The first two belong to perfection; the last, however, belongs to imperfection, since it excludes simplicity. And therefore truth is called a property of the divine essence, not because it differs from or inheres in the divine essence as an accident in a subject, but because it belongs to it alone and is the ground of knowing it. And this is why the converse does not hold — essence is not a property of truth — because essence is not the ground of making truth known, as truth is of making essence known.

But if you ask, since essence and truth signify the same thing, why the one is the ground of knowing the other and not conversely: some have said in response that, although essence and truth signify the same thing, truth is more the ground of knowing by reason of what it connotes. But this cannot stand, because truth connotes nothing. It must therefore be said that this is owing to the mode of signifying and understanding.

And it must be noted that these names can be spoken of in two ways: in one way by reason of what they name or signify; in another way by reason of that in which what they name is signified to be posited. Hence it is different to say "sense" and "sense of a human being"; because the first is said as common to the sense of human and beast, the second as proper to the human being. If therefore we take names of this kind in themselves, the account of essence is one thing and the account of truth is another, since essence expresses what a thing is, and truth expresses a condition of being. But when we draw essence and truth up to God, although they are the same, yet by reason of their general significations one is taken as a property of the other; and they are not synonyms there, nor are they synonymous names, but the account of subject and property remains according to the mode of signifying, and remains also according to the mode of understanding; because through essence in a creature we understand essence in the Creator, and through truth in a creature we understand uncreated truth. Hence just as created truth is a property of and ground for knowing created essence, so uncreated truth, according to the account of signifying and understanding, is the ground for knowing and understanding uncreated essence.

[Scholion omitted]

---

*[The chunk then continues with a second question, which begins after the scholion:]*

QUESTION II.

*[Whether divine being can be thought not to exist.]*

*[Initial arguments for the affirmative are lost in a lacuna; the text resumes at argument 2:]*

2. Likewise, Anselm's argument from the *Proslogion*: that than which nothing greater can be conceived is such that it cannot be thought not to exist, since what cannot be thought not to exist is greater than what can be: therefore, since nothing greater than God can be conceived, divine being is such that it cannot be thought not to exist.

2. Likewise, Damascene says that the knowledge that God exists is naturally impressed in us; but natural impressions do not fail or become habituated to their contrary: therefore the truth of God is inseparably impressed on the human mind: therefore it cannot be thought not to exist.

3. Likewise, there is greater truth in divine being than in any necessary truth; but some necessary truth is so true that there is no contradicting it in the heart — as "every whole is greater than its part," and the like — so that it cannot be thought not to exist: therefore, much more will this be true of the first truth.

4. Likewise, our intellect understands nothing except through the first light and truth: therefore every act of the intellect, which consists in thinking something not to exist, is through the first light; but through the first light it does not come about that one thinks the first light or truth not to exist: therefore in no way does it come about that one thinks the first truth not to exist.

5. Likewise, what it is possible to think it is also possible to assert; but it is not possible to assert that the first truth does not exist: therefore neither is it possible to think it. Proof of the minor: every assertoric utterance asserts that it itself is true; hence it follows: if a man is a donkey, then it is true that a man is a donkey; but whatever posits truth posits the first truth, since every truth implies it: therefore every utterance asserts that the first truth exists: therefore, etc.

6. Likewise, every assertoric utterance is either affirmative or negative; but an affirmative utterance affirms this of that; and it follows: if there is a being that is this, there is a being that is not this, because when I say "this being," I say a limited, finite, and restricted being; and with such a being posited, the supreme being is posited: therefore every affirmative utterance about a creature implies God.

7. Likewise, the negative case holds similarly, because no utterance is more negative than this: "there is no truth." But Augustine in the *Soliloquies* proves that this utterance posits that some truth exists; because if no truth exists, it is true that no truth exists; and if this is true, something is true; and if something is true, some truth exists: therefore, etc.

ON THE CONTRARY: 1. Damascene: "The pernicious malice of men has so prevailed that some say God does not exist, according to that of the Psalm: *The fool has said*, etc."

2. Likewise, an idolater says that there is no other God but the idol, and he believes and thinks this; but it is clear that an idol is not God: therefore, etc.

3. Likewise, everything that can be understood not to exist, when something else is understood instead of it, can be thought not to exist. But Boethius says in the book *On the Hebdomads* that by the intellect, per impossibile, the supreme good can be understood not to exist, and still something round and white can be understood: therefore, similarly with regard to the highest truth, it can be thought not to exist.

4. Likewise, what most escapes our grasp can easily be thought not to exist; but the truth of divine being is of this kind, since God dwells in inaccessible light: therefore, etc.

5. Likewise, I ask what it means to say that God cannot be thought not to exist. If because he cannot be thought in any way, neither truly nor falsely, that is manifestly false; if because he cannot truly be thought not to exist, then neither can the soul nor the heavens and the like.

6. Likewise, what can be expressed can also be thought; but it can be expressed that divine being does not exist: therefore it can also be thought. That it can be expressed is evident: when it is said specifically "God does not exist," and in general "nothing exists"; and that neither of these implies that God exists is evident, because the opposite does not imply the opposite, and what posits nothing implies nothing; but each of these posits nothing.

---

*The truth of divine being is such that it cannot be thought not to exist with assent, except by reason of a defect on the part of the knower, who does not know what God is; but on the part of the knowable there can be no defect, either of presence or of evidence, whether in itself or in the way of proof.*

I respond: It must be said that to think something not to exist is twofold. In one way, in the manner of what is false, as I think of the proposition "a man is a donkey"; and this kind of thinking is nothing other than understanding what the proposition says. In this way the truth of divine being can be thought not to exist.

In another way, something is thought not to exist with assent, as I think something not to exist and believe it not to exist; and in this way thinking something not to exist that does exist can arise either from a defect on the part of the knower or from a defect on the part of the knowable.

The defect on the part of the knower is blindness or ignorance, by reason of which, because one does not know the thing, one thinks it not to exist. Now there are two ways of thinking about any existing thing: whether it exists, and what it is.

Our intellect is deficient in its cognition of divine truth with respect to the cognition of *what it is*, but it is not deficient with respect to the cognition of *that it is*. Hence Hugh: "God so tempered his knowledge of himself in the human being from the beginning, that just as he could never be comprehended as to what he is, so he could never be unknown as to the fact that he is." Therefore, since our intellect never fails in its cognition of God as to whether he exists, neither can it be altogether ignorant that he exists, nor think him not to exist.

But since it is deficient in the cognition of *what he is*, it frequently thinks God to be what he is not — as an idol — or not to be what he is — as just. And since one who thinks God not to be what he is, such as just, consequently thinks him not to exist, therefore by reason of the defect of intellect God can be thought not to exist — or the highest truth can — yet not simply or universally, but as a consequence, just as one who denies that blessedness is in God thereby denies that he exists.

And it is in this way that the arguments proving that some intellect does or can think divine being not to exist proceed.

In another way, something can be thought not to exist by reason of a defect on the part of the knowable, and this kind of defect can be twofold: either a defect of presence, or a defect of evidence. A defect of presence occurs because something is not always, not everywhere, not everywhere wholly present. What is not always present, is sometimes present and sometimes not: and therefore it can at some time truly be thought not to exist. Similarly with what is not everywhere present, because by the same account that it can be thought not to exist here, it can be thought not to exist elsewhere. Similarly with what is present in part and absent in part.

But God is always and everywhere and wholly always and everywhere: therefore he cannot be thought not to exist. This argument is assigned by Anselm in the book *Against* —

questions.notes:
- **Chunk structure**: This chunk covers two questions of D.VIII, Part I, Article I. Q.I concerns whether truth (*veritas*) is a property (*proprietas*) of God's essence; Q.II concerns whether divine being can be thought not to exist (*cogitari non esse*). Both are only partially present — Q.I opens mid-argument, and Q.II breaks off mid-sentence in the *Respondeo*. The initial arguments for Q.I's affirmative side and Q.II's first *pro* argument are lost to OCR gaps.

- **Distinction VIII's structure**: Unlike prior distinctions, D.VIII is divided into two Parts (*Pars I* and *Pars II*), each with its own article. Part I treats the divine attributes of truth, immutability, and simplicity as properties of essence. This is reflected in the chunk ID (*p.1 a.1 q.1*) and will continue across several chunks.

- **Truth's threefold relation (*triplex comparatio*)**: The *Conclusio* of Q.I turns on this schema: truth as indivision of act and potency (relation to subject), truth as representation of supreme unity (relation to principle), truth as ground of discernment (relation to intellect). These three relations track the three transcendental accounts of truth: ontological (*veritas rei*), exemplar (*veritas in ordine ad causam*), and logical (*veritas in ordine ad intellectum*). The second *Conclusio* then adds the key distinction: against *falsity* (privation), truth is found in creatures too; against *admixture* (impurity), it belongs to God alone.

- **"admixture" (*permixtio*)**: The key term of the second *Conclusio*. God's truth is "pure and unmixed" — his indivision has no shadow of potentiality, his imitation no trace of dissimilitude, his expression no obscurity. This is distinct from the Anselmian argument in Q.II and is properly Bonaventure's own analysis.

- **Property without real distinction**: The reply to objection 4 (truth = essence, so neither can be the property of the other) develops a refined account of *proprietas* in God: the third criterion of property in creatures (that the property differs from its subject) is an imperfection arising from non-simplicity, and therefore does not apply to God. What remains is that truth belongs to essence alone (*soli convenit*) and is the ground of knowing it (*ratio innotescendi*) — two marks of perfection without requiring real distinction.

- **Mode of signifying (*modus significandi*)**: The resolution of why truth is the property of essence and not vice versa, even though they signify the same reality: the names retain their distinct *modi significandi* (truth = condition of being; essence = what-it-is) as derived from creaturely usage, and these modes of signification constitute an asymmetric explanatory relation even when the reality signified is identical. This is a careful piece of semantic theology.

- **Q.II — the Anselmian argument**: Arguments 1–7 for the affirmative all derive from variations of the Anselmian ontological intuition: that the first truth is self-confirming in every cognitive act. Arguments 5–7 are particularly sharp: every assertoric utterance, whether affirmative or negative, implicitly posits the first truth. The *sed contra* deploys empirical counter-instances (the fool of Psalm 13, the idolater) and logical objections.

- **"whether it exists / what it is" (*si est / quid est*)**: The standard distinction in scholastic epistemology between existence-cognition and essence-cognition. Bonaventure's resolution turns on the claim — via Hugh of St. Victor — that while the *quid est* of God is inaccessible to the human intellect, the *si est* (the bare fact of his existence) is naturally and indelibly known. Errors about God are always errors of the *quid est* kind, and these only *consequentially* involve denial of existence.

- **OCR**: Argument numbering is somewhat irregular in the OCR (the second argument for the affirmative is labeled "2" twice). The truncation at line 396 (Anselm *contra*—) leaves the *Respondeo* incomplete; the passage on defect of evidence (*defectus evidentiae*) and the full conclusion of Q.II will be in the next chunk. The scholion apparatus at lines 154–227 has been omitted.

DIST. VIII, PART I, ARTICLE I, QUESTION II.

---

*[Continuation of the Respondeo of Question II, begun in the preceding chunk:]*

Not only by reason of a defect of presence can something be thought not to exist, but also by reason of a defect of evidence — because it is not evident in itself, or not evident in the way of proof. But the truth of divine being is evident both in itself and in the way of proof. In itself, because just as we know principles insofar as we know the terms, and because the cause of the predicate is contained in the subject and therefore they are self-evident; so likewise in the matter at hand. For God or the highest truth is being itself, than which nothing better can be conceived: therefore it cannot not exist, nor can it be thought not to exist. For the predicate is contained in the subject. Nor does it have evidence only from itself, but also from proof, since every created truth and nature proves and concludes divine being: because if something is a being by participation and from another, then there is a being by essence and not from another. Every right understanding also proves and concludes it, because the cognition of God is impressed on every soul, and every cognition is through him. Every affirmative proposition likewise proves and concludes it; for every such proposition posits something; and with something posited, the true is posited; and with the true posited, truth is posited, which is the cause of every true thing. A negative proposition, however, does not conclude it except sophistically, as they say. Hence from the fact that nothing exists, or that no truth exists, it does not follow nor can it be inferred that truth exists. For the proposition "nothing exists" destroys every truth. And therefore no affirmation follows from it, and the following is false: "if nothing exists, it is true that nothing exists." And if it be said that every proposition implies its own content, this is true — but if nothing exists, there is no proposition and there is nothing. Augustine, moreover, does not make that argument by way of endorsing it, but by way of inquiry.

It must therefore be conceded that the truth of divine being is so great that it cannot with assent be thought not to exist, except by reason of the ignorance of the one thinking, who does not know what is meant by the name of God. And the arguments for this conclusion are to be conceded, although some of them are sophistical.

1. To the objection on the contrary side, from "the pernicious malice has so prevailed, etc.": it must be said that Damascene is speaking of a thinking that arises from blindness, which is evident from the very word he uses, namely "malice."

2. Similarly, to the objection concerning the idol: it must be said that the idolater errs because he does not know what God is; hence he does not think that God does not exist in the universal sense.

3. To the objection that, with God understood not to exist, other things can still be understood: it must be said that Boethius is speaking of an understanding by which we think something *per impossibile*, but without assenting to it.

4. To the objection that God most escapes our grasp: the response is clear, because what most escapes our grasp is *what he is*, but *that he is* is most evident.

5. To the objection asking what it means to say that divine truth cannot be thought not to exist: it must be said that this means no one can believe that God does not exist, so long as he makes use of reason. This does not hold of creatures; because although it is certain that one creature is present to one thing, it is not present to all things, because it does not have a power great enough to offer itself equally to all, as the first truth does.

6. To the objection that what can be expressed can also be thought: it must be said that "thinking" can be taken broadly for any act of the mind, whether erring or not, whether assenting or not — and in this sense that claim is true; or it can be taken for thinking with assent — and in this sense it is false, because one can contradict necessary truths with respect to external utterance, but not with respect to the interior, as the Philosopher says in the *Posterior Analytics*.

[Scholion omitted]

ARTICLE II.

On the immutability of God.

Consequently, in second place there is a question concerning the second property of divine being, namely immutability. Concerning which two things are inquired:

First, it is inquired whether immutability is in God.
Second, whether it is a property of God.

---

QUESTION I.

Whether God is immutable.

That immutability is in God is shown in the following manner.

1. Every change is either according to substance or according to accident; but God is not changed according to substance, because everything that changes in that way is corruptible, whereas God or the divine substance, since it has no beginning, is incorruptible: therefore, etc.

2. Likewise, neither is he changed according to accident, because in God there is no accident: therefore there is no change in him.

3. Likewise, everything that is changed is first in potency before it is in act, and in such a thing act differs from potency; but God is pure act: therefore he is in no way changed.

questions.notes:
- **Chunk structure**: This chunk completes Q.II of D.VIII P.I A.I (on whether divine being can be thought not to exist), then transitions to Article II (on immutability), opening Q.I of Article II. The chunk breaks off at the beginning of Richard's argument (argument 4 of the *fundamenta* for Q.I of Article II).

- **Defect of evidence — self-evidence (*per se nota*)**: The completion of the *Respondeo* from the prior chunk argues that divine being is immune to both kinds of defect on the side of the knowable: defect of presence (already treated) and defect of evidence. The self-evidence argument mirrors the structure of Anselm's *Proslogion* 2: the predicate (existence, or more precisely, *non posse non esse*) is contained in the subject (the highest truth, being itself). This is Bonaventure's version of what would later be called the ontological argument, but framed epistemically rather than purely ontologically.

- **Negative propositions and Augustine's argument**: Bonaventure sharply qualifies the argument from Q.I argument 7 (Augustine's *Soliloquies* proof that "no truth exists" is self-refuting). He clarifies that Augustine was using it dialectically (*inquirendo*), not endorsing it as a demonstration. The proposition "nothing exists" is not self-refuting in the strong sense — it simply destroys all truth, including itself, and therefore yields no positive conclusion. This is a careful piece of logical analysis.

- **"exterior utterance vs. interior assent" (*exterius / interius*)**: The resolution of the final *sed contra* (argument 6) draws on the Aristotelian distinction from *Posterior Analytics* I.10: one can verbally contradict first principles (*exterius*) without being able to genuinely assent to their negation (*interius*). Bonaventure applies this to the proposition "God does not exist": it can be *expressed* but not genuinely *assented to* by a mind properly exercising reason.

- **Article II opens**: The transition to Article II on immutability follows immediately after the Q.II scholion. The four opening arguments follow the standard scholastic taxonomy of change: (1) substantial change — excluded because God is incorruptible; (2) accidental change — excluded because God has no accidents; (3) act/potency change — excluded because God is pure act; (4) Richard of St. Victor's argument (incomplete). The *Conclusio* will establish immutability as both a fact about God and a divine property.

- **"pure act" (*purus actus*)**: The Aristotelian-Thomistic formula here appears in Bonaventure's own argument, showing his use of the *actus purus* concept as common scholastic currency at this period, though Bonaventure will integrate it within his distinctive emphasis on divine self-sufficiency and the *fontalis plenitudo*.

- **OCR**: The chunk opens mid-*Respondeo* (continuing from the prior chunk's truncation at the Anselm reference). The scholion material (lines covering the Quaracchi editors' discussion of the relationship to the *an Deum esse sit per se notum* question) has been omitted. The chunk ends at the opening words of Richard's argument, which will be completed in the next chunk.

4, 5, 6. To the objection concerning incorruptibility: it must be said, as has been touched on above, that this belongs to creatures; for some creatures are so simple and so united by a good conjunction that no contrariety falls in them, and there is in them no greater ground of corruption than there is in the primary principles. Hence just as the primary principles cannot be resolved into anything, yet they would lapse into nothing if left to themselves; so is it to be understood with respect to certain substances. Hence it is not to be said as simply true that every composite is actually resolvable; but as Anselm says, "it is resolvable either in reality or in understanding." Hence the arguments adduced for this are to be conceded.

7, 8. To the objections concerning mutability (*vertibilitas*): it must be said that every creature is mutable by nature if left to itself.

If the cause of this is asked, it must be said that for this mutability — since it is a pure defect — no efficient or reducing cause leading to non-being is to be assigned, but only a deficient cause. For this reason it must be noted that "nature" is said to be natural origin. Now the origin of a creature is both from nothing and from its own principles: accordingly, something is said to be natural to a creature in two ways — either because it belongs to it from the fact that it is from nothing, or because it belongs to it from the fact that it is from its own principles. And because nothing is not any thing's efficient cause but only its deficient cause, therefore the properties that belong to a creature by reason of its being from nothing are not positive determinations but defects, and are not from a power but from the deficiency of power, and have no efficient cause but only a deficient cause. Such are vanity, instability, and mutability. If therefore it is asked from what source a creature is mutable, I say: not from any efficient cause, but through a deficiency in itself. But according to the sense in which "natural" means what belongs to a thing through its own proper and intrinsic principles, privations and defects are not said to belong to it naturally, but only capacities; and therefore in this sense of "natural," no creature is naturally mutable into non-being — yet it is not said to be naturally immutable either, because "natural" refers to what a thing's nature can bring about; but the principles of a thing are not capable of conserving the thing or of conserving themselves; and therefore immutability is not natural in this sense. Yet neither is it contrary to nature — on the contrary, it is consonant with nature; because every nature desires to be preserved, although it cannot be so of itself, and most especially that creature which desires to be beatified, namely that which is made to the image of God. And because the desire of nature is not in vain where nature falls short, the gratuitous inflow of God supplies what is lacking. And thus it is clear that mutability belongs by nature, but immutability belongs by grace.

9. To the objection concerning the comparison of grace to nature: it must be understood that grace is called an assistance coming from above, with respect to what is beyond the capacity of nature. This assistance is twofold: either with respect to being simply, or with respect to perfect being.

If with respect to being simply — for instance, with respect to the conservation of being, since no primary principles can, being as they are vain things, conserve themselves of themselves — then it does not operate through any infused or given habit. Because it regards being, and because being is common to all things, this grace is common to all. Hence this is grace having the mode of nature, and this is the grace by which the rest of things are said to be immutable.

In the other way, grace is called an assistance with respect to perfect being, and since the perfection of being belongs to those things ordered toward beatitude, it regards well-being and does not belong to all things. Therefore this is a special habit of some, not of all, and this is grace in the mode of grace properly speaking. From these considerations what is objected regarding grace is clear: for the objection proceeds according to grace understood as a special habit distinguished against nature, because in that sense it denotes something newly created; but grace in the sense just described does not.

10. And from this the final objection is also answered: because grace is called an assistance with respect to what is beyond the capacity of nature; and because the conservation of the primary principles is beyond the capacity of nature, while the going-forth of operations is not — indeed, it is below it — therefore the matter is clear, etc.

questions.notes:
- **Chunk structure**: This chunk contains only the replies to objections (numbered 4–10) for Q.II of D.VIII P.I A.II. The question itself, the arguments, and the *Respondeo* proper are entirely absent from this OCR section, which opens mid-discussion. The subject matter — from context and the replies — is whether immutability is a *property* of God alone (*proprium Dei*), i.e., whether any creature can be said to be immutable. The replies defend the claim that immutability in the strict sense belongs to God alone, while conceding a weaker immutability to some creatures by grace.

- **Missing chunk**: A full chunk corresponding to D.VIII P.I A.II Q.II's question, arguments, *sed contra*, and *Respondeo* is absent from the OCR sequence. The gap between the previous chunk (which ended at the opening of A.II Q.I's *fundamenta*) and this one is substantial; Q.I's full *Respondeo* and Q.II's entire body are missing. This should be flagged for recovery from the PDF.

- **"mutability" (*vertibilitas*) and "immutability" (*invertibilitas*)**: The central terms. *Vertibilitas* (literally "turnability") is Bonaventure's technical term for the creature's inherent capacity to lapse into non-being or to undergo change; *invertibilitas* for resistance to such lapse. The distinction maps onto the pair *ex nihilo / ex principiis propriis* — what belongs to a creature from its creaturely origin (from nothing) vs. what belongs to it from its own intrinsic constitutive principles.

- **"from nothing as deficient cause"**: A characteristic Bonaventurian metaphysical move. *Ex nihilo* does not imply that nothing is an efficient cause of defects in creatures; rather, nothing is a *deficient cause* — it is the privative ground of instability, vanity, and mutability. These are not posited by God's creative act but reflect the creature's own ontological poverty as something that was not. This is closely related to Bonaventure's teaching on *vestigium* and the creature's intrinsic finitude.

- **Twofold grace (*duplex adiutorium*)**: The reply to objection 9 introduces an important distinction between (1) grace in the mode of nature (*gratia habens modum naturae*) — universal divine conservation, by which all creatures are preserved in being and thus in a secondary sense "immutable"; and (2) grace in the mode of grace properly speaking — the special infused habit ordered toward beatitude, belonging to rational creatures alone. The first corresponds roughly to what later theology calls *concursus* or *conservatio*; the second to *gratia gratum faciens*. This distinction resolves the objection that immutability, if from grace, must be a special and divisible gift rather than universal.

- **"desire of nature is not in vain" (*desiderium naturae non est frustra*)**: A standard axiom of scholastic teleology, here applied to the creature's desire for conservation and beatification. Where natural desire exceeds natural capacity, divine grace supplies the deficit. This grounds the immutability of spiritual creatures in God's gracious sustenance rather than their own ontological resources.

- **"the empyrean by reason of its contents"**: The opening fragment (before the reply to objections 4–6) belongs to a reply to an objection apparently concerning whether the empyrean heaven is immutable or incorruptible by reason of its simplicity or by reason of what it contains (i.e., the blessed). This is characteristic of the cosmological discussion of incorruptibility that likely featured in the missing *Respondeo*.

- **OCR**: This chunk is fragmentary. All content prior to the reply to objections 4–6 is missing, and the preceding chunk (D.VIII P.I A.II Q.I) is also incomplete. The full A.II section should be reconstructed from the PDF before finalization.

sicut vult Hieronymus ", Augustinus et Anselmus. Secundum vero quod dicuntur de Deo, important solum
durationem. Unde dicitur: Beus fuit, quia eius du-

quia cum pendeat a Deo, non pendet sicut a subiecto.
E contrario est in Deo; et ideo dicit Hilarius, quod
esse non est accidens Deo ; et hoc propter contrarias
proprietates: quia accidens natum est alii inesse, propter hoc dicit: subsistens veritas; quia natum est
ab alio exire, contra hoc dicit: manens causa; quia
nalum est etiam ab alio recedere, contra hoc dicit:
naturalis genei'is proprietas, quae non dimittit esse ".

Di;b. IX.

Item quaeritur, quomodo intelligitur immortalitas, cum dicitur: Solus habet immortalitatem , et

dicit Auguslinus'', quod accipitur pro incommutabilitate; sed hoc non videtur conveniens. Mors e.nim
hon dicit omnem mutabilitatem, sed solum corruptibilitatem' viventium: ergo non idem est dicere.

Respondeo: Sicut vita accipitnr communiter et '
proprie, ita et mors, ita et immortalitas. Uno enim
modo dicitur vita aclus continuus et internus ", qui
est a forma spirituali ; et sic dicitur prqprie , et sic
immortalitas dicit vitam talem cum impossibilitate
ad eius privationem. Alio modo dicilur vita actus
completus potenliae, quae est secundum rei naturam,
sicut dicitur aqua viva, quae habet operationem
aquae convenientem ; et hoc modo importat repugnantiam ad corruptionem. Et ideo' debet dici se-
cundum hanc vitam immortale quod est ita in actu
completo , quod nullo modo potest aliquam peiorationem recipere; et sic accipit Apostolus et exponit

DuB. X.

Item quaeritur de hoc quod dicit beatus lacobus
et est in Uttera* : Nec vicissitudinis obumhratio ; quae
differentia est inter vicissitudinem et obumbraiionem, et quae convenientia , ratione cuius dicatur
vicissitudo obumhrare ?

Et dicendum, quod vicissitudo importat numerum vicis, et iste est numerus cum interruptione ;
sed ohumbralio dicitur per privationem actus lucis.
Quoniam igitur actiis formae lux est, privatio eius
recte dicitur obumbratio ; et quia vicissitudo ratione
numeri dicit interruptionem, et ratione interruptionis dicit privationem, et ratione privationis ohumbra-
tioneni, hinc est, quod recte dicilur vicissitudinis
obumbratio.

non intelligit , etiam natum esse etc. In quarta et

rum, ibi: Sed quaeris a me, inquit Amhrosius,
ubi ostendit quod imperscrutabile ^ est sacramentum

ARTICULUS UNICUS.

De generationo in
QUAESTIO I.

Utruni in divinis generatio ponenda sit.

Circa primum, quod generatio sit in divinis,
ostenditur^:

1. Primo a minori. Multo fortius debet esse
generatio in eo qui generationem aliis tribuit, quain
in his quae recipiunt; sed generatio est in creaturis: ergo et in Deo qui tribuit. Et hoc est quod
dicitur Isaiae ultimo^: Si ego generationem aliis
Irihuo , sterilis ero ? dicit Dominus, quasi dicat, non.

2. Item, ostenditur illud idem a. posteriori. Per
prius enim est paternitas in Deo quam in creatura;
sed paternitas et generatio vere est in creatura:
ergo et in Deo. Quod prius sit ibi , dicit Apostolus
ad Ephesios tertio^: Ex quo omnis paternitas in
caelo et in terra nominatur.

3. Item, ostenditur hoc ipsum a simili, quia
omne quod perfectionis est, attribuendum est Deo,
in quo est summa omnis perfectionis ; sed generatio
est perfectionis in creatura, ut vult Philosophus%
quia «perfectum est quod potest generare quale
ipsum est»: ergo etc.

4. Item , illud idem ostenditur alia ratione
sic ^ : divina natura est summe bona et actualissima: ergo summe potest et vult se communicare;
sed prima et summa ratio communicandi est in generatione : ergo necesse est in divinis ponere gene-
rationem.

CoNTRA : 1 . Generatio in creaturis aut est per- m ,
fectionis , aut impe^'fectionis. Si perfectionis , tunc
ergo, cum substantiae spirituales et incorporales
sint nobilissimae , debet in eis generatio esse: ergo
cum non sit in eis , non est nobilitatis ; sed quod non
est nobilitatis non est in Deo: ergo etc.

2. Item , ubi est generatio , ibi est variatio ; generatio enlm est species motus , et inter omnes spe-
cies motus maior est variatio in motu secundmn
substantiam, quia est entis in potentia, minor in
motu secundum locum ' : ergo cum in Deo non sit
variatio nec aliqua species motus, etiam illa quae
minima est, ut loci mutatio: ergo nec generatio.

3. Item, ubi est generatio, ibi est corruptio,
unde Philosophus ' dicit , quod >< propter longe stare
a principio reliquo modo complevit esse Deus, continuam in his faciens generationem » ; et huiusmodi
signum est, quod sola corruptibilia generant et generantur in creaturis; sed in Deo nulla cadit cor-
ruptio: ergo nec generatio.

4. Item, ubi est generatio, ibi est» nutritio;
unde ad tot et plures se extendit vis nutritiva
quam generativa; sed in Deo non est vis nutritiva:
ergo nec generativa, ergo nec nutritio, nec generatio: ergo generatio non est in divinis.

DIST. IX. DUBL\.

DuB. VIII.

Item quaeritur de hoc quod dicit Hilarius, quod
cum sacramento scientiae suae ex eo nascitur. Videtur enim secundum hoc, quod Pater secundum sacra-
mentum scientiae generat Fiiium: ergo scientia est
ratio generandi.

Respondeo: Dicendura, quod Hilarius vocat hic '
sacramentum sacrum secretum ; dicit autem, Filium
nasci cum sacramento scientiae, quia Filii generatio
non tantum sacra, sed etiam secreta est, non, inquam, Deo secreta, sed nobis, quia nos eam non
comprehendimus ; ipse autem' perfecte noyit eam.
Ideo dicit cum sacramento etc.

DuB. IX.

Item quaeritur de hoc quod dicit: Quod ex vivo
vivum natum est habet nativitatis perfectum sine
novitate naturae. Videtur enim falsum, quia puer nascitur de patre et matre viventibus, et tamen utrum-
que habet, scihcet imperfectionem et novitatem.

Respondeo: Ratio Hilarii, sicut patet per litteram
sequentem ', intelligenda est de vivo per essentiam;
ubi enim est vivens per essentiam, non fit ex non vivo
vivens, sicut flt in vivente ^dv participationem, ubi
non generatur vivum ex vivo nisi per non vivum,
ut patet, quia homo non generatur ex homine nisi
mediante semine.

DuB. X.

Item quaeritur de hoc quod dicit: Neque ex derivatione, sed ex vi?'tute nativitas est. Videtur contra-
rium , quia secundum Dionysium * et Anselmum Pater
se habet ad Filium et Spiritum sanctum, ut fons, et
illi ut rivi ; sed rivus est a fonte per derivationem.

Respondeo: Dicendum, quod nativitas , quae est
per derivationem , attenditur quantum ad transmutationem aliquam circa illud quod transmutatur, et
ita dicit passionem quandam, ac per hoc infirmitatem^; sed vivens, quod est vita, est actus purus,
et ita vita pura, in qua non est infirmitas, sed pura
actualitas; et ideo vult Hilarius dicere, quod Paler
generans est totus ^ vita, et quod generat non est per
vel demutationem, quae attenditur in de-

rivatione, sed per omnimodam virtutem : ergo Filius
genitus est virtus, non per mutationem natus.

DuB. XI.

Ilem quaeritur de hoc quod dicit: Ubi Pater
auctor est, ibi et nativitas est. Videtur quod improprie dicit", quia auctoritas dicit causalitatem; sed
haec non recipitur in divinis: ergo etc.

Respondeo: Dicendum, quod auctoritas dicit
quandam principalitatem sive auctoritatem in persona , quae nihil habet ab alio , sed ab ipso omnes ;
et ista auctoritas in Patre est innascibilitas ; unde non
dicit causalitatem , sed privationem principii , et per
hoc summam principalitatem *.

DuB. XII.

Item quaeritur de hoc quod dicit: Quod vero ab
aeterno natum est, id, si 7ion aeternum natum
est etc; et innuit Hilarius hic tale argumentum: si
Filius non est generatus sive natus ab aeterno, generatio eius non est aeterna; et si hoc^, Pater non
generat ab aeterno: ergo Pater non est aeternus:
ergo qui derogat aeternitati Filli , derogat aeternitati
Patris. Sed ista ratio non videtur valere , quia similiter ego arguam ex parte Creatoris et creaturae:
si '" creatura non est aeterna, non ab aeierno creavit
Deus, et ita non est Creator aeternus.

Respondeo: Dicendum, quod non est simile, sicut patet exsequenti" eins quod Hilarius supponit,
quod esse Patrem sit proprie proprium illius personae : ergo cum tale semper conveniat , aut aliter res
non habet esse perfectum, sequitur de necessitate:
aut Filius est aeternus, aut Pater ab aeterno non habet esse perfectum. Creare vero, etsi solius Dei sit,
tamen ratione connotati habet imperfectionem coniunctam, secundum quam non tantum impossibile, sed
etiam non intelligibile est, aliquid ab aeterno creari '^

DuB. XIII.

Item quaeritur de hoc quod dicit: Sed se ipsum
deniutare nascendo; quia secundum hoc, cum Filius
Dei prius esset et postea ex Virgine natus sit ": ergo
esset mulatus.

Respondeo: Dicenduin, qnod ipse ' Hilarins intelligit secundum eandeni naturain, secnnduin quam
prius erat. Si enim secundnm eandein naliiram priiis
erat et postea natus est, neoesse est. quod secnndum illam naluram mutatus sit ; sed si secundum

aliam \ oportet mutationem fieri in illa natura, sed
non in persona, cum illa natura non dical aliquid
in persona, sed magis aliquid cuni persona. Unde
nulla fit mutatio in alia' natura.

plurificat formam; dicendum, quod hoc non est
verum in adiectivis '.

DUB. III.

Qui hoc dicit, non intelligit, natum esse etc.

Hic ponit Magister quatuor rationes demonstrantes ,

Baiioiies 4. Filium coaeternum Patri, et ita argumentum ,\rii

traTrTum™" non valere * : FiUus est natus, ergo non est ae-

ternus.

Prima sumta est a.simili et est talis: splendor
Ratio 1. est eiusdem durationis cum igne sive aequalis, et

tamen est generatus ab igne : ergo multo fortius ,
cum Filius sit splendor Patris', quamvis ab ipso
generetur, erit ei coaeternus: ergo conclusio praedictae rationis est falsa, et illa consequentia est in-
terimenda: si natus est, erat quando non erat.
Sed contra: Si emanatio procedens a Deo est ei
coaeterna, sieut emanatio procedens a creatura est
ei coaequaeva '" : ergo cum res exierint a Deo, videtur quod ab aeterno.

Respondeo: Dicendum, quod egressus splendoris" a luce vel igne est egressus connaturalis ; el
talis est egressus Filii a Patre, non autem egressus
crealurae a Creatore, immo est voluntarius; et argumentum est bonum in proposito.

Item, si Dei Filius, inquit Augustinus, virtus Ka''o s.
etsapientia. Haec est secunda ratio Augustini: Filius
Dei est virtus et sapientia: ergo si non est aeternus,
aliquando fuit Deus sine virtute et sapientia; sed
hoc est impossibile: ergo etc. Sed contra hanc rationem sic obiicitur: si enim sequitur: si Pater non
habet sapientiam genitam, non est sapiens, videtur
quod sit sapiens sapientia genita, quod expresse negat Augustinus in sexto de Trinitate '-.

Respondeo: Augustinus istam rationem redarguit
in sexto de Trinitate ", ostendens, illam procedere ex
malo intellectu verbi; attamen, quia Magister adducit
eam, potest dici , quod ratio valet , non quia Pater sit
sapiens Filio, qui est sapientia genita, sed quia eadem '*
esl sapientia genita et ingenita; et ita, si una incipit,
et alia.

Eidem quoque Arianicae quaestioni. Haec est Rai>o 3.
tertia ratio quam adducit, et est Ambrosii, sumta
ab auctoritate Isaiae : Anle nie non est Deus , et post
me non erit: ergo nec Pater ante Filium, nec Filius
post Patrem. Sed contra: In divinis personis est ordo;
sed ordo non est nisi prioris ad poslerius: ergo etc.

Respondeo: Dicendum, quod, sicut infra patebit '^ non est ibi ordo durationis, quo alter est prior
altero, sed ordo originis, quo alter ex altero.

Jnvicem enim in se, Pater in Filio, et Filius Raiio 4.

Respondeo: Aliqui volunt dicere, quod ista ratio
valet, quia generatio est de substantia generantis; et
ideo si incipit generare, substantia mutatur. Sed hoc
non videtur, quia generatio in divinis non dicit motum. Alii dicunt, quod quia genitus est consubstan-
tialis gignenti, si mutatur genitus, et gignens; sed
genitus mutatur , si de novo generatur : ergo et generans per consequens. Alius modiis dicendi est,
quod paternitas veram dicit habitudinem in Patre,
non sic creatio vel dominatio; et ideo paternitas adveniens ' mutat , non sic dominatio.

Sed nulla praedictarum rationum * dat vigorem

. huic rationi contra haereticos, quia haereticus dicebat, quod Filius non erat coaeternus, ac per hoc nec
consubstantialis , nec idem in substantia. Propter hoc

cebat Patrem et Filium differentes in substantia et

iste^ mutetur accessione generationis , qui generat
alium in substantia; et in divinis similiter Pater generat alium in substantia: ergo accessione generatio-
uis mutatur, ut ° iste.

Quocumque tamen modo dicatur, non est ma-
•gnura periculum, quia non omnia argumenta, quae
flunt ad veritatem, sunt necessaria'.

DuB. IV.

Itera quaeritur de hoc quod dicit: Vox silet non
mea tantum , sed et Angelorum. Videtur enim male
dicere Angelorum, quia vox non est nisi habentium
organa et respirationem; sed Angeli haec non habent.
Si dicas, quod habent voces spirituales, non prolatas, sicut dicit Damascenus ', quod tradant sibi intel-

ligentias suas sine voce prolatas; quaero, quae sit QaaMUoii
necessitas vocis spiritualis, et quis modus loquendi,
